speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Budget 2019 continues to press on with efforts to build competitive enterprises within our economy with greater focus and emphasis on changes at the microeconomic level.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The slew of schemes and programmes announced aims at helping enterprises deepen capabilities and to scale up.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The merged EFS is also extended to companies which have been incorporated for less than five years and may not have yet met the credit evaluation criteria or vintages as required by banks.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government's willingness to risk sharing up to 70% of the loan amount significantly enhances the lending proposition which would encourage more financial institutions to participate.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The ability to obtain financing means a great deal to companies, especially those in the early growth phase.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Being able to readily access funding and liquidity can make or break a company.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is an essential enabler for a flourishing enterprise ecosystem to exist.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, there is no guarantee of success in such co‐investments, but it is necessary to make available such risk capital so as to give promising startups a lift.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: More new‐to‐economy activities have also been developed in recent years, such as the proliferation of FinTechs, sharing economy apps, deep tech ventures and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Progressing from startup to scale‐up is the next logical move.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Startups and enterprises can only thrive when they scale up and seek greater market opportunities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To achieve this, we must be open to trying new approaches to grow our enterprises.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From an economic resource allocation standpoint, it makes excellent sense to help grow the sizes of our companies, especially the smaller enterprises.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Bigger companies enjoy better economies of scale advantages and are in a better position to expand, innovate, internationalise and manage business risks.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In general, larger companies tend to be bigger value contributors to the economy as a proportion and offer better job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The new Scale‐Up SG programme is a bold move to help fast track growth for promising enterprises.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would imagine that such a programme will offer highly customised assistance which may entail differentiated support and assistance, better financial support for the adoption of technology and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We will await more details from the Committee of Supply (COS) debate on the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the instinctive question I have in mind is whether such schemes, being customised and, hence, selective in nature, would involve some extent of picking winners?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Scale‐Up SG be a separate track of work from the Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs)?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How do we eventually expand or scale up the Scale‐Up SG to move the needle for the economy?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It underscores the Government's resolve to help workers adjust to the future economic landscape, no matter how difficult the adjustments may be.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Among others, the Professional Conversion Programme (PCP) will be expanded to cover new growth areas.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would help jobseekers reskill to transit into new occupations or sectors with good prospects and opportunities for progression.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we should continually raise the bar here, aiming not only to help even more jobseekers find new jobs but also to improve the overall experience of the jobseekers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The newly harmonised Global Ready Talent Programme (GRTP) will help young Singaporeans gain overseas work experience in the key growth regional markets where we are seeking greater economic interdependencies, such as Southeast Asia, China and India.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Under the scheme, participating local firms can receive funding support of up to 70% of costs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are markets in our immediate neighbourhood where we need to strengthen our connectivity and expand the talent pool of people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: CSP is a much‐appreciated scheme by both companies and workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The programme encourages companies to hire mature workers who may have been in long-term unemployment by subsidising a significant share of the workers' salary.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rather than renew this programme every two to three years, I hope that the Government can turn the CSP into a permanent scheme.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, the terms can be refined from time to time to meet changing circumstances.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It will give workers, especially mature workers, who are concerned about their job security a sense of assurance that the Government will be there to help in their transition to a new job.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It will also demonstrate the Government's resolve to keep long-term and structural unemployment to the lowest possible level even as our economy becomes more innovative‐ and technology‐driven.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are consistent with our strategy to tackle the twin challenges of a tightening labour market and our ageing demographics.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is not sustainable, both economically and socially, to keep having more and more foreign workers in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, such mid‐level skills labour is also increasingly in demand in other countries as well and companies will, in a matter of time, face competition in getting those workers to come in.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our S Pass system should be structured in a way where companies are given more S Pass only if they have more local workers at mid‐ to high‐wage levels and demonstrate high value contribution to the economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can I also suggest that the companies that have been shown to hire more displaced or retrenched local workers, for example, via Workforce Singapore (WSG) or the Employment and Employability Institute (e2i), be given favourable consideration for their renewal of S Passes as well?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the end of the day, we want more of the S Pass type of jobs to be undertaken by Singaporeans, whether they are seniors, Institute of Technical Education (ITE) or polytechnic graduates or back‐to‐work mothers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Tightening of the foreign worker quota is understandably painful to companies which are unable to find local workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope that with the EDG and PSG extended and expanded, it would help firms adjust to this round of tightening of the labour market.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I look forward to hearing more details at the MTI COS on the measures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Growing the economy is a means to an end, and the end must be to create good jobs and better salaries for our people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have seen how economic growth in other developed economies has not always led to better workers’ outcomes and resulting in deep divisions within their societies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the end of the day, economic development cannot be delinked from the social well-being of the people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For many years, the Government has been highlighting the challenges of our ageing demographics and have put in place a series of long‐term policies to deal with this imminent development.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One serious implication of an ageing society is that healthcare needs will grow, will increase.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government has put its money where its mouth is.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Over the years, the Ministry of Health (MOH) has expanded the healthcare infrastructure, such as hospitals, polyclinics, senior care centres and many others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the community level, there are also more social support, such as the Community Network for Seniors (CNS) and the People's Association's (PA) Wellness Programme, as well as the many voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) working with the community organisations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) and Silver Generation Office (SGO) are today better resourced to assist and engage seniors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides the infrastructure, healthcare support must also include providing assurance that healthcare services will be affordable and that individuals will have adequate savings and insurance coverage to meet their old age needs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Building more polyclinics and the introduction of the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) have made affordable primary care more accessible to the people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The enhancement in CHAS to cover all Singaporeans for chronic conditions, regardless of income, is another indication of our improving social safety net.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a further icing on the cake, we now have the Merdeka Generation (MG) Package (MGP), which will have benefits better than the Blue CHAS card.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I support the decision not to have means-testing for the MGP, just like the Pioneer Generation (PG) Package (PGP).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are a very special generation who went through some of the most trying times during our pre and early Independence years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To protect against the uncertainties of long‐term care costs, we will soon transit into CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Premiums for both schemes can be paid using MediSave, which is why it is helpful that the Government constantly look to top up the MediSave account of Singaporeans whenever we have Budget surpluses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Both MediShield Life and CareShield Life are now administered by the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My ask to the Ministry of Finance (MOF) and MOH is that we should continually looking to enhance the terms of the coverage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Whenever there are surpluses, we should consider one‐off injections into the risk pool to continually improve the claims economics for the insured.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Overall, credit must be given to MOH and Minister Gan Kim Yong for their tremendous efforts to strengthen our massive healthcare system and for giving Singaporeans much better peace of mind today.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For a Budget to be impactful, having the required financial resources is, of course, a given.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we also need the right strategic plans and the ability to carry out the plans coherently across financial years and across terms of government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are in this enviable position because, in each Budget since our founding years, we have always been prudent and steadfast in resisting the temptation to spend more than necessary.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, we cannot count on NIRC to fund all our expenditures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Growing the economy to generate tax revenues and create good jobs for our people continue to be critical to our long‐term survival.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This arrangement has worked well for Singapore, requiring the Government of the day to be disciplined and prudent in managing our finances, and sharing of the fruits of our better economic performances whenever surpluses are generated.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The surpluses are also used to fund massive social and healthcare programmes, like the PGP and MGP, without adding the burden to future generations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Under the Constitution, this amount not spent will be locked up as past Reserves in the new term of government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These series of incidents have naturally raised concerns whether the standards in the delivery of public services have slackened.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I appreciate Minister Heng Swee Keat's article to the Straits Times on 9 February 2019, reaffirming the Government's commitment to strive for the highest standards of excellence in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore has always been effectively governed and has achieved very commendable outcomes for our people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Whether it is growing our economy and creating jobs, building a liveable home or building a harmonious society, providing law and order or securing our sovereignty, we have always gotten our fundamentals right.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We always do what is right for the long-term good of the country.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am sure Singaporeans feel proud of our achievements.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we also know that the public wants their day‐to‐day services to run well, too, and to have minimal disruption in the delivery of services as they go about their daily lives.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In other words, besides doing big things right and well, which is critical, the public also expects those who are mandated to deliver public services to achieve operational excellence and do the last 5% well, too.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This entails a different mindset at both the organisational and leadership levels as to how we look at operations and the daily functioning of services.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Operational responsibilities cannot be just delegated to line managers, supervisors or individual employees.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is a collective responsibility of the management and their employees, with each employee at the individual level taking ownership and pride in carrying out their duties and responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat, in his article, also mentioned about leaning from the Japanese and the Swiss who have a strong sense of personal responsibility in what they do at work and a meticulous attention to details.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It reminds me of this story about President John Fitzgerald Kennedy's visit to the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) in 1961.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He met a janitor or cleaner who was mopping the floor as he walked in and asked what he was doing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The janitor replied, "I am helping put a man on the moon!" The leadership and the management set the culture.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But it must manifest through the actions of every individual and on a daily basis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Management must take deeper interest in what each of their employees is doing, what their daily challenges and pain points are, whether the employee is adequately resourced to do the work and how can we improve their work situation and employee journey.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We just need to bring everyone on board, instil ownership and pride in what we do, ensure that there are adequate support and resources for people to do their job well, and to build a strong sense of purpose that each of us can make a difference.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I agree with Minister Heng Swee Keat that we do have this ethos and DNA within us, and I am sure we can do a better job, going forward.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, with that, I support the Budget, Sir.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In my speech today, I will touch on the following areas: (a) building SME capabilities; (b) lowering the foreign worker DRC; (c) supporting an inclusive society; and (c) tightening of relief for travellers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will impact the number and quality of jobs, as well as the competitiveness of businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The feedback I have received from dialogue sessions I have had with SME leaders and members of business associations that operate in my ward is that existing schemes with pre-approved digital solutions are helpful, but more flexibility is needed to support the diverse needs and stages that their businesses are at.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will enable them to address the opportunities and challenges, with the major shifts that Minister Heng Swee Keat had spoken about in last year's Budget as well as in the opening of his Budget speech, that are impacting these businesses – the shift in global economic weight to Asia, which brings opportunities for our businesses, but also increases competition; rapid technological advances that enable new capabilities but disrupt business models; changing demographic patterns, with an ageing population impacting both our talent base as well as our manpower requirements; and the decline in support of globalisation that is impacting and creating greater geopolitical uncertainties.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Just last week, a resident, who is an SME business owner, came to our Meet-the-People Session (MPS) seeking help for his business.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We initially thought that he was seeking for financial support and grants.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But after discussions with him, I realised that what he was really seeking help for was to restructure his business and digitalise.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He was, however, at a loss and did not know how to go about it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He did take advantage of the current schemes available to digitalise to have his website and online presence set up.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But he, too, realised that it was not enough.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He needed to rethink how he did his business in order to better leverage technology to help him stay competitive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He clearly needed help not with funding but in transforming his business.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Transforming how he did business in the markets and market his products and services, he needed new skills to understand how to do so.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And he needed to also understand how to leverage the technology.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Budget builds on programmes already in place to support businesses but introduces new initiatives to help businesses restructure.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must recognise that this will not be easy for companies in the services sector as they rely heavily on manpower and currently are facing challenges in attracting Singaporeans to take on jobs in the service sector.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The countries of sources for foreign manpower are also developing fast and will progress well and businesses must understand that supply for this manpower will eventually diminish as well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While it is painful and difficult, if companies in the services sector do not reduce reliance on foreign manpower for their businesses now, they will be more severely impacted if they are not prepared for it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To raise productivity of the services sector, companies will need to innovate and restructure.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We will see some companies struggle to make the shift.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Apart from the extension of the EDG and PSG, more needs to be done to help businesses in the services sector improve productivity and reframe their business models and strategies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The same challenge will be met by other sectors that are labour-intensive and have low productivity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Why is it challenging for companies in the services sector to reduce their dependency on foreign manpower?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Is it a question of not being able to attract Singaporeans to the jobs?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Are the factors due to the demographic changes with an ageing population?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Is it because of the demand and working conditions of the jobs?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Or is it due to the high expectations of Singaporeans for work?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Or is it an issue of cost of getting Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The questions and issues have been debated and many of these factors have been attributed as possible reasons.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I believe that the answer actually is in all of the above.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is important now is that, for businesses to build a sustainable model in a market like Singapore which is developed, where we are not a cost leader, we have a tight labour market, our market is small.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, therefore, we have to differentiate by being more innovative and delivering better quality.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How we do this will decide whether we are competitive or not.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The answer though is not a simple one and it cannot be achieved by doing more of the same.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And it is also not about just innovating and applying technology and automation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It requires rethinking of how business and work are done.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The services sector, as the name suggests, is all about service and customer experience.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many do fear that technology will result in lower customer touch, lower personalisation of services and poorer customer experience.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With innovation, technology, if applied right, can achieve greater productivity and better quality but requires rethinking of the way we do things.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is an example that was shared with me of a business, Kopi Ong.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is a food and beverage (F&B) business.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It services professionals in the Central Business District (CBD) area with freshly brewed coffee and tea.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They differentiate themselves in a very simple way, by the signature kopi and teh to each of the customers' preferences.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What it means for them though is that their staff will take longer in preparing the coffee, leading to queues and longer waiting time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They did not need to have more space as well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What this allows them to do is use technology, make it easier for their workers to plan the work and, at the same time, be able to get better personalised customer service.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, if applied right, with the right partnerships, the right support, businesses can change.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I thought it is important to make the point that it is not just about technology, it is not just about the way we do business, it is not just about people and the skill, it is all of them.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Therefore, the support that is in place needs to do that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Now let me talk about supporting an inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Education, employment, healthcare benefits and affordable healthcare and caregiving affect all Singaporeans at different stages of life and regardless of status.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The various programmes announced in the Budget did signal an inclusive approach to support Singaporeans through the stages while building on the fundamentals for the long term.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Whether it was the MGP, the extension of CHAS for chronic conditions and some of the measures in the Bicentennial Bonus like the five-year MediSave top-up, these gave Singaporeans who are eligible, regardless of income and type of property they lived in, the support and the assurance.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This inclusive approach in important in building our social fabric.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Similarly, Edusave top-ups to support families with school-going children as well as employment support for workers and seniors to enable access to opportunities were equally welcomed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And it is very important as they help give opportunities to all at different stages to be able to take advantage of the opportunities that they are presented with.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But as with all Budgets, we do have to recognise that finances are finite.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To be sustainable, most support packages are means-tested to ensure that they are targeted and go to those who most need it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The challenge is finding the right criteria to use for the means-testing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While not perfect, per capita income and annual value of property living in are used in Singapore to assess eligibility.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For several healthcare and care support programmes as well as the cost-of-living relief initiatives, when there is no household income, the annual value of property is used.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With an ageing population, there are many middle-income seniors who live in modest private properties that will be above the $13,000 or the $21,000 annual value criterion used for means-testing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They, therefore, will not be eligible for many of these support schemes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: An example is the Caregiver Grant that has recently been announced.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Another is the support given to lower-wage seniors who work, which is WIS.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For some of these seniors who do not own properties, they are not eligible for WIS if they live with a relative in a private property which will obviously have an annual value above the criterion.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Is it possible for there to be consideration for more flexibility in such cases to allow for eligibility?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The last point that I would like to touch on is the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Import Relief for travellers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I had not intended to speak on this, but it did intrigue me and the feedback I got was quite surprising.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the increasing trend of Singaporeans travelling, and if I understand correctly, the intent of the change is to make the tax system more resilient.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I believe there will be some digital methods to submit the tax.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But there will be administrative cost, workload for customs officers and inconvenience to travellers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I hope consideration is given to that.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The social and economic measures unveiled in Budget 2019 build on the Government's efforts and investments in prior years to address ageing, social mobility and economic transformation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I welcome the targeted measures that build on that momentum to transform our economy and care for our people.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This Budget offers a systematic set of programmes, each reinforcing and building on existing ones.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am also heartened to see how, over the years, social safety nets continue to be strengthened for Singaporeans, and how our drive to raise productivity and transform the economy begins to bear fruit, even as much remains to be done.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As we celebrate our bicentennial year, we should count our blessings of a strong economy, a united people and the enormous advantages this presents in enabling us to chart our future confidently over the long term amidst a complex and volatile world.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Our unique position contrasts starkly with many other countries.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These include two of the world’s largest economies.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I witnessed the anxiety and suffering of many American families resulting from their government shutdown, and the nightmare scenarios that the British people and businesses are contemplating in anticipation of the Brexit outcomes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This gesture of sharing surpluses with Singaporeans, whenever our finances allow, should be the regular feature of all future Budgets.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There is no better way to build social cohesion than to share these upsides with the people.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Finance Minister's vision of building Singapore as the Global-Asia node of technology, innovation and enterprise is very exciting.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We can be very proud of the progress we have made in nurturing a flourishing startup ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We now have a huge pulling power to bring the global innovation community to Singapore, as witnessed by the success of the Singapore FinTech Festival.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As a globally recognised leader of intellectual property (IP) protection and scientific research, we are, indeed, very well poised to fully deploy our strengths and make this vision a reality.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should also strengthen our funding strategies for our universities and research institutes to encourage multidisciplinary collaborations, including partnerships with corporates, to solve impactful real-world issues.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The reward system for our researchers and academics should provide the motivations for them to supercharge commercialisation of research and development (R&D) and industry applications.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am excited about the plans to encourage young Singaporeans to gain overseas working experience with GRTP.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Such internships afford an eye-opening and mind-broadening experience that no amount of book learning can offer.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Our youths, equipped with unrivalled education and multilingualism, will better understand our place in the world and how to make the most of it.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: During my own corporate days, overseas assignments were a key component of development programmes typically reserved for the selected top graduates only.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I am very pleased that this is now readily available to many Singaporeans through the Government's support.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: My advice to our lucky young people is, "Go seize the opportunity!" Going digital and automation continue to be big themes in Budget 2019.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The call for businesses, big and small, to go digital is loud and clear.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many companies have highlighted skills and talent shortages as significant barriers for them going digital and adopting new technologies.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The expertise and skillsets we need for this digitalisation drive are in short supply the world over.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, we must critically evaluate how Singapore can build a sustainable pipeline of local talent as well as attract the best of foreign manpower, in order to build the critical mass necessary for a thriving innovation hub.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must benchmark our attractiveness to compete for these globally mobile talents with other established centres, such as Silicon Valley, as well as new clusters like the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Even with 23 ITMs launched, their contributions so far are unclear.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The feedback from the ground is that the pivotal roles that industry stakeholders and Trade Associations and Chambers (TACs) are expected to play have proven to be uneven across industries.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Far too few TACs are able to lead the development of industry-wide capabilities and help their members access local and international networks.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There is really an urgent need for the Government to evaluate the partnership model and support structure of how the different Government agencies, TACs, industry players, unions and training providers can come together to accelerate deep capability development.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With the rise of the gig economy, more Singaporeans, young and old, are engaged in work without the security of regular contributions to Central Provident Fund (CPF) and healthcare support.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, keeping in mind the overriding social objective of helping Singaporeans with earnings in the bottom 20%, it really would make sense to offer a form of WIS to lower-income gig economy workers to also help them save for retirement and healthcare, encourage work and raise their income.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This enviable financial position is made possible by our strong fiscal discipline, robust contributions from NIRC and a strong economy in 2017 and 2018.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With the significant funds already set aside in the last two years for future healthcare and infrastructure needs, I believe we are now in a much stronger fiscal position than planned.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This scenario, coupled with the Government’s differentiated fiscal strategy of using borrowings to fund major long-term infrastructure projects, should offer relief from the need for major tax increases in the near to medium term.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I urge the Minister for Finance to maintain our current tax regime for a much longer period, postponing the unpopular GST rate hike for as long as possible.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is truly our "burning platform", and we must press on.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans from different walks of life would inevitably have different ideas on how best to achieve this, with perspectives and views shaped by one's values and sense of justice and equality.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, the Workers' Party is no different.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Apart from the strategic objective of the Budget, three statements resonated strongly for me, each albeit in a different context.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These were: first, developing our people on a lifelong basis; second, taking care of not just this generation but our children and their children’s generation; and, finally, that the changes ahead will be deeper and faster.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My speech will use these overarching statements to cover areas where the Government should consider and reassess its approach to build the strong and united Singapore that all Singaporeans, not just the Government, must navigate towards.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, "developing our people on a lifelong basis".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The ground feeling is that even though it helps our senior citizens with their medical bills, albeit less generously than the PGP, there are also quarters who conclude that it is pungently timed with the election cycle, giving off the odour of an unfair advantage aimed at the electoral prospects of the People's Action Party (PAP).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another feedback I received about periodic benefits like the PGP and MGP is the inherent inequity for some of our senior citizens who, by virtue of their year of birth, stand to miss out on a few years of medical benefits because of the interval between one-time packages.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, senior citizens who missed out on the more substantial PGP when they were between the ages of 60 to 64 in 2014 also feel that the eligibility age of 60 for the MGP is inconsistent with the PGP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Quite rightly, the MGP announcement has led some Singaporeans to enquire whether our Budget can support such a package for our senior citizens.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is good reason to opine that it can.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If it does, it would appear that funding such a universal and permanent healthcare initiative for our seniors cannot be dismissed as dishonest, unreasonable or imprudent.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Instead, it can and should be viewed as the key pillar of a strong and united Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Here, the additional subsidies for common illnesses and chronic conditions for outpatient care and meaningful discounts off subsidised bills at polyclinics and specialist outpatient clinics should be its central features.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The additional components of both the PGP and MGP, such as top-ups to PAssion Silver Cards, MediSave top-ups and other specific enhancements, such as the participation incentive to join CareShield Life for other unmet healthcare needs, can turn on the fiscal position of the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would also provide a sufficient buffer to allow each Government to look into addressing more unique healthcare needs of specific cohorts or categories of workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They would include those that had taken up gig-economy jobs or, for example, to address the CPF shortages of workers who made sacrifices when the Government moved to cut the employer contribution of their CPF in 2003 to keep Singapore as a whole economically competitive.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, it is axiomatic that immigration is a permanent feature of Singapore for the foreseeable future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, to be constantly reminded that a covenant exists between the state and citizen.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Vowing to assist all Singaporeans equally with their medical needs in their silver years augurs well for a confident and assured society, without compromising the work ethic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is especially so as living in a developed country with one of the highest per capita gross domestic products (GDP) in the world comes with costs, particularly for the sandwich middle-class.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As all Singaporeans commit their best years and pay taxes like the GST to the state throughout their working lives, a permanent package that helps our seniors manage their cost-of-living issues in their golden years will inject a powerful message of unity into Singaporeans of all ages.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My colleagues Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, Mr Faisal Manap and Mr Dennis Tan will speak more on the MGP in the course of this debate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It coheres with the values many Singaporeans hold dear, regardless of race or religion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But looking after the next generation puts the question of intergenerational equity on the table.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But this strategy also implies that there is a limit to how much the current generation should pay for the benefit of our children and their children, too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, when speaking of specific infrastructure investments envisaged, the Minister only spoke of funding Changi Airport's expansion through borrowing, while speaking more generally about how the Government funded the first Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) line through borrowing as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have a few clarifications in this regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the COS debate in 2016, I filed a cut on rising water levels and shared with Members a video of waves breaching the foreshore along a beach at the East Coast Park, flooding the back shore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The prospect of raising our roads, port areas amongst others, sounds like a massive undertaking both in effort and expense, particularly when one does not just imagine raising road levels, but thinks about building kilometres of dykes and so forth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Continuing on the effects of climate change, how little is recycled and how much food waste is generated in Singapore, it is apparent that the conversation Singaporeans need to have on conservation has to be elevated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This objective should be an explicit goal of the Waste Masterplan.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I look forward to the Masterplan and hope Singaporeans are sufficiently moved into action by it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, like the Government's successful water story, closing the waste cycle would be a significant chapter of the Singapore story and provide a blueprint for other cities to consider.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister also mentioned in his speech that greening is an important public policy, given our dense urban environment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A few weeks ago, Channel NewsAsia ran a one-hour documentary on the effects of rising temperatures in Singapore with an emphasis on not just climate change in general, but the perils of greater urbanisation, identifying the urban heat island effect, with the loss of open areas and secondary forests like Tengah likely to have an immediate impact on liveability in future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How does the Government and the upcoming Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) Masterplan accommodate the drawbacks of greater urbanisation, particularly rising temperatures, and how does it gel with our desire to leave a liveable Singapore behind for our children and their children’s children?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the Government is not finished building Singapore, how will it ensure that this effort will not come at the expense of our green spaces?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Government addresses this matter clearly and actively welcomes a future where we place far greater emphasis on environmental impact assessments and its attendant social issues with a view to leave a sustainable Singapore for future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In this regard the Bicentennial offers a unique opportunity to reflect on the colonial experience, both the good and the bad, the choices made, and where we are headed as a people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As Singaporeans of the PG grew up through the 1950s and as the MG grew up in the years after self-government, the colonial masters in the United Kingdom (UK) had earlier taken a leap of faith, ambitious and bold, even if imperfect, implementing a universal healthcare system for about 50 million people as the flag of the empire was lowered across the colonies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The 50-odd years since decolonisation saw newly independent societies and governments fashioning their countries to improve the lives of their peoples.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The vast majority had to contend with extreme poverty and problems on a far greater scale and with a much larger population than Singapore's.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As we move past the Bicentennial and into unchartered terrain, our challenges will be far more unique and complex than before.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The availability of good jobs for Singaporeans first will be at the heart of many conversations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Employers and SMEs, many of whom have delivered phenomenal economic success to Singapore in the past, will have to adjust and effect real change at the workplace for the benefit of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would include redesigning jobs for older and more experienced Singaporeans, more part-time or half-day or work from home opportunities, so as to better support our workers from mothers to senior citizens and gig-economy workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On its part, the Government must be prepared to do more to support businesses that do so with tax relief or rebates so that the economic transformation many businesses are undertaking is directly dovetailed to jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My colleague, Workers' Party Chair Sylvia Lim, will speak more on the employment landscape tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The faster and deeper changes premonitioned by the Minister would no doubt include the irreversible advance of the smart nation, the rapid evolution of technology and its disruptive and dislocative effects on jobs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But what this prospect also means is that Singaporeans must commit themselves to participate in civic affairs if we are to be united and strong.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans criticise because we care about the country and we care about the direction it is headed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But we also care about ourselves and our families and friends and do not want to be shortchanged.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A strong and united Singapore will not be built with some Singaporeans being made to feel that they must conform or support the Government's narrative with little room for alternative views.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a sure way of heralding not just a divided and insecure population, but a divisive conversation about the choices we have to make collectively.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Increasingly, as we move into the future, the Government will not have all the answers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While such laws are no panacea nor a silver bullet, they are but one piece of a larger citizen-centric ecosystem, which moves the needle forward on civic participation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If change is, indeed, going to be deeper and faster, then Singaporeans must be ready to become active participants of that process, with the Government facilitating conversations by sharing more information.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Last year, an article in the Business Times put this quandary in stark perspective.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was appropriately titled, "Lack of data on Singapore's Reserves limits discussion on its use".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Bicentennial offers us an opportunity to imagine the richness and breadth of conversations about the Singapore we are entering into in the years to come, a Singapore that is not just economically successful, but socially and culturally confident, too, with Singaporeans of all stripes proud to call it home.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These values must run through whatever future we envision for our children’s generation, wherever the winds of Global-Asia lead us and wherever we lead them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They must stand the test of time even if changes come thick and fast.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They are at the foundation of the Singapore we all want.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But each generation must also be given the freedom to shape the future they seek and to feel that they are an integral part of the country.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A confident population being one with more choices to determine its destiny; a society that accepts that it is only as strong as its weakest link and its most vulnerable; and a people – both employers and employees – all rooted to the Singapore that will always be home for us as we transit into our golden years.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is a Budget that tries to uplift every Singaporean – the children, youths, seniors and, in particular, the MG.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is also a Budget that relentlessly pushes local enterprises and workers to step out of their comfort zone and build deeper capabilities to fend against the unforgiving disruptions caused by globalisation and technology.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, on SMEs, a key pillar of the Singapore economy, contributing about 50% of our GDP.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In addition to creating wealth and jobs, a vibrant entrepreneurial spirit is a national asset that feeds a flourishing society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, the responses by SMEs are important points of consideration in finetuning our policies or communications efforts.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are two Budget features that I would like to touch on concerning businesses.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One is on the DRC or the restrictions on foreign manpower.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It has been more than six years since foreign manpower dependence was tightened to drive higher productivity and redirect foreign manpower to higher tech-content businesses and also to protect the employment of our own local workers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, whilst automation and digitalisation have helped industries, such as the construction and manufacturing sectors, the same cannot be said of the service sector.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I spoke to Mr Benedict Choa, the owner of Cube Boutique Hotel, which specialises in the capsule hotel model with its highly space-efficient yet comfortable bunk-bed accommodation in both Chinatown and the Kampong Glam vicinity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Ben, who has fully used up his foreign worker quota, primarily in the housekeeping department, has tried all means to transform his business model.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: He has found a new market niche in the highly space-efficient capsule hotel market.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: He has also automated his guest check-in system, and he took a leap with the Government agency, Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), to install a communal dining ordering system in the Kampong Glam tourist belt.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And Ben is all ready to employ any local staff willing to work if he only can find them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This manpower challenge on the ground is also faced by larger service enterprises, too.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Despite this, the group is still short of manpower as shift jobs in his industry continue to be unpopular amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Andreas and his team shared that the pool of willing workers from Malaysia and China is shrinking.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And these are the hard truths on the ground.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How does the Government encourage enterprises like Cube Boutique Hotel and Pan Pacific Hotel which are aligned with our national directions and yet still face manpower challenges?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, on the tiered support for different tiers, different types of SMEs according to size.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Those in the mid-sized tier will get slightly less.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And the biggest base, comprising many of the small and micro firms, are assisted through more plug and play solutions at mostly self-help platforms or the heartland SME Centres.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Dr Sue Ann Toh and her team, one of my grassroots, recently started Novi Health, a small firm, a medical clinic and health tech company which combines clinical care with technology-enhanced holistic solutions, to prevent and manage diabetes and other chronic conditions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Sue Ann spoke to me about her team's wish to access a roadmap and a competent Tech Coach which will likely not be available in view of her startup size and in view of our strategy of differentiated support for different tiers of SMEs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, whilst differentiated support favouring larger SMEs makes sense as larger firms arguably give more returns to the economy and provide more jobs, all large firms themselves, however, started small, often with humble beginnings.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How would the Government identify and nurture small startups which deserve a leg-up but which might be overlooked because of their being defined as a micro or small business?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I have further suggestions to help the SMEs, for the Minister to consider.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And the four prongs being the 4As – Awareness, Affiliation, Action and Advocacy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Those who are aware may not be convinced of the need to change and upgrade and will need to affiliate or buy in through a more impactful and regular targeted sharing of successful transformations in their specific industries.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And three, SMEs which are aware and willing to take action often find themselves burdened by daily operational demands and fires.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My search on the SME Portal was interesting, but it was insufficient to develop a roadmap or action plan if I were running my own business.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, some way must be found to competently facilitate clusters of similar SMEs on a regular basis to adopt or to pluck some low-lying fruits together, such as shared services in HR, accounting and common industry-specific applications.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Just as Dr Robert Yap from YCL Group has risen to become an advocate for transformation in the logistics industry, more aggressive efforts ought to be made for more of such evangelists to be profiled for the rest and its industry and to harness these advocates' ideas for further industry transformation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need more of the Robert Yaps in the other industries as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Our Finance Minister had himself shared that these needs cannot be met by the Government alone and will require the rest of the society – the village – to join in the solutioning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Besides donors, one significant partner to the Government is the VWOs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Unless they are more financially independent, much of their time will be taken up to seek funds instead of strengthening their services.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is no reason why this sector cannot be more entrepreneurial and why they cannot spawn a MacDonalds' chain of sorts to create many more jobs for the differently-abled.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is no reason why they cannot set up e-commerce sites with plug and play solutions to market and distribute its own services and products.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Will Budget 2019 make any major difference to the transformation of our country's business and social service sectors?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe the devil is in the details and the key is in the execution.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And I hope the Minister will consider some of my inputs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In recent times, waves of populism have swept across regions and countries, leading to the rise of nationalistic fervour, pressuring countries to adopt citizen-first policies and to implement protectionist trade measures over practices of global citizenship and internationalism.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although trade relations seem to be improving between global giants China and the United States (US), the global economic marketplace and international political landscape are far from stable and certain.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, with uncertainty comes opportunity, and it is important for Singapore to continue to explore how we can continue to remain relevant and ready on the global stage, and leverage our strengths in multilateral and bilateral arrangements that benefit our country.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First of all, supporting and enhancing the capabilities of our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe my Parliamentary colleagues Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Jessica Tan and Ms Denise Phua had already made this point.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the midst of economic uncertainty, our SMEs certainly cannot afford to be complacent and it cannot be a case of "business as usual" for them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I thus applaud this year's Budget for keeping our SMEs in mind, and for putting in place measures that help them grow, especially to develop digital capabilities so that they can eventually cut down on the reliance on foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would allow them to revamp their business model so that they could find their own niche in the midst of the evolving global economic landscape.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the Government enables the financing system to help catalyse the growth of SMEs, I would urge International Enterprise (IE) Singapore do more perhaps to help our companies make their mark overseas, and to further enhance the Made in Singapore brand regionally and globally.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can IE Singapore do more to help identify areas of growth and help groom our local companies to develop capabilities in those areas?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The development of Centres of Innovation in Aquaculture at Temasek Polytechnic and the Energy Centre at the Nanyang Technological University (NTU) have helped to synergise the R&D know-how of our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) with industry-led innovations to commercialise cutting-edge solutions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can this be a model that IE Singapore can further explore moving forward?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can more such centres and incubators be created to spearhead growth in other areas?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Recent developments in the region have shown that it is important for Singapore to have a credible defence force and to enhance our capabilities against cyberattacks.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Bilahari Kausikan put it adeptly at a recent public lecture that a strong and capable defence is Singapore's only leverage on the international stage, giving us an equal footing and bargaining power against other nations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While much of the talks have focused on building our external defences, let us not forget to stay vigilant with regard to our internal security.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the Chinese saying goes, "it is easy to parry a spear thrust in the open, but hard to dodge an arrow shot in the dark." While we can prepare and defend ourselves effectively against any form of external aggression, internal aggression by an enemy in the dark will always be the one that could catch us offguard.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, we thus need to maintain our vigilance against any potential acts of terror on our soil that might rear its ugly head from time to time.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our SGSecure initiatives must thus continue to be strong.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Very often, Mr Speaker, Sir, much more damage can be done by attacking the digital and cyber network of a country than attacking via a method of conventional warfare.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am thus in favour of the proposed spending on defence as I strongly believe that we need to ensure that we stay safe and secure always.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Without robust international defence and domestic security, all our significant economic progress and social development would be significantly threatened and that would have grave consequences for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I now would like to focus on a caring and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore has always adopted somewhat of a centre-left policy structure and we must continue to take necessary steps to look after our citizens.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At my Meet-the-People session, I have often encountered residents who need a little more support beyond what is presently available to get back on their feet.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All of us here, Mr Speaker, would either have relatives or would know someone from the Mederka Generation, and one such person is one of my residents, Mr Sreevardhanan Vasu Pillai, or as he is known in our community, Mr Sree.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Sree was born in 1951 and brought up in a kampung in Sembawang.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As his father  was the sole breadwinner supporting a family of eight children, Mr Sree entered the workforce after his Senior Cambridge Certificate, working as a bicycle mechanic while enrolling at Lembaga Gerakan Dewasa Pelajaran (Lembaga) which was a night school set up by the Ministry of Education (MOE) for workers seeking to upgrade themselves.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 1969, he was called up to report for National Service as his request for a deferment to complete his studies was turned down.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Sree was eventually commissioned as an Artillery Officer in 1971 and he always speaks of his period of National Service with a great source of pride.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As he himself says, and I quote, "I was very proud to be in the Artillery Battalion.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The training I underwent in National Service was very tough, but having lived in a kampung within a big family unit, I was able to tolerate the training regime.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Along the way, I made many friends and they remain a source of strength for me up to today.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The early batch of National Servicemen were considered the Pioneer guardians of Singapore." That is a wonderful tagline actually to tag for our early National Servicemen, the Pioneer guardians of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Sree then went on to join the Port of Singapore Authority as a clerk and, through continuous upgrading and learning, worked his way up to becoming an Operations Officer.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think to some in our younger generation, that seems like an eternity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Forty-five years of loyalty to this particular company.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This also included an eight-year stint in India that he saw as a form of "National Service", as felt he was part of a strategic initiative to develop a Singapore company overseas.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore has, indeed, come a long way since our founding 200 years ago, and we have survived several existential crises in the process.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we celebrate the Bicentennial, I hope that we can all also take some time to think about not just where we came from, but where we are going to next.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us embark on the search for deeper meaning behind what defines Singapore, our goals as a Country and our purpose as a People as these are important fundamental foundations and would certainly help our future generations remain anchored and rooted in the values that have brought us our success.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I listened to the Finance Minister's speech and noticed that he pointed to the role of unions, the crucial place of workers, many times in his Budget Speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Therefore, it is true that we must continue to put workers at the heart of all we do.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: My fellow Labour Members and I will speak up for the different segments of our working population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The common point that we want to make is that every worker matters to the overall good of the economy, society and country.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I will focus, as I have done over the years, on the mature working population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I would frame the context of my speech by making two points.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: First, we are running into predicted headwinds as far as economic growth is concerned because of population and workforce trends.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If we do nothing, our ability to generate national wealth to invest in the future and fund the welfare for the present will face problems, and inequality in our society will grow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is, therefore, crucial that we focus attention in this debate on how we can continue to grow this national economic pie.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Second, that by taking the right coordinated steps, we can turn threat into opportunity, continue our ability to grow economically and cohere better socially.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is the practice of social and economic defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, one may ask, "What if that happens?" Well, GDP growth is the sum of the growth of productivity and the growth of manpower.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Thus, if the manpower growth component becomes zero, then GDP growth, which is how national resources are ultimately generated for use to care for Singaporeans, can only come from productivity growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, you have productivity and manpower, and if you get zero on the manpower side, then it is like flying a plane with one jet engine shut down.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Obviously, we would do better not to let manpower growth become zero.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The question are: how do we do that?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: One way of looking at it is that we have four manpower taps.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The first one would be school leavers coming out of school and entering the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: To all intents and purposes, these were the babies born about 20 odd years ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, whatever those numbers are, it was already preset about two decades ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The second source is, indeed, productivity, and that is done through better work organisation, better design, technology, equipment and skillsets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And this is what Industry Transformation is about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: By becoming more productive, the same number of people can create more economic value through their work, and this is very important and it is the other jet engine to fuel our growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is obvious that we have to judiciously manage the size, mix and growth of this manpower source so that while we benefit from their important contributions, Singaporeans have a fair go at opportunities and prospects at all times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In other words, we cannot just open the floodgates to foreign manpower in order to solve our zero net local workforce growth challenge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Workgroup has been carefully considering these important and difficult topics, and there is much work ahead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I am also grateful to the Finance Minister for extending the SEC and the Additional SEC so that mature workers’ cost-effectiveness continues to be reinforced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There is more, however, that we can do besides reviewing the retirement and re-employment ages in order to get the best of our mature working age population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: At the same time, that challenge also offered an opportunity for households to increase their incomes and living standards and for Singaporean women to become more financially resilient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Many women at the time were full-time housewives, having to look after the children at home while their husbands worked to provide for the family.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Who is going to look after the children?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, the basic transformation then was the scaling up of childcare provision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Parents could entrust their children to childcare in an affordable and accessible manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That liberated the women from being stuck with no choice, to being able to choose to work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: At the same time, the economy got the additional manpower it needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The country grew its wealth and could better afford to invest for the future and to care more for those in need.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And because Singapore took coordinated steps then to overcome that obstacle, the Singapore economy and our society are better off today, both in living standards and in having less inequality than if the women did not have the choice to work and to earn.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Now, 33,000 is the equivalent of one year's birth cohort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And if we add to that caregiving that is cited as a secondary reason for the rest of that 170,000, net of the 33,000 citing caregiving, excluding childcare, as another important reason for their not working, then we are really talking about very substantial numbers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This leakage of national potential will grow as the Singapore population ages further, and more caregiving needs emerge within families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: At the same time, companies across many industries are facing a tighter labour market and crying out for manpower to meet their needs, and many Members of the House spoke about that just now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, there is a structural mismatch between the supply of and the demand for manpower, and it is not just a technical problem because there are profound social and financial consequences for the individual, family, economy and country if a large and growing pool of middle-aged Singaporeans is unable to earn for their immediate upkeep and retirement needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This will then fuel inequality, and it will erode social cohesion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The question then is: how do we turn this socio-economic threat into a dividend that will benefit all?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is, therefore, clear that in order for this pool of latent workers to be activated, we need three key breakthroughs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Current capacity buildup and funding plans for such provision, be it for senior activity, senior day-care or live-in care, is mostly predicated on the expected health and social needs of senior care recipients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Considerations of how to relieve and liberate their caregivers to be able to choose to work are not central.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, this review must look at that and must also consider whether the funding model for service provision can ensure that supply is sustainably built up at the pace that is required.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Here, I would also want to borrow the point from Ms Denise Phua earlier when she spoke about VWOs to become even more financially viable and so on as they undertake the important work because many of the providers in the eldercare sector are, indeed, the VWOs and social enterprises and so on.
