speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, the sustainability of the funding model is actually very critical as we scale it up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is a critical question, because if supply of manpower is increased without a corresponding increase in the demand for manpower or increase in absorptive capacity, then it will not solve the problem, but will, in fact, raise the frustration and just increase the unemployment rate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Earlier, I pointed to the U Family survey that showed a high proportion of caregivers wanting part-time or flexi-work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This also means that if more companies have such options for their workers, many of those who had to quit to care for family would have been able to stay on in work, thus continuing to earn and provide better for their immediate and longer-term needs, and also supplying the manpower on a continual basis to the companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But when we look at the Singapore labour market, it has long been based on primarily the full-time staffing model.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, this tells us that most Singaporean companies may not have yet learnt how to ably utilise and integrate part-time and flexi-work options into their mainstream manpower model, or are also perhaps unwilling to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And this is so despite years of promoting flexi-work arrangements (FWA) by the tripartite partners at both the national and company levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I note with interest that there is an article in today's Business Times entitled "Payoffs in productivity, engagement and creativity make flexi-work a worthwhile goal".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Flexible work needs to be implemented and not restricted in order for it to work".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Therefore, a thorough review of how part-time work and flexible work options can become integral to the mainstream staffing models of Singapore companies, alongside the traditional full-time work model, is needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We also have to determine how to set expectations of HR practitioners in Singapore, so that they can then pick up and have the competence to operationalise this and make this work for companies, and to work well for companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We have to investigate mindsets, close knowledge gaps and consider incentives in order to open the way and grow the capacity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We can learn much from advanced economies like the Netherlands and Japan in this regard, as they have been able to achieve high employment rates for both full-time and part-time work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In other words, they are able to more fully activate their mature working populations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, it is not just a question of substituting full time for part time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But increasing needs, so how do we then introduce and enable this latent force, which is looking a lot for flexible and part-time work, to enter?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Success will only be achieved when potential supply is matched to potential demand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This matching is not trivial, and the outcome does not happen on its own.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In doing so, Mr Speaker, we will stay alert to structural trends.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We will then maximise our chances of staying a "one united people" that will, together, "achieve happiness, prosperity and progress".

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As our society becomes more affluent, many of us are concerned with the plight of low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of us have heard of the phrase "It takes a village to raise a child".

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the same vein, I say that it takes everyone in society to help low-wage workers!

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Everyone, regardless of whether you are in Government, an employer, a service buyer or a concerned citizen, must realise that we all have a part to play to uplift the lives of our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While NTUC continues to rally our workers to upskill, I believe that an important next step would be for the Workforce Skills Qualifications (WSQ) courses to be reviewed.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC stands ready to work with the industry stakeholders, training providers and SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) to ensure WSQ courses are comprehensive and flexible to suit the needs of the industry.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC hopes to see more industry stakeholders coming forward to work with the Government and NTUC to develop PWMs for their industries.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Coupled with WSQ modules being made more relevant, it would be a sustainable way to raise the wages of our workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC is encouraging companies to work with their union leaders to set up training committees to identify training that will equip workers with the relevant skills for sustained productivity increase.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although my previous call for better medical benefits under the Employment Act did not materialise, I welcome the enhanced CHAS subsidies and hope that MOH will allow CHAS cardholders to receive subsidised healthcare treatments at polyclinics even if referrals are made by CHAS-approved private clinics.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Service buyers have a key role to play in uplifting the lives of our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC has been encouraging them to adopt Outcome-Based Contracting and to place greater emphasis on quality attributes rather than contract prices.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Adopting progressive procurement practices will ensure more favourable outcomes for all, including better welfare for our outsourced low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Service buyers should avoid cheap sourcing which would lead to service providers undercutting one another in order to win contracts.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Because with low margins, service providers are unlikely to provide better staff welfare beyond the statutory benefits.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, service buyers should consider longer contract periods.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This would incentivise service providers to invest in technology since they can amortise cost over a longer period.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Technology makes work easier, smarter and safer, leading to better service outcomes and higher productivity.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, it gives outsourced workers greater job security.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Service buyers can also consider aggregating their demand to potentially enjoy economies of scale and more efficient manpower deployment.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Third, service buyers should treat their service providers as partners instead of mere contractors.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They should ensure that their contracts have fair clauses and avoid unreasonable liquidated damages.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When service providers have fair contracts, they are more likely to do a good job and train their workers to deliver higher service standards.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Otherwise, workers would usually bear the brunt of bad contracts.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This happens when service providers find ways to minimise cost at the expense of workers' welfare.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These workers are more experienced and familiar with the job requirements.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thus, in awarding a new or renewed contract, service buyers should ensure that incumbent workers’ wages and benefits are not worse off than before.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC hopes to see more Government bodies take the lead to adopt these Outcome-Based Contracting and progressive procurement practices.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our unions have been working closely with the industry associations to engage buyers and catalyse this on the ground.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Besides this, service buyers have a moral responsibility to look after the welfare of their outsourced workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This includes the area of training, allowing service providers to send their workers to attend training without requesting for headcount replacements, and workplace welfare.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, I call for building owners or service buyers to provide designated rest areas for their outsourced workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am sure if workers are treated well, they will put in their best efforts to deliver quality service.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To lead by example, I call upon all Government agencies and related bodies to ensure proper rest areas are provided for outsourced workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The unions can work with building management to propose solutions for proper rest areas to be built.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On the part of service providers, NTUC has been vocal against the practice of price undercutting or suicide bids, because when service providers have difficulty maintaining the contract subsequently, it is their workers who suffer.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC has been instrumental in the recent changes to the Employment Act and the introduction of Tripartite Standards.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Low-wage, vulnerable workers must also help themselves to earn better wages through upskilling and knowing their employment rights.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC has been urging our workers to "train up to keep up" and "skill up to move up".

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We want workers to embrace the adaptive technology and technical skills relevant to their industry to become Worker 4.0, hand-in-hand with Industry 4.0.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the huge training subsidies provided by the Government, the onus is also on the workers themselves to seize the opportunities available.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Let us not take for granted clean, green and safe environments that we work, live and play in every day.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are the result of a lot of hard work put in by our cleaners, security officers and landscape workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As individuals, we can show our appreciation to them with simple acts.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Return our own trays at the food centres; greet and give them a smile when you see them.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do not litter and do not think that you are doing them a favour by creating work for them.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These acts do not cost us a thing, but they can go a long way in brightening up their lives.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A gracious society does not happen by chance.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is up to you and me to make a difference.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Low-wage workers should also take up opportunities that are available to enhance their skills, especially in the application of technology.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would also like to encourage the public to be more considerate by lightening the workload of low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of us are perhaps unaware, but in our daily duties and lives, we can play a part in helping our low-wage workers earn a living with dignity.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a society, we are judged by how we care for the less fortunate.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Helping low-wage workers earn better wages, gain better welfare and be shown greater respect is not the responsibility of the Government alone.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is our collective responsibility to create a better society, one that is inclusive and caring, and one that ensures all workers feel a sense of belonging.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Whoever you are, do what you can, and with whatever you have to help a low-wage worker live with dignity.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That has been most aptly portrayed by how our freelancers have contributed to the successful making of the Hollywood movie “Crazy Rich Asians”.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They have also benefited from collaborating with global talents in this regard.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Freelancers have responded positively to the Minister for Finance's message on how the Government will help workers deepen capabilities and seek new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will touch on this in the first part of my speech and thereafter on the impact of diesel tax.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The emergence of digital platforms has created more options and easier access to an alternative or additional source of income.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, freelancers that we spoke with cited challenges, such as loss of income due to prolonged illness or injury, training gaps and unclear contracts.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Tripartite Workgroup formed by MOM has come up with recommendations to address these concerns.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some ideas implemented have had good traction, but we can do more and do it faster.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, a member recently suffered an injury and was on medical leave for two months.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Previously, he would have to rely on his own savings.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But with the insurance cover, the payout enabled him to receive income during his recuperation.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, not many have taken up such a policy as they fear losing out on bids if not everybody takes it up.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is one area where Government Procurement entities can encourage freelance bidders to be protected.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In January this year, the National Private Hire Vehicles Association (NPHVA) worked with ride-hailing operator Grab to help their active drivers enjoy free Prolonged Medical Leave coverage.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am also the Executive Adviser for NPHVA and, this morning, we managed to get, together with the help of MOM, GOJEK to also offer similar product protection for their driver partners.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope all operators will do the same for all taxi and private hire drivers to be covered under such insurance coverage.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To this end, I would like to appreciate the efforts by MOM and the Land Transport Authority (LTA) to engage these operators.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is actions, such as these, that will affirm their assertions that drivers' interests matter to them.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I feel that Budget 2019 is pro-worker with initiatives like the GRTP and the Professional Conversion Programmes (PCPs) to help workers with skills upgrading and to move into new growth areas.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Freelancers also want to participate in these initiatives.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They do not have easy access to courses and support.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It can be extra daunting if they work in specialised fields where there are few local providers or experts.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Potential loss of income when they attend classes also deters some from attending such training.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we have had some early successes in providing training support to them with the help of some Government agencies and NTUC Learning Hub.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, we contextualised first-aid courses for outdoor learning and adventure instructors.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We also customised SkillsFuture for Digital Workplace training for taxi drivers and sports coaches.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Masterclasses and workshops were also co-organised with freelancer associations.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We hope to receive more help even as we intensify our efforts to deepen the competencies of more freelancers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are glad that there are initiatives like those by IMDA to develop the media sector skills framework.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: IMDA also provides training allowance to alleviate the loss of income when media freelancers attend approved training.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that other Government agencies will quickly put in place skills frameworks and training allowance for freelancers in sectors under their purview.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have also made some progress in technical training for individuals like riggers – those who set up lightings and sound systems on ceilings and walls – and boot camps to equip new media freelancers on how to go about submitting quotations and how to go about training and deepening their own competencies.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This also includes upstream efforts with MOE’s Education and Career Guidance officers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Together, we co-curate sessions where youths in tertiary institutions can get a clearer picture as to what a freelance career entails.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They, too, want opportunities to gain working experience overseas.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We hope that the Ministry can consider partnering us and freelance associations to send our young freelancers to key regional markets.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We in the NTUC also stand ready to select and prepare young workers from among unionised companies, especially those who have displayed leadership skills, to gain overseas exposure so that they can support our unionised firms’ expansion plans.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Freelancers and self-employed persons (SEPs) are often frustrated by late or non-payment for work done.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes, they have to deal with buyers who exact additional demands beyond the agreed scope of work.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Usually, disputes arise because the agreed terms are not documented or when the contract terms are vague.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad our joint efforts have seen some early take-ups.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I also want to applaud the MOF team in getting all Government Procurement Entities to adopt the Tripartite Standards.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us encourage more to do so, especially the recipients of transformation efforts supported by Enterprise Singapore’s EDG.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to thank the MOF team for guiding freelancers to navigate Government procurement procedures.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many would like to tender and bid for projects offered by the Government, and I am happy that we will next co-produce with MOF a brochure with information on procurement procedures and practices so that freelancers know how to provide and bid for Government projects.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Taxi drivers wished that the Government can provide more support to help them manage higher operating costs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, while there is some rebate to cushion the impact, they need more assistance.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have called upon taxi operators to help beyond just passing on this diesel rebate that the Minister has offered to the drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They can also consider cutting pump prices because they offer pump stations to their drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When their costs increase, taxi drivers cannot pass on this cost increase to commuters because they also do not set the fares of the taxis.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The type of vehicle is selected by the operators.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I cannot choose between vehicles A and B because you have 16,000 diesel vehicles that the taxi drivers choose from.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, if the operator offers non-diesel taxis, then the taxi driver would not have to incur this additional diesel tax.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can then appoint the appropriate operator who will sell fuel at the right price to members and manage them manage costs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, support from the Government in training and setting the tone for all buyers will be an important boost.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I urge business buyers and operators to also offer freelancers a fair and reasonable deal.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That is a Budget outcome that will matter most to freelancers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am glad that the Minister for Finance has acknowledged in his Budget Speech that strengthening Singapore's economic competitiveness is an ever-continuing journey and there is more that we can do to support Singaporeans on this journey.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My speech today will focus on two areas which I think we can do more, especially for working Singaporeans – in Training and in Workplace Safety and Health.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the increasing pace of technological advancement, we must ensure that workers – be it those in multinational corporations (MNCs) or those in SMEs – are able to tap on training opportunities and ensure that they continue to stay relevant amidst the Fourth Industrial Revolution.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: From the feedback that I have received in my weekly visits to workplaces and through speaking to a broad spectrum of blue- and white-collar workers, I have identified three key challenges facing our workers when it comes to training.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The first challenge that workers face comes when selecting their courses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, there is an overemphasis on having a breadth of courses available, rather than having in-depth SkillsFuture courses to help build mastery in the domain.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some have also given me feedback that the process of course selection can be disheartening, especially when they find that a course offered by a polytechnic or university is not eligible for reimbursement by their SkillsFuture Credit.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The $500 SkillsFuture Credit offered by the Government may not be sufficient for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many courses cost more than $500 and, often, going on a single one-off training course would deplete one's entire SkillsFuture Credit account.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many workers do harbour hopes of returning to school to get that diploma or degree that they did not pursue when they were younger.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But the cost of these courses can be prohibitive, as they are no longer eligible for the same subsidies enjoyed by our young Singaporean students.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The third challenge is simply the lack of time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many working in the SMEs tell me that they do not have time to go for training as their organisations are already so manpower-lean.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Those in the MNCs do not have it easier either.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They tell me that while they are given the time to go for training in the day, they end up pulling what they call “double shifts” – having to still complete their work at night after class, in the office or at home.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Cost and time are two of the most common reasons given by those who have yet to utilise their SkillsFuture Credits.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How then can we collectively work to address these challenges that our workers are facing?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am proposing three strategies: (a) build depth; (b) bring training closer to workers; and (c) formalise the importance of training with management.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This should cover all types of courses, be it part-time diplomas, specialist certificates, executive education programmes or one-off specialist modules.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will certainly cement our commitment to invest in lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Helping to identify training needs and craft in-depth training courses is an area where tripartite cooperation is useful.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The National Transport Workers’ Union (NTWU) has been actively working with LTA and the public transport operators to help our workers upskill and reskill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This includes setting up the Singapore Bus Academy and the Singapore Rail Academy to provide workers with relevant and timely training.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last year, the union worked with Singapore Bus Services Transit (SBST) to roll out the Operator-Maintainer training course, which empowers our bus captains to perform simple vehicle repairs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the course’s graduation ceremony, I met 63-year-old Bus Captain Varathan.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He has been a bus captain for over 40 years and this was the first time he was taught to do maintenance work on his vehicle.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He was one of the pioneers to complete the course and shared with me that there were plenty of hands-on practices during the course which made the training very much easier to understand.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He was also appreciative of this chance to develop skills and knowledge that would come in handy in his daily work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope the story of Bus Captain Varathan will inspire many more workers to have a lifelong learning attitude and be open to training and upskilling.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, let us bring training closer to workers to support them in this lifelong learning journey.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For courses that require physical premises, our schools and IHLs can be a convenient location for workers to go and upgrade themselves.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Labour Movement has begun taking steps to bring training closer to our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For SMEs worried about sending their employees for training over a long period of time, we can bring training closer to them by having modular courses offered online.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: SMEs can leverage NTUC's e2i U Leap app.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a mobile learning platform that allows users to learn bite-sized modules on the go and take anywhere between 30 minutes and two hours off work to focus on learning during the week.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last year, e2i also released U Leap Enterprise, a mobile learning platform where e2i works with companies to curate specific courses for their workers, which I think is very suitable for SMEs to address their workers’ training needs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will not only save employees' travel time and hassle, it also minimises downtime for the company.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To ensure that upgrading workers' skills is seen as a priority towards a company’s transformation, training must be formalised and recognised by the management.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, I encourage companies to work with the Labour Movement to make training a shared responsibility and make training real for our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is imperative that we continue to invest in WSH practices to ensure that our workers can return home to their families, safe and healthy, everyday.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our closely coordinated tripartite efforts in recent years have started to bear fruits.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are four areas that we can do more to safeguard our workers' safety and health at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, we need to place more emphasis on workplace health.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our workforce is ageing and many have shared with me that they are increasingly facing higher stress levels at work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Recent studies have shown that poor workplace health contributes to work-related injuries and fatalities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can do more to place more emphasis on workplace health, for example, by mandating yearly health check-ups for better detection and prevention of chronic occupational diseases.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, to encourage employers to build safer and healthier workplaces, we need to increase the cost to companies with poor WSH track record as deterrence.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Insurance companies should put in place a tiered insurance premium framework under WICA, where companies will have to pay higher insurance premiums if there are many claims of the same incident nature.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, every company must have a trained WSH representative.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The current legislation only mandates for a WSH officer to be appointed in some workplaces, such as shipyards, petroleum processing plants and factories which employ over 100 people.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: According to the 2018 National WSH Statistics Report released last week, even lower risk sectors are not spared from WSH accidents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As such, we should consider expanding the requirement of having a trained WSH representative to all companies, to make WSH pervasive in every workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Fourth, we need a National WSH Training Academy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Having a National WSH Training Academy will better ensure high and consistent WSH standards across all sectors, particularly in high-risk sectors like construction and manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I will speak more about this during the upcoming Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a Government that cares for our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us continue to invest in lifelong learning and put in place strong measures for WSH to ensure a well-trained, future-ready, safe and healthy workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Because, I am very sure, this House will agree with me that Every Worker Matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These include strengthened support in education for young Singaporeans, as well as the MGP and Bicentennial bonus that will help older Singaporeans and low- to middle-income families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In particular, I was glad to see strong support for businesses and workers, with measures that will help them embrace and adapt to industry transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Businesses and workers must embrace change together so that everyone can reap the benefits of industry transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: While these measures and announcements are encouraging, there is more that we can do and I want to focus my speech in two areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, to enhance the employability and employment of our older workers; and two, to make industry transformation "real" for our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This proportion is likely to grow as Singaporeans enjoy better healthcare and higher standards of living.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Older workers are valuable assets who can contribute experience and maturity to our workforce, and we must better ensure their employability and employment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With our transition to a knowledge-based economy and the wider use of enabling technology, our workers rely less and less on physical strength and their work experience becomes an even more important asset.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our older workers with their years of industry experience are well-placed to leverage technological tools to maximise their productivity potential.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Successful Industry 4.0 transformation must be complemented by a capable and competent Worker 4.0.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But this transformation is not a straightforward process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The key challenge is mindset change of both employers and workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some employers prefer hiring younger workers, while some older workers are apprehensive and resistant towards emerging technology trends.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In the face of rapid technological changes and the evolving demographic profile of our local workforce, the Government, businesses and workers must all be ready to adjust their mindsets and adapt to changes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This change in mindset must be led by employers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With supportive employers coming on board the transformation journey, workers will also be encouraged to pick up the relevant skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Here, I would like to encourage enterprises and companies to focus greater efforts in two areas to integrate more older workers into the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, companies must put an emphasis on job redesign to ensure that older workers are able to adapt to new technology and to different work environments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This could mean improving the user interface of a process so that technology adoption is much easier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, some SMEs I have visited in the manufacturing sector have made the control of industrial robots via the use of iPads very much more intuitive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The operator does not need to understand the inner workings of the robot.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: He only needs to be familiar with the controls on the iPad.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: By using a familiar platform like the iPad as the user interface between the operator and the industrial robot, older workers found it much less daunting to adapt to robotics and automation and are able to improve on their productivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Innovation and technology adoption do not have to be complicated for businesses or workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We must do more to ensure that job redesign and technology adoption remain user-friendly and intuitive for our workers, both the young and old.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: A more conducive work environment through job redesign will attract a younger talent pipeline to enter the industry while enabling experienced older workers to expand on their job roles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Second, companies must provide better training for older workers to upskill or reskill to leverage technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, PSA has been testing and adopting many automation technologies, including unmanned automated guided vehicles (AGVs) as well as automated and remotely-controlled yard cranes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To ensure that their drivers and crane operators remain relevant and employable, PSA worked with the unions to train them for higher-skilled roles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The result is new skills, better pay and greater fulfilment for its workers and, of course, enhanced productivity for PSA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Training and reskilling are key to ensure that our older workers remain employed and employable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: PMEs are, therefore, also at risk of displacement and must continually upgrade to seize emerging job roles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC has been working with the Government and industry partners on the PCPs, Place-and-Train Programmes and Professional Development Programmes to upskill and reskill older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will continue to work with the Government and employers to strengthen the employability of our older workers through our network of unions, social enterprises and our U Associate partners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: There are other funding levers that NTUC can work with the Government to better incentivise and support companies to upskill and reskill older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will work with the Government on implementing the changes to the EDG and PSG to ensure workers' outcome will be one of the key endpoints of ITMs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Government grants for transformation must partner the Labour Movement and result in better outcomes for our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We need to continue helping Singaporean workers keep pace with economic transformation so that they can continue to have better wages, better career prospects, progression, protection and privileges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Since we launched the ITMs, much has been done and we are starting to see early successes across many sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: However, the ultimate beneficiary of our ITM initiatives must be the Singaporean worker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Transformation and ITMs need to be made real, with real tangible benefits for our Singaporean workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And I will be sharing more about this at MTI's Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Only by helping our workers meaningfully and effectively use technology can we unleash the full potential of technology as a multiplier to the capabilities of our companies to be globally competitive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In my many conversations with our workers and employers, two issues stand out.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, workers and companies are unsure of where to go and get started on training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Workers who are keen to undergo training are confused by the myriad of courses available by different course providers and are unsure of what exactly is the most suitable course that they should go for.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some companies also find it difficult to navigate the training space and find the right partners to train their workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Second, workers are often not involved in the change management process in the company's transformation and wondered if they will be able to meet the needs of the company or get displaced by automation and robotics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some companies have embarked on transformation but have yet to translate increased productivity into tangible benefits for their workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This has all led to a sense of unease among some of our workers on what industry transformation holds for them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To address the two issues which I highlighted, the Training Exco will focus our initial efforts in these two areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC will work with unions, industry partners, Government agencies as well as IHLs to curate courses and simplify the training space for businesses and workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC's e2i will be rolling out some enhancements to U Leap, a mobile app that can be a useful tool for workers to upskill, reskill and acquire knowledge in bite-sized formats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: There will also be quicker registration and on-boarding process for learners to intuitively navigate U Leap for a better user experience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We plan to introduce more certifiable modules in collaboration with educational institutes and professional organisations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC will also work with agencies like the Economic Development Board (EDB) and ESG to bring more SMEs onboard U Leap Enterprise version.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To date, we have 15 companies, including SMEs, such as Feinmetall and Fong Engineering, who have reaped the benefits of customised content for their workers' training to learn on-the-go.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This has allowed workers to acquire useful knowledge without the need to be away from work, helping SMEs to better manage their manpower while, at the same time, upskilling their workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is the start of various U Leap communities to enable users to network and participate in crowd-sourced learning as well as be attuned with trending topics on U Leap itself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Both management and workers must work together to engender continual training as an important ingredient for business transformation and increased productivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Workers must be a co-driver in this change process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We must ensure that industry transformation leads to real outcomes for our workers, be it wage growth or retention of older workers and upskilling of our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is a Budget that is both pro-enterprise and pro-worker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It sends a strong signal that Industry 4.0 and Worker 4.0 must continue to go hand-in-hand for us to succeed in the competitive global environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With close partnership amongst the Government, businesses and workers, with our strong tripartite relationship, I am confident that we can overcome challenges and achieve win-win-win outcomes for all.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: By revising national enterprise schemes to focus on worker outcomes places workers' interests at the core of Government policies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our younger Singaporean workers, unlike generations before theirs, face more disruptions in their work lives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, they are almost certain to need multiple career and skill trampolines.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Job facilitation for fresh graduates, many of whom are 26 years and below, is crucial as it sets their direction in life early.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is especially so for the students of Private Education Institutes (PEIs).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must continually review the PEIs to either enhance the skills and job value of these qualifications or to increase the students' awareness of alternative options.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC is prepared to assist with career navigation via its Youth Career Network platforms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations' (ASEAN's) growth will turn it into one of the top economic regions in the world.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are significant entrepreneurial and employment opportunities for our Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: ASEAN can be the important second wing of growth for our economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How do we make it easier for people to move out of Singapore, explore the world, and open more gateways for themselves and fellow Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our young people must seek regional working experience.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many major companies already require their senior executives to understand overseas markets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Without that, they cannot progress to become head of the companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While programmes like the National University of Singapore (NUS) Overseas Colleges (NOCs) and the GRTP allow for meaningful internships, we need our youths to pursue full-time job overseas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope that we can harness the strength of our overseas trade offices and larger Singaporean companies with regional presence to build employment networks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The latter can jumpstart growing our ASEAN-ready talent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This Budget is also about addressing the needs and challenges of businesses and workers in the face of growing structural changes globally.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To achieve this, we must prioritise and master lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat aptly mentioned that Singaporeans need to "reconceptualise" what learning is about, adding that they need to be prepared to learn from "anywhere from anyone at any time".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While this applies to all workers, we need to pay special attention to those who started off with lower qualifications.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How do we extend more comprehensive learning support beyond SkillsFuture Credit for workers who want to return to school or to upgrade themselves?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our workers and unionists are well aware of the need to continually retrain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is made more urgent now with disruption.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Most workers would not have a single linear career trajectory.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They would need to be nimble and switch careers or job functions as seamlessly as possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, the majority would need to obtain additional skills or qualifications to progress within their specific industry or to switch to another industry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, this process is not easy, as my fellow Labour Member of Parliament Mr Melvin Yong had shared.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many workers have significant financial and family commitments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, many workers choose to put off picking up another skill or qualification for as long as they can.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The PCPs and CSPs have helped to provide these bridges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The combination of course subsidies and training allowances have lowered the barriers to career conversion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, the limited number of PCP and Earn and Learn Programme (ELP) places meant that many workers would have to pay full unsubsidised fees, and some workers might not qualify for the PCPs and might need a longer time for them to qualify or succeed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Recently, a 33-year-old resident staying in Tampines sought assistance from me.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: He has been working since graduating with a diploma in business in 2007.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In his own words, he wrote to me, he said, "I had no idea what I wanted to do after my GCE "O" level.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: So, I did a diploma in business." He worked in a corporate function, and his job was in a polyclinic where he was inspired to become a nurse.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: After trying for two years, he finally obtained a place in Ngee Ann Polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: He said, "I do have some savings, but it is not enough for three years." Yet, he still has a burning desire to serve the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: He also said, "It took me a long time to finally get a placement at Ngee Ann Polytechnic to study nursing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But unfortunately, I do not come from a well-to-do family.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: My father is semi-retired and my mother is a homemaker.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I do not behold high hopes in life.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I will be gratified enough to be a nurse.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But the cost of $60,000, I believe, is too difficult for me to manage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the end, I do have some savings to tide myself through, but it is not enough for three years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thus, I am seeking all forms of assistance which I can possibly conquer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is possibly my last chance, and I am thoroughly sincere in becoming a qualified nurse." While this is one appeal, there might be many other people in similar circumstances in different fields.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It will also allow workers to discover new career choices instead of those predetermined in the earlier years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Returning to school for career switch can be socialised as a mainstream norm.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers require more support when they leave their jobs to expand their options on reskilling.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This streamlining of courses allows for over-specificity early in life.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Perhaps, we can also offer these to workers looking for career resilience and changes in modular fashion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Learning agility is the key to building a modern workforce capable of navigating and leveraging opportunities arising from disruptions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And the Labour Movement will continue to do its part to make it real for workers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.00 pm until 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Whether 700 years, or 200, Singapore's place in the world remains geographically small.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But with careful development and husbandry, we have seen our little place become more prosperous and more secure.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We often think that our dream of peace and safety can be secured by technology.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And, indeed, in our armed forces, in the way we have harnessed technology to our service in infrastructure, housing, and even parking, we have seen how things can be cheaper, easier and better.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But technology carries with it not just a chance at greater comfort and ease, but also a risk of great evil.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Technology is about process; it is an instrument which helps us to make things better and is valuable for that reason.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Science works to a different purpose – it is the pursuit of knowledge and truth – working towards an accumulation of not just how we do things, but in understanding the true nature of the universe – physical and human – that we work and live in.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this sense, science can be "hard" or "physical sciences", or "the human, social sciences".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One can, therefore, be a very good scientist, but a poor technologist and vice versa.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I make this distinction only to say that the pursuit of technological advances cannot be a blind one but must contribute to a useful end.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For example, we would all agree that Parking.sg is a very useful technological product.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It replaces paper coupons, makes it easy, quick and secure to pay for parking.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: You pay for what you use, and you get a refund for what you do not.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: That is an example where we used technology in a cost-effective manner to get us a service which we find useful.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Technology needs a master, and we ought to be always careful of the purpose to which it is employed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It covers issues, such as the infringement of personal privacy, because smart technologies can determine an employee's whereabouts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Working life is also becoming more precarious for workers with no laws to protect them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It affects the way workers process information, their working time and workplace relationships.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The regulatory regime of our working life harks from the industrialisation era.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I am not sure whether this is the sort of working life we want.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Meanwhile, in the F&B sector, in the past, we had inhouse delivery riders, say, in fastfood chains.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These are permanent employees hired by the fastfood chains with rights and protection given to all full-time employees.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: However, when online food delivery platforms are up, fastfood chains increasingly do not need the same number of inhouse delivery riders.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, riders themselves may opt to join delivery companies because they see their earnings improve.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They do not see the important considerations in the short term – a career plan, stability, insurance and training.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC FairPrice, in our transformation journey, is building automated distribution centres, online platforms and at the stores, adopting technology to help improve processes.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our HR side, working together with our union, has had to retrain our staff to take on new jobs and work with new machines and technology.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is important so that our staff, especially the older ones, are not left behind.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For sure, this is not a walk in the park.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In an age of technological advance, the HR divisions need to rise to the call, to remember that we are dealing with humans, and to ensure that our regulatory regime keeps up with very human needs and wants.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There has been a lot of technological innovations in the payment ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: With technology and the drive towards a cashless society, and with cashless payments becoming more widely accepted, a rising social issue could arise.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The obvious question that comes to mind is: will the poor be left out?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have moved from drawing cash from banks, counting cash, issuing cash to workers on pay day to getting everyone to have bank accounts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: When the banks imposed a "fall below fee", it was the lower income who are likely to pay the cost.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: With cashless payments, like using quick response (QR) codes or mobile pay, the poor may become excluded.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And yes, they may yet pay the cost of going cashless.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, we need to guard against being technology-centric over being people-centric.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In our move towards self-checkouts, we started with having self-checkouts that accepted only credit cards.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But should we pause to reconsider that even as machines become more powerful, people remain equally frail?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But the case of the leaked human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) identities and the MOH data leaks show us that user problems are as present as ever.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We will always have unfriendly states, underhanded attacks, subversions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The difference is that technology gives us all greater power.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, I say, while we should not stop in our journey towards a smart nation, we ought always to remember “user problems” and give pause.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is a great app if everything works.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If it does not, well, you ought to know that the following pieces of information have been given by you – your credit, your debit card details, the location you were at at that point in time, your vehicle number and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think it is a risk many of us are willing to take, and I certainly do not want to paint alarmist hypotheticals.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But how do we guard against the bitter, the disaffected, the maladjusted or the pathological?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The greater the power, the greater the evil that men can do.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We talk about industrial revolution but the quieter yet more violent one lies in the companion revolution in the way we work and relate to one another.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The humanities allow us to know why and how we ought to deploy our new powers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This calls for a way we think and invest in education, but also, what we can do, in Government.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have long vaunted our ability to tell “hard truths”, to value “doing the right thing” over doing the popular one.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But with increasing use of AI and machines, our ability to tell what is the right thing we ought to do may be severely compromised.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our ability to incorporate technology in our lives has far outstripped our ability to reason morally about the choices that we will be forced to make as a technological society.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is no longer a choice between the right and the popular, the short and the long term, but the choice on how to programme machines to make choices that are not just about efficiency and speed, but about values – good, bad, right, wrong.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We know of the accident with the autonomous vehicle at one-north where, thankfully, no one was hurt.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If there was, to whom do we attribute the blame?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is recently a rendition of the classic "trolley problem", where people all over the world voted on how they would resolve moral dilemmas.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Would they save the young or the old?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There are different ethics committees now, embedded in different Ministries and agencies, for example, in biomedical studies and research.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I must clarify that the frontiers are not those of technological progress alone, but on how they affect humans and human relationships.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And what, whether and how technology should be deployed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It has made important provisions to keep us safe in the online space.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Ministry of Home Affairs' (MHA's) Home Team Science and Technology Agency is one.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the next 200 years, changes will be even faster and more severe.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to not just understand science to take advantage of these changes, but also what it means to be human.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Only then can we have a Strong and United Singapore.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Given the changes that have been made to our manpower policies and resources, perhaps it is time that the Ministry conduct an in-depth study of the data and find ways to increase the labour force participation rate.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: If more Singaporeans are gainfully employed, we will also be able to reduce the corresponding resources needed from the Government and channel it for other uses.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Simplistically speaking, one more Singaporean worker joining the workforce equals to the same Singaporean depending less on Government resources.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: It is heartening that this year’s Budget will provide more support towards the older workers, with increased annual payouts from the WIS scheme, by topping up SEC to support employers in hiring older workers, and other initiatives that will help them save more for retirement.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: While these are helpful to older workers, the best support is ensuring that they have a good job.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Many of the older workers have told us they are not ready to retire for good.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Some need to continue working, as they are the sole breadwinners of their families.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Some need to support their children’s education in universities, and others hope to build up the family's medical and retirement funds which, at 67 years old, many of them still felt were inadequate.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: But most importantly, many of them expressed the fact that they are still physically able, relatively healthy and want to continue to be gainfully employed.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: One area to look at is to help our older workers to continue working for as long as they wish to and are able to.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad a Tripartite Workgroup has been set up to look into this.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Examples of such companies are ComfortDelgro, Gardens by the Bay, Hewlett Packard Singapore, among others.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: These companies have chosen to move the retirement age to 65 and beyond, with some of them having no contractual retirement age.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: From time to time, the Labour Movement also receives appeals from workers seeking assistance to extend their re-employment contracts.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: And I urge the Civil Service and other Government-linked companies to quickly take the lead.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: The extension of retirement and re-employment ages provides certainty to our workers who want to continue working and allows a longer runway for employers to plan for training and upskilling, as well as adapt to digital transformation holistically.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: No worker should be left behind on our road to the development of a Smart Nation for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: As such, I urge MOE to look into enabling continual education for our mature workers.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, companies are engaging IHLs to develop programmes for their workers.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: This approach only reaches out to a small number of workers.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: If MOE could step in, it can be further scaled up.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: It has been particularly challenging training workers in the SME sector.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: A large number of Singaporeans work for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Due to their workforce size, many SME companies are often unable to send workers for training due to shortage of staff.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, the other challenge is that SME workers are reluctant to go for training as it might affect their gross income and overtime.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: We have also heard feedback from workers in their mid-50s who felt that it is not necessary to go for training as their career runway is shorter and training might not provide more opportunities for career advancement.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: We need to change their mindset and help educate them that training and skills upgrading are necessary for them to remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: To facilitate and accelerate training, I hope that training can be brought nearer to the doorsteps of companies and their workers, especially for companies that are situated at industrial areas.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: This will help to reduce travelling time for workers when attending training.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore as a Smart Nation will position us well in the competitive global economy and, hence, we need to push everyone to step up the pace of industry transformation and push for productivity growth through automation and developing a skilled workforce.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: If our workers are gainfully employed, it will benefit employers, the Government and the nation overall as Every Worker Matters.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Today, we are facing the headwinds of stiff global competition and a rapidly changing economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Protectionism is on the rise and globalisation is giving way to "slowbalisation".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As a small and open economy, these geopolitical forces impact Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While there are challenges, we must maintain our sights on the bright spots.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Businesses are turning to ASEAN to diversify risks and Singapore can play a pivotal role as a regional hub.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Technology and innovation can unearth new opportunities for our growth.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Singapore must continue to sharpen our strengths as a trusted brand and a skilled workforce, and I am glad that this Budget provides a strategic plan to help Singapore and Singaporeans to do so.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our labour market is tight with lower birth rates, an ageing population and tightening foreign labour inflows.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This Budget is pro-worker and has put workers at the heart of it.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I strongly believe that Every Worker Matters and this Budget can do more for PMEs because every PME matters.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In 2018, professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) continued to be more affected by retrenchments with higher skilled, mature PMETs the hardest hit.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Older PMETs also face greater difficulty in the job market with the long-term unemployment rate for resident PMETs aged above 50 higher than younger age groups.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With technologies, such as AI, middle-income jobs can potentially be hollowed out, at the risk of workers' downward labour mobility.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These are real concerns I have heard from PMEs I have met and spoken to.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our skilled workforce is our competitive advantage and Every Worker Matters.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Investing in our workforce enables us to grow the pie collectively and reap the fruits of labour together.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I propose three key thrusts to do so.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, enhancing protection in the future workplace; second, enabling progression in the future of work; and third, expanding potential for our future workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The future workplace must take pre-emptive steps to redesign jobs and future-proof workers' skillsets.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Stakeholders must strengthen information flow, overcome information asymmetry and collaborate on transformation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At the recent NTUC Future Jobs, Skills and Training Forum, industry and union leaders, employers and workers shared actionable keys for industry transformation based on early successes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For example, in the financial services industry, the Tripartite Advisory on Human Capital Practices for Banking, adopted by 160 banks, calls on banks to proactively identify impacted jobs and redeploy workers into areas of job growth through PCPs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Last month, the Singapore Bank Officer's Association, now renamed the Banking and Financial Services Union, repositioned its mission to serve more workers to cope with disruption.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Labour Movement also welcomed the Singapore FinTech Association, which helps workers to reskill to take up financial technology (FinTech) roles, as an affiliated U Associate partner.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Under the Employment Act and other labour legislation, there remains distinctions between our rank and file and PMEs, and "manual" and "non-manual" work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
