text: These distinctions influence the treatment and protection of these workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is particularly challenging today to make these distinctions as many jobs involve a mix of both manual and non-manual work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are also workers who have been wrongly classified as "managers and executives", excluding them from protection under Part IV of the Employment Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some employers have also tried to exclude workers from union protection under the pretext that the worker is in a conflicted position as he wields "managerial" powers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The relevance of these dichotomies needs to be examined to ensure that our workers continue to be adequately protected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Future of Work is fast-paced and the half-life of skills is shortening.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Much like our Formula 1 drivers, we must have quick and effective pitstops to retool and get back in the race.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Training providers must have speed-to-market and move away from traditional certifications to peer network approval systems and industry crowdsourced on-the-go learning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: An example of such a "pitstop" is the Healthcare Academy, set up by the Healthcare Services Employees' Union and NTUC Learning Hub, which upskills workers through industry co-created programmes, delivered through varied modes of learning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Such concerted efforts are needed to ensure that our workers upskill in tandem with transformation efforts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While PWM is associated with low-wage, rank and file workers, PMETs, too, can benefit from PWM, especially PMETs earning between $2,500 and $3,500 per month in highly impacted jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our Future Workers will increasingly participate in new ways of work and employment models.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With flexible and digital-enabled work, we can tap on sources of untapped labour supply to expand our workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I want to also call for more pre-emptive and proactive training, and we can only do this with strong support from our tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To enable workers to take charge and expand their potential, workers can tap on their SkillsFuture Credits to upskill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These credits have helped to seed and catalyse lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our unions have also been working with employers to set aside time for workers' upskilling.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some companies have even voluntarily provided a top-up of employees' SkillsFuture Credits to fund their training, and more companies are encouraged to do so.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: All stakeholders have a part to play in co-creating our future.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We need to create wealth rather than focus on spending more.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We are generating wealth by transforming our economy to higher value activities and constantly attracting such investments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Help our workers earn more, in better jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What obstacles are there to prevent our workers from going for continuous training and education?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: If we argue about how to share a stagnant pie, we are fighting a losing battle.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We should be working together to grow the pie.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   	I would like to propose a "five-core" strategy when we implement the Budget.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, the Singapore Core ‒ build a workforce with a Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, of one heart and mind ‒ the tripartite partners must work together with one heart and mind and adopt a worker-centric approach.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, determination ‒ our workers must be determined to learn new skills, pick up a second skill and develop a lifelong learning mindset.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fourth, confidence – face the future challenges with full confidence.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fifth, ambition – we must have the ambition to fulfil greater objectives.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In particular, Minister Heng Swee Keat paid close attention to workers, not just workers in the generic sense, but workers as real people – the elderly, the unemployed, lower-income workers, even our youths, who represent the future workforce.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Feedback from our workers on the Budget has been positive.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The MGP, WIS enhancements and other forms of support reflect a more "caring and inclusive" society.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They appreciate what the Government is doing for them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, some middle-class workers pointed out that they did not feel the benefits as strongly.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Some also noted that notwithstanding the disbursements, structural rises in costs of living – water, diesel tax, carbon tax and the eventual Goods and Services Tax (GST) rise – would ultimately be passed on to the end users.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Some of our workers also wanted to clarify that disbursements, such as the MGP, would not burden future Governments or the workforce.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I thought these were very insightful feedback from our workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In short, the Labour Movement appreciates the direction of our Government and, as Secretary-General of NTUC, I urge the Government to continue to put workers at the heart of all we do.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: NTUC Labour Members and many other colleagues in the Chamber today have placed workers at the heart of our debate speeches.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They have each addressed the various segments of our workforce and the issues they face, whether it is the elderly workers, low-income workers, workplace safety issues, balancing family with work, training and progression, all segments of the workforce, including freelancers and PMEs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our vision and purpose in NTUC are a simple one.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is about doing the best we can for every worker.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our changing demographics mean a tighter labour force in the future and, with limited manpower growth, Every Worker Matters.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Each worker's skills, knowledge, experience, contribute to our human capital.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our economy can only be at its best when all our workers are performing to their potential and are rewarded fairly for their productivity.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is testament to the efforts of the tripartite stakeholders – the Government, businesses and our workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But even as we have done well, the Labour Movement cannot rest and must look ahead.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: At these moments of rapid economic change and disruption, I am glad that there are also many new opportunities for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: NTUC will partner our tripartite partners to enable our businesses to seize new opportunities and create wealth, so that our workers can aspire to what we, in the Labour Movement call, the 3Ws: better wages, better welfare and better work prospects.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: At the same time, the Labour Movement is cognisant that some workers in Singapore will feel dislocated by the rapid changes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: NTUC will and must always and will do our best to support these workers to keep up.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The heart of the Labour Movement's purpose is for our workers to earn and secure a fair wage.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This allows them and their families to keep up with the cost of living, save and flourish.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have no illusions that workers can do well if businesses do not do well.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In this regard, I agree with the Minister for Finance that a company's leadership is key.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: So, when the boss of a company is ready to seize new opportunities through technology, NTUC wants to partner you and wants to facilitate with the necessary worker training and upskilling.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: NTUC and our union leaders are eager to share our experience and expertise with our tripartite partners in ensuring that these outcomes are achieved.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I will cite a simple example of what we have done for almost 10 years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: NTUC's e2i launched the Inclusive Growth Programme (IGP) in 2010 as NTUC's advocacy for low-wage workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The programme provides funding for companies' productivity initiatives that translate into actual workers' wage increments.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Brother Norizal bin Zainal, a security supervisor at Temasek Polytechnic, benefited from this.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: He took part in a project that was looking to allow officers to update information to supervisors through their handphones.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This gives security supervisors more mobility and they were able to up their productivity.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As a consequence, he enjoyed a $100 increment to his basic salary as a result.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Some may think that $100 a month is not so significant an amount, but to many of our workers, this matters a lot.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The successful demonstration of sustainable, productivity-driven wage increases also facilitated the eventual legislation of PWM for lower-income sectors.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These successes were possible because union leaders and our industrial relations officers acted as critical catalysts.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Labour Movement looks forward to a productive partnership with MTI and ESG on the EDG.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Labour Movement must act on the advent of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, or Industry 4.0, as mentioned by Minister Heng Swee Keat.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These workers, what we have called and termed "Worker 4.0", go hand in hand with Industry 4.0.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They fear it, they do not understand it, and they are worried that technology will take away their rice bowl.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Some of our very own workers in Singapore also feel threatened by the unknown and some of the fear mongering online.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: When Members get their hands on the pamphlet, you will see that this is a simplified example of what the archetype for Port Engineering Professional 4.0 looks like – the current version, what is the 4.0 version, the skills gap, and the necessary and required training for them to upgrade.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Our intention is to help our workers visualise the potential of Industry 4.0, for the companies and for themselves, for their careers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: When Minister Heng Swee Keat visited PSA over the Lunar New Year period, he may have noticed some automation projects which were on trial.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Automation is an important area of productivity growth for PSA in the intense arena of competition for Ports.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: One of our Union members and a Senior Mechanical Engineer at PSA, Brother Ng Hwee Sheng, has completed a one-year Systems Engineering course at the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT).

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: With his newly acquired skillsets, he now takes on a larger role managing various automated and intelligent systems.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: This is part of PSA's scheme in upskilling and multiskilling their PMEs to be more agile and adaptive to keep value-adding in the long run.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: With a better vision of Worker 4.0, and examples of fellow workers that have achieved it, we want our workers to make it real for themselves, to know that it is doable that they must take personal responsibility for it.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Many colleagues in the Chamber today have called for workers' upskilling and upgrading.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: As the Secretary General, I am very grateful for the support this Chamber has for the workers, including Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Ms Foo Mee Har, for standing in support of workers' training.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: These committees, made up of management and union leaders, will work together to articulate what Worker 4.0 looks like for the company, and partner management in the transformation towards Industry 4.0.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: For example, in the aviation and aerospace cluster, we have SIA Engineering Company, ST Aerospace, SATS; in energy, we have the Singapore Power (SP) Group; in transport, we have the Singapore Bus Services Transit (SBST), Singapore Mass Rapid Transit (SMRT) and so on.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: In the past, we also have companies that work with unions on training and wage increments to support the implementation of PWM.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: This provides a ready infrastructure for us to push Industry 4.0 and Worker 4.0 outcomes within these companies as well.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: These Training Committees may have different sounding names and structures.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: But more importantly, I am concerned about the outcomes and not the form.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Whichever the form they may come in, what they have in common is that management and union must sit down together to discuss, plan and execute these very important training programmes for workers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: They must share information in a way that facilitates this mutually beneficial initiative.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Training Committees harness workers’ expertise to support companies’ business development and investments.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Union leaders, by the nature of their work, have a deep understanding of the factory floor and intimate knowledge of ground worker readiness and realities.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: By harnessing both management and labour expertise, the Training Committee can chart out skills and competency requirements, put in place training programmes, such as PSA’s one-year Systems Engineering Course at SIT, schedule workers' training to minimise downtime in ongoing operations.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: This may seem simple in a speech, but it is no trivial matter in our companies' manpower shortage with shift work.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: And, when we do all these, it facilitates good outcomes for the workers and the companies.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: In addition, we can also map out, through the training committees, prospects for career progression, incorporating possible jobs of the future and, where possible, even tagged to wage increments of these future jobs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Hence, in the next phase, we want to scale up further to all our unionised companies.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Importantly, we must know that these Training Committees will benefit the businesses and they will benefit our workers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: This may sound easy but, in actuality, will not be so simple to execute.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: The Labour Movement, with our reach to partner unionised companies, can play our part in the Industry Transformation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: It is important to start now, to put many good ideas discussed in this Chamber into practical action and, even if we may not get it 100% right at the first go, well, we will get it right.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: And let us get to the transformation process.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: (In Mandarin):   Union leaders and workers told me they are heartened that the Government is pro-worker.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Besides supporting companies to deepen capabilities and increase competitiveness, the Government is also helping workers to enjoy better wages, welfare and career prospects in the new age of industrial transformation and digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: NTUC looks forward to partnering MTI and ESG for EDG to be both pro-business and pro-worker.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: It has always been NTUC's belief that the best welfare for our workers is a good job.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: With the rapid development of technology, we are entering the era of Industry 4.0.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: But there can be no Industry 4.0 without Worker 4.0.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Besides helping companies to stay competitive by leveraging smart technologies, it is also important to help workers accept and harness technology to realise their potential in Industry 4.0.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: But what are the skillsets and attributes of Worker 4.0?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: What types of training should they undergo to become Worker 4.0?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Over the last few months, NTUC has been in discussions with companies and relevant partners across industries to develop archetypes of Worker 4.0.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: In this rapidly changing world, it is critical that companies innovate and transform in tandem.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Likewise, workers must also quickly adapt and seize opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: The theme of this year's Budget is building a strong and united Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: I believe that if we put workers at the heart of everything we do and with concerted efforts, we will be able to create a better future for all.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, I will conclude.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: As a result, the trust and mutual respect between the Government and NTUC enabled the setting up of various co-operatives, such as NTUC FairPrice, to help workers manage the cost of living and serve workers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: The Labour Movement has since then played a crucial role in Singapore’s success.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: As Mr Lee Kuan Yew said back in 1979, "The close cooperation between the political and the union leadership made modern Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Lee's statement remains true in the way forward for us.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Singapore is at a transition point, where our economy is taking on a major transformation, where our society is an ageing one, and our political leadership is also undergoing renewal.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: NTUC has enjoyed the strong support of MOM in labour issues.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Moving forward, from all the different speeches, we know that there is a need for NTUC to engage other agencies upstream, particularly MTI for transformation and MOE for lifelong learning for our workers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: In these and other aspects, the political and union leadership must continue the close collaboration that made modern Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: It must be today’s reality; it must be the future reality.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: At the heart of what our 4th Generation (4G) leaders do, be it in the Government or in the Labour Movement, workers must be at the centre.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: With this close political and union cooperation, we can chart Singapore’s success together so that when Singapore succeeds, all Singaporeans can have a share in that success.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not sure what the government of the day 20 years down the road will call my generation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My generation was raised by Singaporeans of the MG.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My parents are from PG and they both worked.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many of my childhood caregivers and teachers were Merdekas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If there was one value the Merdekas taught me, it was to grow up to be an independent Singaporean, proud and defensive of our Independent Singapore, and to think and act independently, beholden to no one but to my country and conscience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This generation truly deserves to be named MG, not because they happened to be born in the 1950s, just as Singapore fought and got its Independence, but because this generation was imbued with the spirit of independence and imparted the spirit of independence to future generations such as mine.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is my sincere hope that a generation who embodied and imparted the spirit of independence will be able to age with independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What I mean by ageing with independence is the ability of our seniors to retire on their own, with as little financial dependence as possible on their children, siblings and other family members, and also on the Government and welfare organisations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Except for incidents of serious illness and accidents, seniors ageing with independence will be able to care for themselves or pay for the care that they require to lead purposeful golden years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe the best way to honour the Merdekas is for the MGP and other Government policies to facilitate their ageing with independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I shall discuss this now in five aspects, in terms of our Merdekas' physical well-being, socio-economic well-being, financial well-being, psychological well-being and the special concern for the well-being of women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first aspect of ageing with independence is physical well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The healthcare system secures our physical well-being, and our investment in preventive health services is paying off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent years, the Government has been investing in long-term care to prepare for the ageing society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In an ageing society, primary care is the critical frontline service to keep our seniors in tip-top health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Preventive care is a subset of primary care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Primary care is essential for the early detection and good management of chronic diseases, which are the leading causes of disabilities and deaths worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our seniors are particularly vulnerable to chronic conditions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our seniors also need immediate remedies for colds and other common ailments, lest these snowball into major illnesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is now an expectation that future generations will be auto-enrolled into CHAS and receive outpatient subsidies when they hit their 60s.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Future governments will be hard-pressed into denying future generations of this benefit, not just because of the political cost, but also the sheer logic of the justification.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Pioneers had worked hard to make Singapore what it is today, if the Merdekas had worked hard so that Singapore stands tall and proud today, who is going to deny that subsequent generations also worked hard to contribute to building a Singapore for future generations?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Did the generation born in the 1960s not work hard in the 1980s and 1990s during the first major economic restructuring and reskilling of the workforce?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Did the generation born in the 1970s not work hard in the 1990s and 2000s to bring Singapore through the Asian Financial Crisis, the tech bubble recession, and the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) crisis?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do not think this is a bad precedent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Again, the MG is setting the foundation for subsequent generations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the last few years, the Government has socialised hospitalisation and disability insurance, making it universal and compulsory.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With MediShield Life and CareShield Life, we are now dedicated to supporting one another as we age, shoring up our interdependence to secure our ageing with independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Making it compulsory for all Singaporeans to help one another to pay for hospitalisation and disability has helped the Government save in healthcare expenditure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans paying for one another has allowed the Government to focus its investment on the healthcare system and long-term care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe the Government should do this, not because of the political pressure, but because, with MediShield Life and CareShield Life in operation, making primary care affordable for all seniors will plug the remaining big gap to make public healthcare in Singapore truly universal and accessible to all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second aspect of ageing with independence is socio-economic well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans are renowned worldwide as a people who work hard and play hard.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a hardworking people, socio-economic well-being is a very important aspect of our overall well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Socio-economic well-being refers to the fulfilment one gets from being economically active.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is also social, as work brings people together to interact and collaborate to achieve specific objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, many of our colleagues are also our friends.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What makes us distinct in the animal kingdom is our desire to be creative, to work to create things that become part of our social identity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Work is, therefore, filled with meaning and purpose.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Life expectancy has increased so much to give us decades of extra time to age with meaning, purpose and dignity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the post-industrial economy, our workers are skilled knowledge-based workers who are continuously learning new skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To allow our older workers to work as long as they desire, as long as they are able to, is to allow our workers to age with independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is because work provides for meaning, purpose and dignity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our older workers should be respected for their experience gathered in a lifetime, and not forcibly retired when they still have so much to contribute in meaningful ways.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our seniors should be allowed to continue to use their skills developed in a lifetime so that they find their lives to be filled with purpose.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our seniors should also be treated with dignity, not subjected to an ageist mindset or have their wages docked mechanically by formula just for crossing some threshold making them "old" when they can be just as productive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will allow our workers to strengthen their socio-economic well-being and age with independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: From the perspective of the economy and society, it is also a waste of human capital for workers to retire prematurely when their skills and experience are still invaluable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nevertheless, our workers should also be empowered to retire in their 60s if they want to retire.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Retirement, for many, is not the end of work, but the pursuit of creative activities that could be unpaid work, for example, providing childcare for their grandchildren, or part-time work in fields that they could not pursue previously.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To enable our workers to work if they can and want to work by removing the retirement age does not mean, I repeat, does not mean to get Singaporeans to work till they die.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is to reform the system so that Singaporeans do not have to worry about their finances and can retire in their 60s if they want to, but they can also continue to work if they want to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The ideal would be that, from today, no Merdeka-Generation Singaporean, no Merdeka, would be compelled to retire or forced to work by necessity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third aspect of ageing with independence is, therefore, financial well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Once we change our mindset about retirement and allow our workers to work as long as they can work and want to work, and to retire if they want, our approach towards CPF should also change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: CPF has already been delinked from the retirement age and re-employment age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The question that remains is: what role should CPF play in the new ageing society we are facing?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In our maturing society, and especially from the MG onwards, our would-be seniors will increasingly not be dependent on one single source of income to meet their needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a good thing, as it provides the financial basis for ageing with independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some will have enough savings that can be used to purchase private annuities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many will be owners of a housing asset that can be monetised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Others will want to continue to work and they can continue to work to maintain a steady stream of income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In such a context, CPF becomes an avenue of supplementary income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our CPF monies are our savings secured by the Government as a fixed deposit account with attractive interest rates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this respect, CPF can be a crucial safety net in two ways.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, we need to recognise that there will be ageing Singaporeans, whether now among the Merdekas or in subsequent generations, who will not have enough savings and who do not own housing assets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These Singaporeans will not be working because they want and can, but because they have to in order to survive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For these Singaporeans, WIS is important, and they may also seek ComCare help.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But while ComCare assistance is a dignified option for those who are really destitute and cannot work, it is not the same for a senior who can work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such seniors would rather age with independence and not be dependent on state handouts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, if there is no need for CPF Life payouts to act as supplementary income, seniors should have the option and be encouraged to leave their monies in their CPF account to accumulate interest and get larger payouts later.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The youngest of the MG is turning 60 years old this year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is, therefore, an appropriate time to reconsider this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, CPF can function as an insurance against crises.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not unlike why many put their savings in fixed deposits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fixed deposits can be withdrawn easily to meet urgent needs, compared to less liquid investments with higher returns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Major illnesses, accidents and other crises can disrupt the normal life course of an older Singaporean and erode his or her quality of life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of the first things that many people do in such situations is to cut back on expenditure on quality food, which could worsen their health in the long run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some may even be forced to sell their housing assets to tide over the crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: CPF members can currently apply to make partial withdrawals on medical grounds, if "they are physically or mentally incapacitated to ever continuing in any employment".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The condition "ever continuing in any employment" is very extreme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such withdrawals should be determined on a case-by-case basis, with the objective being for the withdrawal to help a member tide over the crisis with their own savings so that they can return to employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fourth aspect of ageing with independence is psychological well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current understanding is that ageing in place is the best option for our seniors because the stability of their community environment will provide for their psychological well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Urban planning and public housing policies can also facilitate this by implementing renewal in ageing estates, so that our seniors are embedded in mixed environments that encourage interaction with younger families, especially if their own children's families are living close by.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Neighbourhood renewal and home improvement projects have also improved accessibility and safety to encourage active ageing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These initiatives are positive for ageing with independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But all things being equal, it is a good policy to allow our seniors to live out their lives in the HDB flats and neighbourhoods where they raised their children in and built their community networks on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Place is a locality made meaningful by memories and relationships.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The familiarity of the neighbourhood and the neighbours, and the neighbourhood eating places and shops, provide for active seniors who know how to navigate their living spaces to support themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Merdekas are among the first beneficiaries of our HDB policy to house the nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The majority of the MG would have started their families in HDB flats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, the flats and estates they live in would very likely hold special meaning and memories for them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should try to ensure that the Merdekas would not need to move from the flats and neighbourhoods they had raised their families and built communities in, so that they can preserve their meaning and memories of home, and age in place and with independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Lease Buyback Scheme is a policy that allows Singaporeans to truly age in place and with independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Merdekas will be reaching or have reached the eligibility age of 65 years old for the scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The MGP is a good opportunity to promote the scheme to our seniors, as there are still too many seniors who are unaware of the benefits of the scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government could build further incentives for Merdekas to take up the scheme into the Package.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This way, no Merdeka-Generation Singaporean will be forced to downgrade to smaller flats or relocate to an alien neighbourhood because of financial need.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They do not have to sell their flats, just the end part of the lease back to HDB.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fifth aspect of ageing with independence is the need for special consideration for Merdeka women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: CPF statistics suggest that women in the MG need extra help.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a substantial gender gap that also suggests Merdeka women earned less from paid work in their lifetime and, therefore, have less savings beyond their CPF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to call for more generous provisions for Merdeka women who are still caregivers for their aged parents or siblings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Subsidies for long-term home and centre-based care should be increased for them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Merdeka women should have a special place in our honouring of the MG.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The far majority of caregivers who have performed the work of childcare and eldercare for decades have been women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This work has been essential for functioning of our society, but this work has gone unpaid.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Merdeka women have given much of their lives caring for their families and others in society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Now that they need care themselves, they may not be able to afford it because they have suffered the opportunity cost of sacrificing full-time work to care for others.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe all our seniors want to age with independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not because they are self-centred and individualistic, but it is because we are Asians who care for family and community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many of us would have heard stories of, or experienced first-hand, seniors telling their children to let them die if they were to become critically ill, so that they would not be a financial or practical burden.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our seniors want to age with independence so that they do not become burdens for the younger generation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a natural extension of the spirit of sacrifice they embody, for which we are honouring them with the PGP and MGP.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, the strategic direction of the Budget; second, an assessment on the schemes currently in place to help enterprises transform; and last, the implication of the increased social expenditure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the strategic direction of the Budget, the hon Member, Mr Pritam Singh, in his speech shared some ground feedback that he had obtained, suggesting this Budget Statement is tied with the election cycle, rather than being a strategic Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Respectfully, I feel that it is important for Members of this House to deal emphatically with such soundings as they may give rise to cynicism.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If left unchecked, it may well undermine the stated objectives of this year's Budget, which is to build a strong and united Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To understand the strategic direction of this year's Budget, I found it useful to juxtapose this year's Budget Statement against the backdrop of previous Budget Statements, especially from the first year of the current term of Government, so that we, as Members of this House, can better appreciate where the Government intends to take our country to, to overcome the challenges we face as a country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Members may recall the slogans for the past three years' Budgets.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The broad themes for each year, including this year, are similar.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the economic front, there is an emphasis on the need to transform our economy to a lean technology-based and innovation-driven economy that will ensure our enterprises will continue to capture their fair share of opportunities here and overseas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A lot of support is given for such transformation efforts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On our people front, focus falls on training, deepening our capabilities, ensuring we are productive, possess skills that make us relevant to the world and earn a decent living.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the social front, the focus remains on dealing with social inequality, social mobility and access to critical needs, be it healthcare, education and so on, and also to build, ultimately, a caring and united society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition, while we spend more on the social front, financial prudence is maintained always.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, as I see, there is no change in the general direction of strategies employed over these years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Those who described this year's Budget as a pre-elections sweetener Budget make reference to the Bicentennial Bonus and the MGP.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My view is that such a characterisation does not take into account what happened in the previous years, as well as the entirety of what Minister Heng Swee Keat announced this year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Every year, there has always been a slew of short-term measures announced in the Budget Statements together with long-term measures.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, in 2016 and 2017, the Minister announced a one-off GST Voucher (GSTV) – Cash Special Payment; and last year, we had the SG Bonus.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are also pain points introduced this year, running contrary to the suggestion that this is an artificial feel-good Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I heard Minister Heng Swee Keat, the MGP is not for the purpose of plugging the healthcare or affordability need gaps.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The existing systems and Budget allocation have already done that and, as I understand, we are spending more and more on healthcare, year on year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such gaps have to be dealt with across the board, irrespective of the age of fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand that the objective behind the MGP is to acknowledge the contributions of the generation that contributed much to the economic development of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And in the words of Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, the MG taught him independence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is analogous to PGP, or rather, the PG, who are credited for the very existence of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: No one in this House can hardly argue against the fact that the MG Singaporeans – defined not just by age, but the depth of their roots in Singapore – did, indeed, strengthen the economic foundations of Singapore against the prevailing odds then.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Members of this House sometimes forget that whatever we budget for in this House does not define what will happen for the financial year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The spiritual amongst us may say, "Man proposes; God disposes".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But really, it is the market circumstances that would dictate whether or not we would have sufficient resources for these packages.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, to ascribe a political motive to say that MGP is timed for the elections, really kind of elevates the Government to the position of being a fortune-teller.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am not sure if that is an accurate way of describing the timing and, indeed, the position of the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: From the feedback that I have received, generally, the MGP is well-received by both by the MG as well as their children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I did note the next generation, those born in the 1960s, seem to have an expectation that they should be beneficiaries of a package, too, and I think Assoc Prof Daniel Goh made a call along these lines.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am a member of the 1960s generation, but I am not raising this out of personal interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are some bets going on outside this House as to how we would be labelled – the strongest horse seems to be "Majulah Generation".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Much depends on the extent and outcome of the generation's contributions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is where the strategic direction that the Government intends to steer Singapore, too, becomes relevant.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is where the call to unity to deliver sound economic and social outcomes becomes key.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And hon Minister Heng Swee Keat candidly acknowledged in his Statement that "financial resources alone do not get us there".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also think that any acknowledgement should be done by the succeeding generation, just like how the MGP is formulated by the 4G Leaders and the details provided in this House by Minister Heng Swee Keat on behalf of the 4G Leaders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I have said before, the package is not meant to plug a needs gap.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Year on year, much resources have been devoted to transform businesses of our 200,000-plus enterprises and skilling up our people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Is he satisfied with the progress that has been made?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is meant to deal with sluggish productivity growth in this sector, which is admittedly uneven.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would the hon Minister, however, not agree that the services sector is a kind of a "broad church" which includes industries where it is not easy to automate and digitise for the purpose of increasing productivity?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, the logistics business, they would still need human drivers – the framework for autonomous vehicles will only be in place by 2030, if at all.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Could there not be a more granular assessment of industries to see if, indeed, they have been laggards on the productivity front before placing a foreign manpower quota on them?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, we need to be mindful that in the drive for enterprises to become cost-efficient and productive, we do not create a situation where full-time jobs are cut down in favour of engaging freelancers whose pay is variable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What strategy do we have to ensure that this would not happen as SMEs tap on Government grants and programmes?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam recently mentioned this outside this House that Singapore has gained a strong international reputation for trust.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat as well as hon Member Mr Liang Eng Hwa referred to Switzerland in their speeches.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Swiss have successfully carved a well-earned reputation for quality, punctuality and reliability.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We would have heard the phrase "Swiss precision" where "Swiss" is used as an adjective.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is as a result of a national marketing effort.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would the hon Minister agree that more can be done to strengthen the Singapore brand so that enterprises here can also leverage this?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This particularly dovetails with the Minister’s call that enterprises build deeper partnerships across the world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What steps can he identify to support these brand-building efforts?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hopefully, one day, the word "Singaporean" will be become synonymous all over the world with "dependability".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On social spending and prudence, I note that social expenditure is up.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As in previous Government terms, when our economy grows, we also have an obligation to contribute to the Reserves to be used for the uncertainties of the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is a big part of our responsibility to ensure a bright future for our children and our progeny.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Does the Minister anticipate that the Government will be able to follow the same practice in this term, notwithstanding his decision to set aside big sums for the various programmes, which were helpfully identified by hon Member Ms Foo Mee Har in her speech?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To me, this captures the essence of what the hon Minister meant when he referred to building a united Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The potential multiplier effect that will arise by facilitating involvement of private individuals and corporations in helping less-advantaged families is very significant.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This effort should not be the sole responsibility of our Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This also ensures that through this, we will prudently manage our social expenditure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I fully support the strengthening of the SG Cares movement.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I rise to affirm my support for the recently delivered Singapore Budget 2019 and to provide a response from the business community.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: On behalf of the manufacturing community in Singapore, I applaud the Government's recognition of the contributions of the manufacturing sector to our economy.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, the three TACs that I represent are also pleased that the Government has also recognised the important role played by TACs.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to affirm that TACs, as partners in nation-building, remain committed to the cause of enhancing the business community’s capabilities and look forward to continuing its stellar collaborative relationships with our members, government agencies both local and overseas, as well as our Labour Movement, NTUC.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat's speech on enterprise and workforce transformation lends Government support to the beliefs that TACs have been advancing to our members and to the work we do over the last few years.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: For example, SMF has programmes to actively assist the manufacturing community in the three thrusts defined in the Budget for moving the Singapore economy forward.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Some of these programmes are: Deep Enterprise Capabilities.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: SMF is, therefore, excited with the announcement of two further PCP programmes and stand ready to collaborate with Government agencies on them.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As the leading certification body for PMCs, SMF provides a certification process to train and enable workers, especially PMETs undergoing a career change, to be professionally certified as consultants.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Following certification, these consultants are then better enabled to assist SMEs identify issues in business processes and the right type of support they can receive from the Government as well as to bring them on the internationalisation efforts.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: SMF has signed more than 180 memorandums of understanding (MOUs) with local and overseas TACs and government agencies for better collaboration on commercial development.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The Enterprise Europe Network (EEN) representative office in Singapore, tasked with bringing local companies closer to doing business with EU companies, has between 2016 and 2018 organised 56 brokerage events and signed 25 EEN partnership agreements.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It currently has 200 active businesses on the network.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: SMF regularly leads member delegations to local and overseas trade exhibitions.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: We welcome the support that the Government is pledging to transform the industry further under Budget 2019 towards Industry 4.0 standards.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, SMF has taken the initiative to develop a Manufacturing Digital Plan to assist SMEs on their transformation journey.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In 2019, we will continue our focus on assisting companies to digitalise and sooner realise Industry 4.0.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: We have since launched the Go Digital Project Management Services to help SMEs that want to go digital take their first step to digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Under the programme, SMEs can tap on "mentors" to help them deploy technology.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The support announced by Minister Heng Swee Keat will go a long way towards facilitating the process.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: These are just some examples of how TACs can contribute effectively to bringing the business community in line with the Government’s vision, and thereby creating a united Singapore.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: SMF, SBF and SNEF have a very healthy collaborative relationship and supports one another in our respective efforts and stand strong ready to work with NTUC and the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: TACs are not in competition with one another and, like businesses, more can be done when acting in concert where there are greater resources to draw from.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I would, therefore, like to call on TACs to further break down individual walls and work with one another to accelerate our common national interests.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   	At a regional level, myself as one of the three Singapore Appointed Representatives to the ASEAN Business Advisory Council (ASEAN-BAC), together with the business community, we are in strong agreement that the Government has, in this Budget, rightfully identified opportunities in ASEAN to be an area that our local businesses should consider expanding to.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As the strategies from the ASEAN Economic Community (AEC) Blueprint 2025 take shape, Singapore businesses need to better define our competitive space and to leverage the potential of ASEAN as an economic block.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: With the AEC Blueprint in place, ASEAN is, indeed, well-poised to be the fourth largest economy in the world by GDP in 2030.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This is a relatively youthful workforce when compared to the median age of more advanced nations, for example, 40.8 years for the US and 36 years for China.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The urbanisation rate in ASEAN is expected to hit 55.8% in 2030, about 12 percentage points up from 44.5% in 2010.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As income rises, so will standards of living.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: ASEAN will, therefore, become an important market for businesses.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: That these would take place within a short span of slightly over a decade presents our Singapore businesses with many opportunities at our doorstep.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, increasingly imperative that our businesses are enabled to move up the value chain to generate higher value output and, more importantly, position ourselves as a gateway to the rest of ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Digitalisation and Industry 4.0 are the way forward and, with the different financial packages and assistance schemes, the Government is, indeed, helping our businesses along the journey.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker Sir, my speech today would be incomplete if I do not talk about the main concern that the business community has in relation to Budget 2019.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses can appreciate the policy reasons for such cuts, for example, with the declining birth rate in Singapore, having a continued inflow of foreign manpower at the current or increased rate may eventually result in a Singapore with more foreigners than locals.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: However, the fears and the difficulties for businesses have already begun.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: For example, last year, changes made to the Employment Act provided more protection and welfare for employees but incurred additional costs for businesses.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Building a relationship with customers takes time, as does training.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Being able to attract new local workers with more welfare demands and higher costs is yet another aspect which these businesses have to deal with.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is in this context that I would like to caution against an over-reliance on legislation for more and more rules.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Members have, in recent debates before this House, lobbied for mandatory PWMs, eldercare leave and FWAs.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: While all of these are, indeed, legitimate interests which enterprises are also concerned about, legislating them may not necessarily be the best way forward.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is encouraging that there is increased focus at the micro level, with support to accelerate the adoption of innovative solutions, building of global partnerships, upscaling of the workforce and business transformation.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is pro-business, pro-worker, and we look forward to a strong united Singapore.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: With that, I affirm my support for the Budget Statement 2019.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I rise in support of Budget 2019 with its focus on "Building A Strong, United Singapore".

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are a small country in an uncertain world.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Developments in the US, China and Europe had contributed to high levels of uncertainty in the past and will continue to do so in the foreseeable future.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the face of such headwinds, Singaporeans would have to stay strong and united.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must be committed to solving our own problems and helping our own communities, something which this Budget aims to achieve.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must rally behind our leaders who will take us into a new Singapore era, one that our children and grandchildren will be proud of.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many plans and schemes had already been put in place.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The oft-heard ones include those relating to AI, Intelligent Automation (IA), Technology, Manpower, Digitalisation, Innovation and Globalisation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To many Singaporeans though, these schemes appeared to be piecemeal.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More can be done to highlight the vision for Singapore and strengthen the connections so that we can understand how all these schemes can, together, shape a new future and set us a common goal.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Driven by the rapid pace of technological advances which radically change processes and operations, many sectors are undergoing developments and changes of seismic proportions.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are critical for companies' survival, to catch up with their peers or seize opportunities to be market leaders.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To automate and digitise is also to overcome the manpower challenges arising from the reduction in DRC which is expected to put an upward pressure on labour costs for companies in the services-related industry.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We still hear businesses from the services sectors feedback that many of their processes cannot be automated.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The challenge is how we can successfully harness AI and IA to help these companies.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on how successful the ITMs and the Lean Enterprise Development (LED) schemes have been in assisting companies redesign jobs and reduce reliance on manpower?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some businesses find these restructuring steps troublesome, even counter-productive, as the time and resources required may temporarily distract them from their day-to-day operations.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For companies which have yet to implement digital plans, what are the main obstacles?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What measures do we have in place to help them surmount these challenges?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The seven industries were prioritised as their expected productivity gains would be the highest.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Do our SMEs have enough awareness about this scheme and the necessary talents and specialists to implement the transformations?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Ministry share with us some of the successful cases and those which had not turned out as well?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are the lessons from those which had performed below expectations?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are important questions as we need to know how to better help these SMEs leverage technology to move ahead.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Mandarin):   	Next, I would like to speak about the occasional unintended consequences of well-intentioned Government policies.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Take the example of the employment of older workers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are commonly seen in our hawker centres, food courts and shopping malls clearing tables and mopping floors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These seniors are mostly unskilled workers with little education.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, there is a limitation to the type of jobs they can take on.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the Government provides WIS to encourage companies to employ older workers, companies are fine with hiring them since they are paying less for their services.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, employing these Singapore citizens also entitle the companies to employ more foreign workers based on DRC.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the tightening of DRC, companies are likely to employ more of these old workers, letting them do simple cleaning jobs, in order to employ more and better skilled foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should note that this would also reduce their incentive to automate.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On one hand, WIS may boost elder employment; on the other hand, there are some concerns about these seniors in menial jobs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The sight of these seniors, as they shuffle around hunched over, tugs at our heartstrings.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The work may not appear to be heavy but some of the older workers are frail and visibly tired.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are the scenarios which led to many Singaporeans and tourists asking why our Government is not taking care of these poor senior citizens.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are comments that poor Singaporeans have to work to their deaths and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Although these comments do not reflect Singapore’s reality, they are out there.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While there might be some seniors who said that they worked to pass their time, due to the nature of these menial jobs, most people have concerns and reservations.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must also ask ourselves what is the perception our young children have of us as a society when they see frail senior citizens picking up after them, clearing tables and mopping toilets?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps, it is timely for us to re-examine the implications arising from these policies.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): I move on to assistance for workers with low CPF balances.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The consistent returns from the higher interest rates will be of greater help to this group of Singaporeans, many of whom are likely to be freelancers, self-employed or low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If the funding for this means that we have to reduce or even remove the extra interests on the first $60,000 or $30,000 respectively for those with much higher CPF balances, I believe that financially secure Singaporeans will be willing to support this assistance measure.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should step up priority and urgency to scale up food production through both the lease or acquisition of farmland overseas and the adoption of innovative processes.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides requiring support and investments from both the public and private sectors, we have to encourage Singaporeans and residents to join in our "Buy Singapore" movement and help to buy local produce.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Initially, buying local may mean paying a higher price.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But we must continue to support local suppliers and vendors so that when volume picks up, prices would drop correspondingly. "Buy Singapore" will not only help ensure the sustainability of producing local food but also reduce our carbon footprint, contributing to environmental sustainability.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By supporting our Singapore food producers and companies, eventually, they will be able to scale up and go regional or global.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the global pivot to Asia, now the fastest growing region in the world, the time is ripe for Singapore companies to tap into new opportunities and new markets.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to work together to achieve that.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Just as Singapore has welcomed firms from all over the world to partake in our economy, many of our firms have taken a leap of faith and ventured overseas.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Through this, Singapore has become strongly embedded in the global economic order.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Economic growth driven by globalisation has enriched our lives.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We enjoy ever-improving technologies that we would have never deigned to imagine.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: You can now have a face-to-face video conversation with someone residing overseas.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Yet, against the backdrop of these benefits, the need for sustainability is clear.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The world's appetite for consumption far exceeds the rate at which resources can be replenished.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Third, the perpetuation of Singapore's position as a global city.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the Budget speech delivered by the Finance Minister, it is clear that many of our policies are aimed to help SMEs in expanding and thriving.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, I have received feedback on two issues faced by SMEs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, their ability to compete effectively against large-scale enterprises, due to being unable to match their economies of scale.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Second, their abilities to attract and retain talent.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: SMEs have the distinct advantage of being more flexible and adaptable to the needs of customers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: By encouraging them to find gaps in the market and providing the right goods and services to fill these gaps, our SMEs can find respite in competing against their larger counterparts, while developing capabilities in these niche sectors.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: A case in point is a cider company known as Orchard Pig.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Orchard Pig penetrated the UK cider market in 2007 at a time when the market was highly saturated and dominated by large corporations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Orchard Pig provided a product which was more expensive but was more artisan, mischievous and just generally fun.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition, initiatives, such as SkillsFuture, encourage Singaporeans to equip themselves with skills to cope with a changing economy.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are industries which are rife with opportunities.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Yet, these industries have negative stigmas attached to them which have prevented employment of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We can learn from Germany which spares no effort in training its people for blue-collar jobs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In fact, they are so respected that a German political scientist has coined this phenomenon as "blue-collar aristocracy".

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This has allowed the German economy to thrive in terms of quality and has allowed them to compete in the global market on their own terms, not one of lowest cost, but of highest quality.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have an obligation to meet our needs of today without compromising the ability of Singaporeans of tomorrow to meet theirs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: One avenue that we can achieve sustainability in, is the built environment.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
