text: Other cities around the world have introduced policies to incentivise the creation of sustainable built environments.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Interested participants are subjected to third-party independent audits.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: They then execute the recommendations outlined in the audit report.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Upon the implementation of these recommendations, a Sustainable Building Certificate of varying levels of achievement is issued and successful participants become eligible for the aforementioned benefits and can obtain up to a 20% reduction in property taxes.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I urge the Government to adopt the SEC's Green Labelling Scheme and engage independent third-party auditors to assess the BCA's Green Mark Building certification.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This can be further reinforced by introducing pro-sustainability legislation.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I understand that BIM is not seamlessly integrated among developers, consultants, contractors, suppliers and the authorities.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This has resulted in the benefits of BIM not being fully reaped, resulting in stakeholders of construction projects suffering from redundancy.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Furthermore, SMEs face difficulties in adopting BIM due to cost and manpower barriers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I urge BCA to consider shared integrated BIM services to support the industry.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore enjoys her current levels of success due to us positioning ourselves as a global city and acting as a node by which the world may become more connected.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To remain a global city, it is imperative that we pay attention to both our hardware and software.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore must continue to upgrade its hardware through ensuring a world-class infrastructure, high levels of security and a beautiful green environment.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Concurrently, we must ensure that our software, our people, become international, so as to be the means by which we reach out to the world and vice versa.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To maintain our position as a global city, we can learn from fellow global city, Tokyo.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: They intend to use the entire city as a stage showcasing Japanese culture.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The recent Chingay parade is testament to our cultural strength and legacy.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have a rich culture that can, and should be, showcased to the world.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We should learn from Tokyo and utilise international events as platforms by which we promote our culture, and cement our position as a global city.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Another area in which we can learn from Tokyo is extensive and in-depth collaboration with other cities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Bukit Timah had fallen, along with crucial military supplies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The water supply was on the verge of collapse.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Thousands of soldiers wandered aimlessly through the city, dazed and confused.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Collectively, the generals decided that counterattack was impossible.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They went against their orders, to fight to the last man.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The surrender marked one of the biggest military defeats in British history and a big military mystery.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As we commemorate our Bicentennial, it is a good time to reflect on history.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: A close reading of history showed that Singapore was lost not on the defence in the battles of 1941.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore was lost on the planning tables since 1921.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: After World War One (WWI), the British Empire was stretched financially.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The British returned to the gold standard at a high exchange rate, which triggered deflationary monetary and fiscal policies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Wage did not adjust downwards due to union pressure, and British exports became expensive.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For most of the 1920s, the British suffered a depression.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The British military defence budget was cut very deeply until 1935, and her military failed to modernise.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And after WWI, America and Japan competed for dominance in Asia.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In 1922, America forced the British to choose a side.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Britain chose to side with America over Japan, its former ally.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With that, Britain faced a dangerous Japan with a formidable navy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Despite her military weakness, the British must convince Australia and India, then part of the British Empire, that the Far East can be secured, especially so since Australian and Indian troops were needed to protect their Empire's interest in Europe and the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, the British could not afford a Far East navy to counter Japan.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: To make the impossible possible, the British came up with the "Singapore Strategy".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And Singapore must be defended until the arrival of that fleet.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But the implementation of the Singapore Strategy over the next two decades can only be described as fundamentally unsound, as a 20-year sleepwalk towards disaster.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: First, according to historian Brian Farrell, the British never found the money to build a big naval base.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Unfortunately, the British air defence plan was fundamentally unsound as well.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The British air force built a string of airbases to the north without consulting their army.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: While these air bases were close to the South China Sea and the Thai border – areas that they expected the Japanese to invade from – they were situated in indefensible terrain.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And after all this hassle, the British incredibly never found the money to deploy an air force large or sophisticated enough.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: All these meant that the under-strength British Army now had to defend not just the empty naval base in Singapore in the south, but also the under-equipped airbases in the north.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: After the attack on Pearl Harbour, the British stood alone in Malaya and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In the final years before the Japanese invasion, the British did build up the Malayan army to almost three times the size of the invading Japanese army.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But decades are needed to build and sustain a strong defence.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many historians, including Frank Pike, concluded that the large British Malayan army was only capable of fighting fixed-piece battles of WWI, and while there were some good units, even the British official historian Woodburn Kirby concluded that most of these units were raw and unfamiliar with how to fight in the tropics.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, the British army lacked comprehensive intelligence on the Japanese and, therefore, were complacent.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In December 1941, when the Japanese swept down from the north, they destroyed the small obsolete British air force in the north within 100 hours and sank the only two major British ships in the Far East.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They then proceeded to destroy the British Army dispersed throughout Malaya, piecemeal.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They defeated the British at Jitra to win Northern Malaya, overran and dispersed the British at Slim River, outmaneuvered the British at Muar to win the crucial fight for Johor, and reached the gates of Singapore, all within 55 days.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, what can we learn from the Fall of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The obvious answer is that we can only count on ourselves to defend Singapore, regardless of security arrangements with others.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But there are at least three other lessons.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The first lesson is sustained and sufficient defence spending is necessary.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In the case of the British Empire after WWI, they faced a rapidly changing world order with the rise of Japan and Germany.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The rise of air power, use of combined arms, shift from battleships to carriers, all required major investments.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: When the British woke up to the reality in the mid-1930s, it was too late to reverse two decades of military neglect.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The situation for Singapore today is vastly different, but some lessons are still worth noting.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The second lesson is that a nation's security depends on a strong economy and ample fiscal resources to deal with the changing world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In the case of the British Empire, while it thrived in the First Industrial Revolution of steam engines and weaving looms, it failed to transform its economy and fell behind America and Germany in the Second Industrial Revolution of chemicals and cars.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Its misguided monetary and fiscal policy led to deflation and depression.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For an empire where the sun never sets, it never built a diverse and sustainable tax base to pay for its defence.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In short, the world changed dramatically for the British Empire, but it ran out of money to adapt to the changing world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Henry Kissinger recently said, "We are in a very, very grave period for the world", and the current times can only be marked as an "end of an era".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: While there are major global uncertainties ahead, there are ample opportunities for a nimble Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But this requires us to sustain our economy and maintain our fiscal discipline.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But what about our economy in 10 years' time?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: No one can guarantee that our companies can continue to thrive in the face of technology disruption and global competition.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, our companies and people must tap on various programmes and grants, and press on relentlessly to transform.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If we fail to grow our savings over time, when a major storm hits Singapore a decade or two down the road, we may find our financial anchor insufficient to stabilise our economy, which would have grown larger by then.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The third and final lesson is that a successful society requires its people to have shared beliefs rooted firmly in reality.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The British Empire had an unworkable defence plan.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Over two decades, her electorate and leaders failed to robustly debate on whether it was realistic and whether there were sufficient resources to backstop the plan.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore's success to date depends on our people's consensus on what it takes for Singapore to succeed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But the world is increasingly diverse and our people's views mirror this increasing diversity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: To meet tomorrow's challenges, we need to strengthen our shared beliefs in many areas.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, how can we balance giving our youths with the best we can afford, while ensuring that they remain hungry and curious for new opportunities?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How can we persuade our people that keeping Singapore open to the world is to our best collective interest?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How can we continue the unfinished business of tackling inequality while maintaining the core promise of meritocracy?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How can we best represent the causes and values of some, while enlarging the common space for all?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The answer lies in more robust conversations not just between the Government and the people, but also among people of differing viewpoints.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I hope our Government can foster more conversations for our people to air their views, listen to differing opinions, understand the realities that constrain Singapore and achieve a nuanced and shared understanding of our common future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Even in peace and prosperity, it is essential to plan for and act on, the turbulence and uncertainty ahead.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Budget 2019 is best described by the same phrase, "居安思危".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With that, I stand in support of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   	Sir, the MGP has become one of the focal points of this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This generation is certainly deserving of being called the MG, not only because they were born in the 1950s, which was the time when Singapore fought for and achieved Merdeka, followed by self-rule in 1959, but it was because this generation was imbued with the values and spirit of Merdeka.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These values and spirit then cascaded down and were inherited by the generations after them.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As a generation shaped by the values and spirit of Merdeka, this generation should have been prepared to enjoy their golden years, the Merdeka way.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In other words, independently and not having many dependencies.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The process of ageing independently happens when our seniors can retire without depending too much on financial support from their children, siblings and other relatives, and also without depending on assistance from Government bodies and welfare organisations.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Apart from seniors who face difficulties because they are burdened by serious diseases and misfortunes, seniors who undergo ageing independently should be able to take care of themselves or be able to support their own daily expenses in order to live their golden years meaningfully.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We must make changes and adaptations to aspects of healthcare, manpower, social pension, housing policies and policies that are based on gender in order to ensure that our seniors can undergo ageing independently.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is an effort to further address the present gaps in our universal healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If we missed the chance to do so for PG, let us not lose this opportunity to do so for MG.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The MG possesses the values, spirit, concept and realisation of Merdeka.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We can still do something better for MG so that they can be more independent, instead of having many dependencies while living out their golden years.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, this Budget will help us to confront and harness the forces of digital disruption as they interact with demographic shifts, Asia's growing ascendancy in the world economy and subsiding support for globalisation.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, even as the Budget takes into account the critical needs of lower-income households, it also seeks to boost the capabilities of our people and the companies that power our economic transformation.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, different schemes for companies, such as Innovation Agents, SMEs Go Digital and the Automation Support Package are especially welcome.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat also spoke of the need for our people to have the skills, knowledge and aptitude to flourish in our fast-changing and technologising world.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I would like to highlight three critical literacies we must seek to nurture in our people, to help us all better adapt to our rapidly evolving environment.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister had, in fact, raised the need to cultivate cross-cultural literacy among our young so as to broaden our regional and international connections.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me, therefore, to unpack the concept of cross-cultural literacy and how it is more crucial today than ever before.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: To fortify our rich multicultural heritage, we must create more spaces and opportunities for meaningful cross-cultural understanding.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Rather than simply trading in essentialist and simplistic caricatures of different cultures, we need to create forums where people are unafraid to ask tough questions of one another, confront their unconscious biases and dispel long-held misconceptions.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Cross-cultural interactions should be well developed, organised and supported by facilitators, failing which these encounters may create confusion, trigger misunderstandings and, at worst, reinforce stereotypes and prejudices.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Greater cross-cultural literacy can help to forge a more inclusive society where diversity is valued rather than frowned upon.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Efforts to enhance cross-cultural literacy should be introduced not only in schools, but also in community and corporate events so that working adults can benefit as well.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, social ties that are undergirded by greater cross-cultural literacy will be more enduring and resilient.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: They can serve as a bulwark against threats, such as online disinformation campaigns, that seek to foment inter-ethnic discord.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond Singapore, our people must also inculcate a deeper understanding of our neighbours.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Our region boasts of a rich cultural heritage and tremendous growth potential.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: And yet, many young Singaporeans view our regional neighbours as nothing more than holiday destinations.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Many industry leaders I meet increasingly lament that Singaporeans are averse to job postings in the region as they view them as being less glamourous and rewarding than those further afield.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: And yet our region is home to fast-growing markets where there are many inroads to make significant impact.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: To better develop Singapore into a node both within Asia and globally and ensure that our citizens are well placed to tap on such opportunities, our schools from primary through to tertiary levels should make greater efforts to strengthen and deepen our students' appreciation of the region.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has done well in terms of providing access to digital devices and services.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Fortunately, we do not face a significant issue of a digital access divide.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These pertain to managing information, communicating, transacting and maintaining cyber safety.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, how do we ensure that emerging adults from across the socio-economic spectrum are prepared for the job market in terms of knowing how to profile their competencies, utilise job portals, seek online career mentoring and access skills upgrading programmes?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, we may wish to offer digital roadmaps for critical issues that everyone has to deal with.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: For example, how can individuals seek reliable health information online and how can families obtain sound advice on managing household finances?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In my research on parents with school-going children, I found that some parents were daunted by the online homework their children were given and felt deeply insecure about their inability to help their children.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, our digitally-connected world is constantly expanding in complex ways, with an ever-proliferating range of apps, portals, platforms and content.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As far as possible, we must offer signposts to help people navigate their way online and make sense of the deluge of information they encounter.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The final literacy I wish to speak on is ethical literacy.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Whether the solutions to our wicked problems are technologically or socially engineered, they must accord with our values and align with the ethical principles we collectively subscribe to.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Who should be given access to information about whom and for what purpose?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: How do we draw the line between customer-orientation and surveillance?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: When should automated decision-making yield to human judgement?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to it being disseminated across the relevant industry and education sectors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is generous healthcare support for Singaporeans with chronic illnesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: MG gets additional healthcare benefits among other perks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Low-income salary workers have an increased income cap and enhanced workfare bonus.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bicentennial Bonus brings additional monetary perks for the different groups of Singaporeans, and there are tax rebates for all.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also a Budget to chart a steady course in uncertain times and prepare for the future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Indeed, restructuring is the key to doing well in the future economy, and this Budget builds on the principles and key features of past Budgets to improve the lives of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   	On the issue of ageing in Singapore, with reference to MG, apart from the proposals mentioned by Mr Faisal Manap, our Budget for 2019 has also provided various packages for senior citizens as well as MG and the families of these seniors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These include PAssion card top-ups that were provided in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, there are already various packages in this Budget for those who have reached their golden years, other than those proposed by Mr Faisal Manap.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, for this Budget, besides the MGP that we have put forward, there are also active ageing activities for seniors that have been established by the Government for the long term.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): In English, please, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the last decade, our expenditure has grown correspondingly to the population's needs and it will only keep growing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We will have to fund our needs in a fiscally sustainable way to achieve all our objectives.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Certainly, we have to be ambitious in the face of many challenges.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Arguably, the most ambitious dimension that this Budget, and many to follow, has to address pertains to the daunting socio-economic challenges derived from rapidly greying demographics and inequality.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Of the two, inequality is a multidimensional and complex problem that needs to be examined more closely.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Finance Minister's allusion to social mobility is a critical precondition to tackling this problem.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To be sure, by definition, one of the main purposes of the Budget is clearly redistribution.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But we must go beyond to address the true underlying causes of inequality.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Short-term redistribution of wealth is not only unhelpful for the future generations, but it inadvertently increases social tensions when it devolves into a zero-sum game tug-of-war between the haves and have-nots.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Already, some people are asking, "Can you do more for the middle-income group?" "What about those who don't have jobs?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They can't even benefit from WIS." These are perfectly valid concerns, but there are other long-term measures to address these.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: After all, the ultimate goal of inclusive fiscal policies is not merely some variant of Robin Hood-type of social transfers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Instead, a holistic approach to inequality is incomplete without an ecosystem of measures and programmes to improve social mobility, which is a far more potent catalyst of socio-economic progress than welfare.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To this end, there is a repletion of programmes to serve every need, from individuals to businesses, children to elderly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Built upon the pre-existing system of high-quality, heavily subsidised public education, these will improve one's chances of climbing up the career or economic ladder.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But these schemes are merely the start of a long journey on battling inequality, a pervasive problem across many developed countries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One can reasonably expect that further enhancements in coming Budgets will be inevitable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Most of the time, focus has been on the vertical dimension of inequality – between the rich and the poor – and the Budget is one good example where we tax the better off ones and we distribute to the needy segments, hopefully, well-distributed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But there are important horizontal dimensions as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the Gini coefficient or the top 1% income share, people appear anonymously, but we may be concerned with how unequal income is across various groups, such as by gender, location or even ethnicity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Budget and previous Budgets have aimed to address these horizontal dimensions in various ways.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I feel more can be done to address some of these horizontal dimensions – earlier, in terms of generational, but now, in terms of social and educational dimensions to narrow gaps as much as we can.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One way to narrow gaps in terms of social and educational dimensions is to increase spending on the ITE segment of the student population.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We already have a very established system for the conventional post-secondary route consisting of junior colleges and polytechnics.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Enhancements in the ITE education programme is something more recent.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that despite the myriad of financial assistance programmes available for ITE students, poor time management and prioritising of resources are one reason for some students to fall behind in their studies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, I know of a young boy who worked two jobs while studying because of financial woes in the family.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He does not blame his lack of finances, but he regrets his poor time management which has effectively rendered his two years in ITE a waste of time because he skipped classes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Last I am aware, he was working hard on his internship, hoping to do well enough to improve his Grade Point Average and qualify for entry into the polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think there are many such students who, at their young age, feel lost, and entered ITE as a last resort and squandered away their time and resources.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By the time they recognise the opportunities and potential provided by the school, it is a bit late.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope a proactive approach can be taken to counsel students, particularly new admissions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Teach them how to manage their resources, help them to apply for the necessary financial help, and follow up on their progress.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This hands-on approach would need extra manpower resources and skilled ones at that.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have also heard anecdotally that a rising number of special needs students are admitted to IHLs, in particular ITEs, to further their education and obtain gainful employment upon graduation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How many of these students were able to graduate and take on fulfilling work on their own terms?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we do more to increase SEN student enrolment in IHLs, particularly in ITEs, as some have demonstrated potential for vocational studies?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Every student matters in a country where labour force growth is low.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   	Singapore is a small nation with a small market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But we are well-positioned for research, innovation and enterprise opportunities on a regional and global level.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have many global and regional partnerships, and we also have a good reputation for efficient and reliable services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It makes sense for Singaporeans to venture overseas to find success.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In doing so, they may also create more jobs and opportunities for other Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This also benefits the high-growth Singapore firms which will receive support to send their local employees for overseas postings.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, this Global Ready programme has a good premise, and I hope that it can be expanded to include regional placements in a wider variety of sectors and to include mid-career switchers who may not want to leave their industry entirely but would like to try a different market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By encouraging Singaporeans to seize opportunities to explore, especially in the ASEAN region, this will also help facilitate collaborations within ASEAN which are beneficial for the economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With great pleasure, I would like to share about some of our Malay/Muslim businesses which have found success in the region.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Positano Risto came up with the unique proposition for a halal Italian restaurant in Singapore in 2017, and they have since opened an additional outlet in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Adrianna Yariqa has been selling modest attire fused with modern and traditional elements for Malay men and women since 2014, and they have expanded to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another firm, Enercon Engineering Pte Ltd, which specialises in power control solutions, has offices in Singapore and the Philippines, and supports businesses in Malaysia and Taiwan.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For instance, JumainSataysfaction has spread its wings to Japan in halal food manufacturing, as did Versafleet in the technological transport management solutions sector in the region.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Malaysia, as Members can see, is a popular choice for expansion, because not only are they close by and have a large population of Muslims, but also because when local businesses make headway in one country, they pave the way for other Singaporean businesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Through networking and sharing of experiences among businesses expanding to the same countries, they can help one another to grow.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, next, I want to talk about helping small savers to grow their income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The debate about distribution of wealth and inequality tends to focus on large fortunes at the top.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But the redistribution of wealth is as much about encouragement of small savings at the bottom as it is about the restriction of the excesses at the top.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is just as important to encourage small savings at the bottom, rather than harping on restriction of excesses at the top.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The rich get richer because they have ample funds to invest, benefit from high interest rates and grow their portfolios and assets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The low-income has less money to risk, and some also lack the financial savviness.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One suggestion is to address the current low interest rate environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: CPF offers relatively high interest rates for members, but not all have sufficient money in their accounts to take advantage of it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The high interest rates would motivate people to save up, without restricting the use of the funds in times of need.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This could also raise the awareness about the positive characteristics of the Singapore Savings Bond to the general public.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I applaud this approach as I have expressed my suggestions on this in my previous Budget response last year, to ensure intergenerational equity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is important to make sure that intergenerational burden is allocated properly to the generation benefiting from the large infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, when planning a long-term project, be it infrastructure or social, it is important to follow individual lifetimes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The future is unpredictable, and there may be significant inequality between generations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Just because the real incomes are rising over time does not necessarily mean that those born later enjoy higher lifetime incomes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Inflation, increased costs of living and so on could have a major impact on livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the UK and the US, there is growing observation of millennials living with their parents because they cannot afford their own homes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This appears to be a trend in developed economies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Thankfully, we do not have such issues here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Governments have the tendency to apply a social discount rate to long-term projects.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Part of it reflects the expectation that future generations will be better off, and so a lower valuation is attached to the better off when measuring inequality at a point in time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, as the economic situation in various developed economies has reflected, this is a dangerous mindset we have to steer clear of.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We risk increasing income inequality for the future generations otherwise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The matter of taxes is also something to contemplate while on the topic of intergenerational equity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As an ageing population that is gearing towards automation, the amount of income taxes collected is expected to decrease along with the number of people in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What happens if the taxable population remains low?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is a huge burden for future generations to bear, especially if they are not doing so well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is important that we examine whether these additional taxes will enhance or deteriorate the progressivity of the overall tax framework, especially for the lowest income households.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, impose a 10% tax on purchase of goods in the luxury tier or fine dining at a restaurant, and a much lower tax like 3% on basic necessities like rice.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, increase tax rebates for social causes, and instead of paying taxes, the wealthy may choose to donate to causes they care about.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To sum up, Mr Deputy Speaker, Budget 2019 manages the tough and delicate balancing act of being sufficiently counter-cyclical, appropriately strategic and unwaveringly committed to tackling structural challenges posed by ageing and economic transformation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Looking forward, we should continue focusing on increasing social mobility and measured tax solutions to resolve the inequality problem.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While there were positive results, my concerns have remained unchanged from 2017 when the diesel excise tax was introduced.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, my concern is that while we care about environmental resiliency, we may be doing this at the expense of economic resiliency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Diesel is the common fuel for most taxis, public and private buses, delivery vans, pickups, lorries and many other different types of heavy vehicles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, such rebates are really short-term measures and, ultimately, operators and owners will face the full effect of the price increase for their businesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They will have to pass the increases to their customers downstream sooner or later.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In short, this diesel tax increase will mean an increase in transportation expenses, which will translate to higher costs for all kinds of businesses in Singapore requiring directly or indirectly transportation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Until all public buses are converted to electric ones, diesel tax increase will raise the operating costs of our Public Transport Operators (PTOs).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will that lead to fare increase again at some point?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why penalise taxi drivers who do not own the taxis they drive?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How soon can the taxi fleet be converted to hybrids or even to the use of fully electric cars for taxis?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While environmental concerns are understandable, and while the Minister can talk about some car owners and taxi companies switching to hybrids, the vast majority of existing vehicles using diesel have no other options for an immediate switch at the moment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the message that the Government wants to send is that diesel is bad for our environment, what are the hybrid or fully electric options that the Government is providing at this moment for users to switch to non-diesel vehicles, especially beyond cars and taxis?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If electric or hybrid options are not realistically available en masse now, the tax will just perpetuate the continuing operation of diesel vehicles with the owners paying more into the state coffers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And that does not really help the environment either.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The increase in diesel tax will only increase the cost for businesses, especially our SMEs, in an economic climate that is not rosy at all.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whether we are talking about commuters taking public buses, workers or students taking chartered buses to work or school, delivery vehicles sending goods and food, and so on, ultimately, the diesel tax raise will just increase our cost of living, diminishing our economic resiliency at a time where we may ill-afford to.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another part where our resiliency is being tested is in our aerospace industry.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In last year’s Ministry of Transport's (MOT’s) Committee of Supply (COS) speech, the then Second Minister for Transport Ng Chee Meng shared with this House exciting plans for the proposed building of Changi Airport T5 and the development of Changi East.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister spoke of it being, I quote, "a bold move to cement Changi Airport’s position as a premier air hub for the future" and that "it is critical our aviation sector can continue to grow and support the growing needs of our economy".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are told that the scale and complexity of the project are unprecedented: new runways, new terminals, network of tunnels and systems, in short, "a game changer" and "a mega terminal with satellite terminals".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government even decided that it would foot the majority of the costs of building which will be expected to cost tens of billions of dollars.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As of last year, $9 billion has been spent.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I cannot agree more that these are exciting developments for our Changi Airport, for Singapore as an international as well as regional air hub, and with good prospects.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I am concerned whether recent announcements from Malaysia will affect our plans and, more importantly, the future of our air hub.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that it will take back its air traffic control service arrangements over Southern Johor.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over our southern border, there has also been media reports of Indonesia demanding to take back its delegated airspace over the Riau Islands Flight Information Region.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am certainly concerned with the possible effects of our neighbours taking back their delegated airspaces on: one, Singapore as a major air hub; two, Singapore’s aerospace industry; and three, the development and future viability of Changi T5 and Changi East.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are our aerospace ambitions sufficiently resilient against such uncertainties and potential shocks?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The tests of resilience also extend to our port and maritime sectors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat mentioned in his speech that the British decision to declare Singapore a free port plugged us into an emerging network of global trade.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, this is also the bicentennial of the modern port of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this bicentennial year, it is noteworthy that over the last 200 years, as different businesses and industries rose and fell, our port has remained one constant key to Singapore's survival and prosperity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has, in fact, grown from strength to strength, thanks to our strategic location and those who have worked hard over 200 years to keep Singapore port in its position today.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last year, in my Budget Debate speech, I spoke of the challenges to our port and asked how long we can continue to enjoy our advantages.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I mentioned of challenges from the Arctic or Northern Sea Route and the Malacca Port.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At MOT's COS Debate last year, the long talked about possibility of a canal across the Kra Isthmus in Thailand was brought up briefly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In face of changing leadership in Thailand and the new Asian political landscape, it is uncertain whether the long talked about project can be resisted indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Besides monitoring developments, are we doing any forward scenario planning and how are we going to deal with such a possibility?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Similarly, I asked how many of our SMEs are in a position to compete in the liquified natural gas and offshore renewables identified in the ITM for marine and offshore engineering?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Besides these areas, what are the future options they should be prepared for?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In these still difficult market conditions, how are our ITMS helping our maritime SMEs beyond the categories which have already been talked about?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope we can receive an update on these either here or at the COS debate later.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Overcoming tests of economic resiliency may not ultimately help our citizenry if there is no country to begin with.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This underlines the importance of our security resiliency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat stressed in his speech the importance of keeping safe and secure and justifying that our spending is significant but indispensable.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He mentioned that a strong Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) remains a bulwark against threats to our way of life.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While our spending on SAF's military equipment and hardware may be important to keep our potential adversaries at bay, our SAF, though led at the highest levels by full-time regulars, is largely a conscript force.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While equipment, hardware and spending may be important, for SAF to succeed in its defence objectives, the buy-in from our Full-time National Servicemen (NSFs) and NSmen is absolutely critical.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister has said that National Service has forged a deep understanding in our people that each and every one of us has the duty to defend our nation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This ought to be the case, but it is something we can ill afford to assume or take for granted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is something we must always continue to strive to achieve and maintain.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In my view, it is a constant work-in-progress.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we expect our NSFs and NSmen to take their NS training and call-ups seriously and do their utmost, they will need to be convinced that the training they do is necessary and that both the SAF as well as their commanders, especially senior commanders, not just their NSmen commanders, must be able to command their confidence and respect.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Equally, our NSFs and NSmen and, indeed, their families, too, must have absolute confidence in both the SAF and their commanders taking responsibility for their men's welfare and training safety while balancing the equally important objective of operational readiness.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This buy-in may be easier said than done and we need to enhance our current efforts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we are at our Bicentennial, I look to our forefathers over the last 200 years who have displayed tremendous resilience to recover from adversity and build Singapore to what it is today.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The hope is that we can continue to ace the tests of resiliency that come our way as a people.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   	Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, the MGP appears to be the highlight of this Budget.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The generation being honoured truly deserves to be named MG.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not because they happened to be born in the 1950s, just as Singapore fought and got its Independence, beginning with self-rule in 1959, but because this generation was imbued with the spirit of independence and imparted the spirit of independence to future generations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a generation who embodied and imparted the spirit of independence, the Merdekas should be enabled to age with independence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ageing with independence is the ability of our seniors to retire on their own, with as little financial dependence as possible on their children, siblings and other family members, and also on the Government and welfare organisations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Except for incidents of serious illness and accidents, seniors ageing with independence will be able to care for themselves or pay for the care that they require to lead purposeful golden years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, we should work towards this goal for all our seniors, both now and in future.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need and we should calibrate our healthcare, manpower, social pension, housing and gender policies to make sure all our seniors, both now and in future, age with independence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Workers’ Party has five proposals to enable our seniors to age with independence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ageing with independence is ageing with dignity for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we have missed our chances with the Pioneers, we should not miss this opportunity with the Merdekas and all future generations of seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is important that we focus on economic growth as this is linked to our ability to create good jobs for Singaporeans, generate resources for our social and security needs, and provide opportunities for future generations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) and MOM will address these issues more fully during our COS debates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This will impact industries like accommodation, information and communications, food services, retail and professional services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I will also discuss how the Government, employers and workers can jointly tackle the challenges going forward.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In particular, I want to highlight a well-written editorial by Zaobao on 22 February, which presented the tradeoffs clearly and explained why the tightening is necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In fact, the S Pass numbers are the highest we have seen in the last five years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The editorial hit the nail on the head by observing that if the total number of foreign workers rises too quickly, it will affect the employment outcomes of local workers and lead to sociopolitical problems in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have seen this happen in other countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Indeed, this is the key reason why the Government proceeded with the DRC tightening.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We knew it would be painful for the affected companies, and we agonised over this difficult decision during our many rounds of inter-Ministry discussions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On balance, we decided that it was better to make a move now to moderate the overall number of foreign workers in Singapore before the problem gets out of hand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As the Zaobao editorial said, the DRC tightening is necessary bitter medicine, "治本的苦口良药".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are aware that many companies in the Services sector are facing labour constraints, and some have started to invest in productivity improvements by adopting technology and re-engineering their processes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Denise Phua and Mr Douglas Foo spoke about this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our economic agencies like ESG and the Singapore Tourism Board have been working closely with the companies and industry associations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I attend regular dialogues with our companies, including sessions organised by NTUC in my capacity as Adviser to U-SME.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: My colleagues and I also visit Services sector companies and witness first-hand how they have been working hard to implement productivity measures and upskill their workers through SkillsFuture training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The hard work is starting to bear fruit and we need to keep it up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the accommodation industry, for example, total manpower declined by about 1% between 2013 to 2018, even though total room stock increased by 4% during the same period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These positive results were due to our companies’ efforts to innovate, upskill their workers and adopt progressive work practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: What I shared above are the average numbers for each industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We can expect some companies to be above and some companies to be below these averages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But the outcomes show that our productivity measures are producing results.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The key now is how to spread these efforts and benefit more companies, and for the more successful ones to eventually scale up and expand overseas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with business leaders and Members like Mr Seah Kian Peng and Ms Jessica Tan who cautioned that technology is not a silver bullet and cannot completely replace the need for human workers, especially in customer service roles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Technology is a tool and an enabler, and what results we achieve ultimately depends on how well we use the tool.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But we also know that in the current operating environment, it is important for all companies – big or small, traditional or modern – to have a good understanding of technology and what it can do to improve their products, reduce costs and enhance service quality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Otherwise, you risk being overtaken by your competitors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Technology is not everything, but if you do not make good use of technology, there are many things you cannot achieve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will work with industry associations to reach out to their members and enhance the support we provide to companies that want to transform their operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will also extend enhanced support under the PSG and EDG, keeping the maximum co-funding by the Government at 70% to support enterprise transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Under MTI’s Pro-Enterprise Panel, we work with industry associations and companies to review Government rules and regulations, to support new business ideas and look for ways to reduce licensing costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Using this approach, we made several rule changes over the past months which have been welcomed by our enterprises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are more changes in the pipeline, including a project to simplify the licensing requirements for food services companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We understand that the transformation journey for our companies can be a daunting and difficult challenge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Government agencies and industry associations will walk this journey together with you – this is our commitment to our companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If you want to transform and you are willing to put in the effort to do so, we will help you.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Let us work together to have a pro-enterprise, pro-worker economy, where we can continue to achieve economic growth to provide good jobs for our workers and a good life for our people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: (In Mandarin):   I am heartened that business owners and workers across various sectors have been working hard to raise productivity and transform their enterprises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Take our homegrown F&B company Jumbo Group as an example.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Last year, I went on a tour of Jumbo's new central kitchen facility and saw how the company has automated its production of sauces and soup bases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Besides reducing Jumbo's labour requirements, this has allowed for better quality control in the production process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Jumbo also developed a mobile app to facilitate short-term job placements, which has helped to alleviate manpower shortages during peak periods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Heartland shops can also adopt technology solutions with support from ESG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ngee Soon Jewellery is an example of a company that has managed to do so successfully.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The system also minimises human error and improves the accuracy of stocktaking.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ngee Soon’s staff can, therefore, devote more time and attention to serving customers and generating sales.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is our commitment to the business community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Let us stand united, press on in the face of any challenges and work together to build a pro-enterprise, pro-worker Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I may need a little bit more time, Sir.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Seniors who go to polyclinics get additional subsidies compared to other patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, it is not quite accurate for Assoc Prof Daniel Goh to describe it as Singaporeans pay for one another, Government saves money.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Actually, Government pays quite a bit of the premiums through premium subsidies and additional premium support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The same principle is applied for CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are premium subsidies, there is also additional premium support, and these are part of the design of the scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will be enhancing the coverage of CHAS to benefit even more Singaporeans, especially for chronic care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In our hospitals, in our Specialist Outpatient Clinics (SOCs), in our nursing homes, there are also structural subsidies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These are means-tested because we want to give more help to lower- and middle-income Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When we introduce packages that are cohort-based, like the PGP and MGP, these are on top of the structural subsidies that are already provided in the system for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Pritam Singh claimed that the MGP gives off a pungent odour of an unfair advantage for the electoral prospects of the People's Action Party.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Now, I wonder why the Workers' Party chose to use such an unpleasant description and to focus on politicising this tribute to our MGs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Opposition calls for the Government to give more, and yet when the Government gives more to help Singaporeans, the Workers' Party criticises the move as an election tactic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Please make up your mind and decide where you stand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is also to show our heartfelt appreciation to our MGs for their sacrifices and contributions to Singapore during the early years of our nation-building.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, let us not diminish the significance of the PGP and MGP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is misleading to link these packages to election cycles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have explained this point before in the House, but let me say it again, because Mr Pritam Singh brought it up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And then you set them aside, the surpluses that you have accumulated, to fund the PGP and MGP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: You cannot do this at the start of the term because you do not know at that point how much surpluses you are going to have and how much surpluses you can set aside to fund these packages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is part of the design of our system for financial prudence and sustainability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To look after our current generation as well as future generations, we must plan for the long term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And this is what a responsible Government needs to do, to ensure that our policies and programmes are financially sustainable for the current and future generations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: What is the size of the bill, where are the funds coming from, how do we achieve maximum value for money, these are important questions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: What we can provide for future cohorts of Singaporeans and how much resources we have to invest in our people and to continue to rejuvenate our communities, our infrastructure, these will depend on whether Singapore continues to have constructive politics, good Government, strong economy and a cohesive society.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I support the broad principles highlighted by the Finance Minister which Budget 2019 was formulated upon.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: First, universal support and cohort-based support schemes like the Pioneer Generation Package (PGP) and Merdeka Generation Package (MGP); second, investing in our future; and third, why we should have a Climate Change Bill.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: First, like many of us in this House, my parents belong to the Pioneer Generation (PG).

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I have many relatives and friends who belong to the Merdeka Generation (MG).

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Both the PG and MG lived through turbulent times of our nation-building.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They have worked hard and built this nation so that the subsequent generations that follow will have a much better future.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, I belong to the next cohort, which Mr Murali Pillai had referred to as the Majulah Generation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But we were coined the Post-Independence Generation when we first came into this House.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The next cohort consists of those born in 1960 to 1969, which includes Mr Speaker yourself, too.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I do agree with Assoc Prof Daniel Goh that the MG and PG have taught us independence.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: That is the reason why I think Independence Generation is a much better name than the Majulah Generation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We all want our PG and MG seniors to enjoy their golden years and age graciously and peacefully.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: All seniors aged 60 and above can apply for a senior citizen concession card.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But is it practical and realistic for the Government or for this House to propose and implement such a health scheme?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Is it sustainable, given our ageing population and the growing numbers of people in this age group over the next few years?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Cohort-based schemes like PGP and MGP are targeted at the needs of these cohorts.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As explained during the launch of PGP, this cohort has contributed to our nation-building during difficult and challenging times.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many did not have proper education and good job opportunities.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They worked hard to support their families and did not have sufficient savings for retirement and healthcare because Central Provident Fund (CPF) and MediSave schemes were not implemented yet.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The package was tailored to their needs and targeted at the concerns they have.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As it is today, we do have a universal health scheme.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: One may go to the Ministry of Health (MOH) website to enquire about the subsidies they can enjoy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If you key in 60 years old, which means your year of birth was 1959, and key in that you are Singaporean, the website will show 15 health schemes that you may get subsidy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: These 15 schemes are MediShield Life, CareShield Life, MediSave, Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS), ElderShield, MediFund, subsidies for services and drugs at Public Healthcare Institutions, Enhanced Screen for Life, Interim Disability Assistance Programme for the Elderly, Foreign Domestic Worker (FWD) levy concession for persons with disabilities, Seniors' Mobility and Enabling Fund, Caregivers Training Grant, Elder Fund, Foreign Domestic Work Grant, and Subsidies for Government-funded intermediate and long-term care services.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Primary healthcare in polyclinics is heavily subsidised and they are not means-tested.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Likewise, subsidised healthcare at public hospitals is also affordable to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: For those who are not able to afford, medical social workers are there to assist and there is always MediFund.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, no Singaporean will be deprived of the medical care they need.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There are also some who asked whether the next generation that follows, that is, those who are currently 50 to 59 years old, will get a similar package when we reach 60, which is in 10 years' time.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many of us and I in this House belong to this generation, the Independence Generation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Our generation, in fact, has already received a much bigger and better package than the previous two generations.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Those in our generation were given better education, better job opportunities, better housing, better healthcare, better transport and a better Singapore by PG and MG.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Like the previous two generations, our generation have worked hard and contributed.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We grew up in a more stable and prosperous Singapore, were able to save more for our retirement and medical needs compared to the preceding two generations.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There is an important difference between a cohort-based scheme and a permanent scheme, that is, sustainability.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In another five to 10 years, the new future government, if it is prudent and capable, may see an Independence Generation Package that will cater to our needs at that point in time.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Human resource is the only and most important resource Singapore has.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Development of human resources through education and upskilling is the key.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Currently, formal education – primary and secondary school education – is heavily subsidised.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Hence, parents only pay monthly standard miscellaneous fees of $6.50 and $5 monthly school fees for secondary school.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Hence, it does not have the support given.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Upskilling and upgrading all Singaporeans for the future is important.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: After education and upskilling, it is important that wages have to be increased to improve their lives.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
