text: There are many countries with a Minimum Wage but few countries with WIS.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Are there low-wage workers who did not benefit from WIS?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: My last topic will be on climate change.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We have been educating our population on the greenhouse effect, carried out various campaigns, engaged transport operators, businesses and corporations and factories to get their buy-in.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But we do not have a Climate Change Bill.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In the United Kingdom (UK), before the Climate Change Act became law, the UK was struggling to meet its very unambitious emission reduction targets.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In other words, it aimed to increase ambition and to ensure that ambition was met.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There are many countries, for example, Sweden, where the Climate Change Act contains provisions on the government's climate policy, what the work will be aimed at and how it should be conducted; Norway where the Climate Change Act offers a framework to promote the implementation of Norway’s climate targets as part of the transition to a low carbon society in Norway in 2050.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In Asia, closer to home, Japan's Climate Change Adaptation Act aims at enhancing adaptation efforts in Japan.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It enshrines into law the 2015 National Adaptation Plan and sets updated obligations.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Even Malaysia has announced in December last year that they are drafting a Climate Change Act which will contain adaptation and mitigation plans to climate change.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It would develop a list of comprehensive risk analytic simulating scenarios in the face of a rise in global temperatures of 2oC.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Meanwhile, Scotland, too, acknowledged the warning of rising global temperatures and, last year, they sought advice to further enhance it.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, in Scotland, their ministers are legally required to seek expert advice on the earliest achievable date for a net-zero target at least every five years.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Why do we not have a Climate Change Act?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can the Government share what percentage of our energy used can be harnessed from renewable sources?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will the Government consider giving incentives to private property owners to install solar panels like many other countries do?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Also, what percentage of recyclable waste that was collected for recycling actually get recycled?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I noticed from a documentary recently that it was a dismal 50%, which means that the other 50% was disposed of as waste.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will the National Environment Agency (NEA) do more public education on this and teach residents to separate the different recyclable wastes rather than to treat the recycling bins as dustbins?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Perhaps, we may have to review the current design of the recycling bin at the Housing and Development Board (HDB) estates, which has just one large opening, and looks almost like a normal trash bin.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Why not have them designed with separate small openings for each type of recyclables, like the ones along Orchard Road?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Lastly, what is our plan to adopt the use of hybrid electric cars?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will the Government take the lead to install more charging points around different parts of Singapore?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) consider hardcoding this requirement in all buildings, including new HDB estates?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, I hope the Government can develop more concrete measures to create a culture of environmental-consciousness in our country.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But, how many Singaporeans take a strong interest in what the Budget is and discuss how each Budget impacts the future state of the country?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: A few days ago, I overheard a conversation between two individuals about Budget 2019.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Mr X asked Mr Y, "Have you checked out the Budget calculator and see what benefits you get?" Mr Y replied, "Not yet, I roughly heard some things about it, but seems there are no benefits for me or my family." Such a conversation may sound familiar to some.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It indicates a lack of interest about the Budget or the only association they can have with the Budget is a measure of one-off monetary benefits.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The underlying message is worrisome, that the Budget is nothing more than a bag of benefits that serves some people in one year or the other.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As we chart our way forward and work towards an inclusive society, this is an increasingly pertinent topic to address.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I believe it is time for us to define who we are, what we can do as one country and what we hope the future Singapore to be.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While some issues can be addressed with short-term fixes, the future state of the country requires longer-term strategies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And this big picture, the end state, must be defined and built together with the citizens and the Government.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We need participants, not bystanders, in the process.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Singapore has a growing ageing population, the external environment is more dynamic and disruptive and future scenarios are more unpredictable; these are all facts and norms of the new age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For Singapore to rise above the challenges and ensure every citizen has a place in this country, we should take a hard look at what it takes to be inclusive.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How can we be inclusive unless it is consciously built into our policies, ingrained as a culture and as individuals, we think and walk them like a way of life.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To me, building social capital and civic participation is key.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In this process, the concept of sharing is fundamental – sharing of wealth, sharing of people and available resources.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Let us begin by looking at what areas we need to improve on to achieve a more equitable distribution of resources.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Those with the wealth are not only on a better footing to accumulate more but they have even better access to resources that help preserve their wealth.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To reduce the wealth inequality gap in Singapore, we tax through personal income, property and consumption.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This way, the top earners and those with more assets contribute.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To further encourage those who have more to give, the tax-deductible donation scheme was implemented.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Compared globally, Singapore has a low personal income tax rate.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But with a shrinking and ageing workforce, it is impractical to consider further taxes on income.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: After all, the ability of an average income worker to build wealth is dependent on sheer labour.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Also, the consumption tax, in one way or another, does impact the lower-income group to meet their basic living expenses.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) and transport vouchers, Silver Support Scheme and other subsidies given to the lower-income group do help to defray some of their costs but, overall, consumption taxes indirectly do raise the general cost of living.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In order to maintain fiscal prudence, we need new revenue sources to sustain the many programmes that may have a long tail in the years ahead.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In the spirit of giving and sharing, will the ultra-high net worth individuals be willing to share more of their wealth to uplift the vulnerable and less privileged communities?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Another case in point is the wages of the low-income workers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Many of these workers are hired in domestically focused industries like cleaning, security and landscaping.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I have come across my own residents in these sectors, and they work very long hours to ensure their income can meet the family’s expenses.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For these individuals, we cannot expect they would have the luxury of time to upkeep and have upgrading of their skills, or even to further define their career path for the long run.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Over time, they are the ones who are disadvantaged by us.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The Government has implemented multiple targeted schemes in larger quantum like ComCare, GST rebate, transport vouchers, education funds and so on to continue assisting this low-income group.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: There are also donations of cash in kind from the public and the voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) to them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I feel that to effectively make a difference that impacts and uplifts the lower-percentile group, in particular, those younger families, giving them access to resources, especially a decent living wage, so that each worker at the end of the month would have more to spare, is actually more critical.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We cannot continue this path of racing to the last dollar for the value of contracts, asking for more productivity from these workers without paying for tools or environment that aid their productivity improvement, assigning more tasks to them when we can do some on our own, something even as simple as clearing our own plates and trays after a meal.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Employers, too, have a fair share to play in this as they balance their profits, reinvest in the workers and give the workers a decent wage to begin with.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is not how large or small the action is, but what we are willing to do and to what extent to effect the change.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This comes back to the basic question of sharing.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The top and middle tiers of the economy, whilst they have more opportunities and pathways to elevate, they can certainly do more for the lower-income group, starting with a willingness to pay more for their services.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Our mindset and actions around this issue ultimately reflect the values of this country and its people.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Another area that I wish to highlight is the need for knowledge transfer between the inter-generations and within the working class.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Knowledge sharing is a very important resource in any organisation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: When we exchange information, skills and expertise, it not only creates awareness of expectations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It also serves to update the workforce of changes within the workplace and, consequently, trains the people.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Any organisation, and a country for that matter, which has a culture of sharing, will achieve better results of faster response time, better coordination and diversity in solutions to their problems.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I do not doubt that millennials are learning and will develop the different new skillsets to meet the future workplace demands.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But in all businesses, there are some fundamentals in people and business management that will always be relevant across time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: These are the key aspects of operating a business beyond data analytics, automation and a technology app.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As we put focus on the structural aspects of the industry transformation maps (ITMs), let us not forget the need to step up on our mentorship guidance and the cross-industry functional knowledge exchange.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Countries with longer histories than Singapore are facing the same issue.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But all these will only continue to be chatters unless we, as a country, as the people of this little red dot, begin to acknowledge that we must all play a part and take actions in our daily lives to make Singapore an inclusive country.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If we cannot convince ourselves to demonstrate the intrinsic values of this country, our future Budget debates and conversation with the public will be nothing more than package subsidies, Net Investment Return Contributions (NIRC) and incremental shifts in our economy and trade.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Not that these are unimportant, but they will not move the needle nor set the long-term direction of our country.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And without building our social capital now, defining the values and roles of this country with active civic participation, each Budget will only fall on the ears of citizens like a lecture in class and endless debate of whose rightful duty it is to care for the ageing population and the future generations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: My cousin had told her not to go to the polling centre since she walks slowly, with a limp.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She jumped and said, "You have no idea how important Government is.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is the best Government in the world.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am going to vote." Needless to say, she got her way.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: My grandmother and her generation of Pioneers as well as subsequent generations of Singaporeans witnessed what the Government had done for the country and the people, and they trusted our leaders.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They had faith in what the country can achieve together – people and Government hand-in-hand.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This trust has been built up over the last 50, 60 years by successive People's Action Party (PAP) governments.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is what made my grandmother's generation feel grateful for a good government.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In this day and age when trust in governments worldwide has been declining, we have to continuously strive to ensure that trust in our Government is not and will not be eroded.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But I still want to repeat it because it is important.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Once lost, it is difficult to bring back.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Unfortunately, in the last few months, a spate of accidents and incidents have grabbed the headlines and shaken this confidence in our Government.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I do not need to repeat them all but there are two I wish to mention as they are of concern to my residents.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: When it was reported that MediShield Life only paid $4.50 out of a $4,500 bill, it was quite a shock.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some of my residents thought that there had been a big mistake.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Worse still, that the Government was trying to cover up or sweep the matter under the carpet.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am glad that MOH and the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) members have come out quickly to explain.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: If it was a mistake, just make things right again.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: If it was a misunderstanding or a special case, let us lay out the facts to the people.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: At the end of the day, if we provide a proper explanation to the people, they will understand, and they can be reassured that MediShield Life does work as intended.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: If we do not do that, there would be lingering doubts on what the Government had said about MediShield Life, and this is not good for the Government because trust and confidence will be gradually eroded.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But the fact is that our people also tend not to pay attention to things that concern them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For example, when I asked them what is the price of water and how much it costs if you drink two litres of water for 365 days, no one got it right.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Therefore, it is understandable that when social media circulated that the Government shifted the payout age for the CPF Retirement Sum Scheme to 70, people thought they had missed some announcement.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But it does show that we should work harder at our communication and make it more easily understood.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some Government agencies no longer have counter services or, perhaps, they are inadequate.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some seniors and even blue-collar persons aged 40 and above, who are not so comfortable with the Internet, still require face-to-face explanations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For example, give people an option to book an appointment at age 65 to meet a CPF officer.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is like buying an insurance annuity, the customer service should explain the details to the citizens.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We cannot afford to have our people confused, then their trust and confidence in our Government would be affected.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We must create opportunities and encourage our schools, families, grandparents to share stories to remember our past and not to take our current peace and prosperity for granted.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Last year, when I chaired the River Hongbao Organising Committee, I was showing my Parliamentary colleagues around and a man in his 40s came up and said "I saw the exhibition in the news.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: After looking at the old 3-room flat mockup and remembering my past, I came out and looked around at the skyscrapers and I am grateful.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Pointing to his primary school daughter next to him, he said, "She does not know how I am feeling.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This year, the exhibition was taken to greater heights with an informative exhibition of our history.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As this is only the beginning of our celebrations, I hope that down the road, we will have more and better opportunities to encourage interactions between our seniors and family and to nurture our Singapore Identity.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, this year, we commemorate Singapore's Bicentennial.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As we reflect our history, we must create opportunities and encourage our schools, families and grandparents to share stories of the past 200 years.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Last year, when I chaired the River Hongbao Organising Committee, I was showing my Parliamentary colleagues around the exhibition, "My Home, My New Year".

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: A man in his 40s came up to me and one of them said that before he came to that exhibition, he thought it was no big deal.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But after looking at the mockup of an old 3-room flat and remembering his past, he walked out of the exhibition and felt emotional at the sight of the skyscrapers around him.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He told us that this feeling was something that his daughter could not understand.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He said we should be feeling grateful for the peace, prosperity and stability that we enjoy today.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This year's River Hongbao was more colourful and exciting by using an exhibition to narrate Singapore's history and its development.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In Singapore, I have received a lot of feedback that people are getting increasingly frustrated by a host of seemingly unnecessary and irrelevant regulations that are putting the brakes on their work or their lives.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In an increasingly complex society where change is happening more and more quickly, the tendency is to come up with more regulations to protect the interests of many diverse groups.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Of course, some regulations are necessary and are good for the society.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When more people started using Personal Mobility Devices (PMDS), for instance, we had to come up with rules to protect the safety of others.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Or Workfare regulations, which have been protecting older lower-income Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But in other areas, the amount and nature of regulations might be adding more red tape and making our lives miserable for businesses.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Before I elaborate, I would like to declare my interest as the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of ComfortDelGro Taxi business.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: My architect friends have been complaining to me about their less than pleasant experience with the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) and the Fire Safety and Shelter Department (FSSD).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I face the same issues when I need to construct a new building, either as part of my community work or in the course of my work in my company.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But I will cite one that is the most painful to the architects.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Appeals by architects to BCA have fallen on deaf ears, for reasons best known to BCA.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Next, I would like to turn to a Statutory Board that is closer to my heart, LTA.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Every new car model has to go through a homologation process – a mouthful – by LTA to verify whether the car model is safe to be driven on Singapore roads.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The homologation process is relatively manual, tedious and lengthy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There are also many rounds of clarifications by LTA which has slowed down the approval process.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As a result, even current models with minor improvements or facelift also takes about eight weeks to homologate instead of two to three weeks previously.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Industry players have given feedback to LTA on many occasions to simplify the homologation process, which can be stretched for months.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, LTA is quite happy to keep the process lengthy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Perhaps this is the way LTA is trying to make Singapore car-lite?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: More importantly, these are the difficulties arising from bureaucratic red tape which many people have been complaining about.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Another example is getting approval to install a Direct Charger (DC) to charge full electric vehicles in double quick time.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: ABB, a large company, had been trying for six months to seek approval from the Energy Market Authority (EMA) without success to install a 50 kilowatt-hours DC to fully charge an electric car in 30 minutes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In this case, the CEO of EMA personally intervened and the DCs are now installed island-wide by the Singapore Power (SP) Group.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But not many regulatory authorities are as progressive as EMA.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Maybe that is one of the reasons why a few former EMA CEOs have now become Ministers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: To be objective, many industry players do not like to be regulated.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Very often, private companies feel that competition will drive quality and there is no need for the regulators to impose many rules.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: They feel that Singapore should be as laissez-faire as Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, competition is often not perfect and some form of regulation is important, necessary and, at times, essential.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: On the other hand, over-regulation can stifle creativity, slow down processes and add compliance costs without obvious benefits.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: A total removal of regulations could lead to many other problems like unfair competition or hurting the interests of consumers, like the Hokkien saying, 树倒猴子耍, it means that when the tree serving as a pillar falls, all hell breaks loose.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: No private company likes to be regulated, no matter how altruistic one is.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, it is often considered as biased, not objective and self-serving when the parties being regulated complain that the regulator is enforcing unnecessary rules.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This includes myself when my industry is being regulated by LTA.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, my views changed when I was preparing for River Hongbao 2019 which has just ended.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As Chairman of River Hongbao, I was a volunteer, not paid, and I had nothing to gain financially.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Nonetheless, I also encountered some issues with the regulators.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: First of all, I would like to thank the 1.35 million people who visited River Hongbao between 3 and 10 February 2019 for their support.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many visitors, comprising mainly local residents of all races, told me they enjoyed the larger-than-life lanterns, food street, stage performances and, particularly, the spectacular international fireworks display.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Very importantly, I have to thank the sponsors for their generous support for the fireworks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, I would like to share that the beloved fireworks display almost could not happen.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This year, we appointed an experienced fireworks vendor to arrange for the fireworks display at River Hongbao.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This fireworks vendor has been the company behind the fireworks display for the National Day parades for the past decade.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It has years of experience in applying for all of the necessary fireworks permits, including getting approval from the Public Utilities Board (PUB), which is the custodian of the Marina Bay reservoir.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, the prospect of the fireworks show being cancelled was imminent and preposterous.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The 100,000 ticket holders would be very disappointed.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: More importantly, the approval for the River Hongbao fireworks had been sought months before, with no positive reply from PUB.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Fireworks shows have routinely been put up in Marina Bay, with approvals granted, with no issues before.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I do not know what actually happened, but I am grateful that the fireworks display could take place during the eighth day of River Hongbao.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But Mr Speaker, Sir, I could keep quiet and move on.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: My concern is, what if I had no recourse?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: What if I was not able to appeal to the authorities?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It appears that we need the intervention by a higher authority in the case of the River Hongbao fireworks and the installation of DCs for “exceptions” to be made and before things can move ahead.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The above industrial examples and recent episode with PUB have highlighted the frustration of many ordinary people with various Government regulatory bodies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We need to strike a balance between laws that are so general and simplistic that they become ambiguous, and regulations which go into such nitty-gritty that it becomes a nightmare to observe and abide by.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We need to review regulations and strike them off when it becomes more of a hindrance than a help.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The best way to get a sense of what may be obsolete is to rely on feedback.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We should listen to the people who have to comply with the regulations and their reasons for why they find some legal requirements very onerous.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, my concern with direct feedback is that many private companies are afraid to speak up against their regulators for fear of repercussions.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many companies have told me that they experience additional hindrance when they voice out too strongly against their regulators.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In fact, over lunch just now, a company said, they do not just voice out against regulations at all.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Some companies told me they refrain from giving genuine feedback as they do not want to bite the hand that feeds them, especially when they have to bid for contracts from their regulators.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In fact, all the companies that have provided me with feedback to the cases cited above have asked me not to name their organisations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: How then could the Government obtain genuine, objective and timely feedback from the parties most affected by the regulations?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Some say they should feedback to Members of Parliament and let Members be their mouthpiece, which is precisely what I am doing today.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We need more systematic ways to obtain regular, timely and objective feedback from the industry players.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: To overcome the fear of repercussion, perhaps the Government can establish a neutral channel, similar to the whistleblower policy, to encourage feedback.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Another way for us to develop and finetune our regulations is to have a deeper understanding between the Public Service which enforces those regulations, and the private sector, through work exchange programmes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As someone who has work experience in both the public and private sectors, I have spoken on the need for this work exchange programme in the past.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Since then, I have observed, and I know for a fact, that there are small but sporadic efforts to do so.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Some Government agencies have started to send and pay for their staff to work at the private sector organisations that they regulate.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There are many benefits for such work exchange programmes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: By "walking in the other person's shoes", the public servant who returns to his organisation are likely to have a deeper understanding on how the private company works; what kind of regulations are necessary and effective; what kind of regulations are difficult to comply and do not serve the policy intent.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The public servants with immersion experience in the private sector can also better help to design incentive schemes to encourage companies to upgrade, adopt new technology, embrace digital transformation and rely less on foreign labour.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In addition, they can also better anticipate and detect the loopholes private companies can exploit and abuse Government incentive schemes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: These are the cases where regulation is absolutely necessary but has to be developed and enforced with a deep understanding of how it would be interpreted on the ground.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Private companies can also send their staff for work stints in the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: On a more personal note, as the President of the Volleyball Association of Singapore, I have seen the benefits of such exchanges first-hand.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: She has helped Sport Singapore to better understand the challenges face by the NSAs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: At the same time, she can tap on her experience in managing the NSAs and her networks in Sport Singapore to help in nurturing the volleyball players, volleyball coaches, securing training and competition venues for volleyball and more.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Her posting has been mutually beneficial, very good and rewarding.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The staff exchange efforts between the public and private sectors have so far been ad hoc.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In the larger scheme of things, such exchanges not only help to develop more relevant regulations, better enforcement policies and better incentive schemes for the private sector, the private and public sectors can also exploit the mutual learning between the two sectors for the better good of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope that my suggestions can spark some discussion, more ideas and more channels where industry feedback can be solicited, evaluated and acted upon as well as deepen the understanding between the public and private sectors.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat can review the same in other sectors as well.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For Singapore to thrive in this uncertain world with constant technological and geopolitical disruptions, the Government has to keep listening.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This year's Budget is generous and provides something for almost everyone – from the employees, to business owners, the less privileged, students, Singaporeans 50 years old and above, and seniors belonging to MG.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am particularly heartened by the focus on uplifting Singaporeans in this year's Budget.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have to continue to help lower-wage as well as older Singaporeans in ensuring their incomes remain competitive and sufficient, and that they will always have opportunities to be financially independent.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Here, I would like to urge the Government to extend similar assistance to other vulnerable groups who are looking to retain their self-dignity and self-worth, where they can enjoy equal opportunities to be employed, be financially independent and also contribute to our community and economy.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One such group would be those with special needs and those with mental health challenges.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These two groups of individuals continue to face stigmatisation and challenges in their effort to be like everyone else and in leading a life as normal as possible.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, the support or assistance that can also be rendered to business owners or employers can be in the form of tax reliefs or wage support to allow for flexiwork arrangements.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Flexiwork arrangements can provide for better employment opportunities for those with special needs and those with mental health challenges to work from home or to gradually adjust to their work environments and work commitments at a pace they are comfortable with.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Being gainfully employed is a start in helping those with special needs or with mental health challenges live independently like many others, and it accords sufficient opportunities to develop that much-needed self-belief and self-dignity.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, beyond SECs or incentives for employers to hire those with special needs or with mental health challenges, as a society, we need to be more accepting of different abilities, whether as employers, co-workers or neighbours.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our personal acceptance paves the way for more of those among us who are considered vulnerable individuals to have a place in our society, be independent and have that opportunity to lead a life that is as normal as possible.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Still on employment and workers, the Professionals, Managers and Executives (PMEs) is another group of employees I would like to urge the Government to continue to monitor and extend assistance to.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can these programmes continue beyond the next two to three years?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there plans to introduce other programmes to further assist PMEs, and older PMEs in particular, in their employment search and careers?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another portion of this year’s Budget in uplifting Singaporeans is to help students from less privileged families, mainly through the Uplifting Pupils in Life and Inspiring Families Taskforce (UPLIFT) initiative in schools.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I support the plan to strengthen after-school care for disadvantaged students in school-based student care centres.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This provision will help such students have better social support after school, whether it is in the form of help in their school work or in socio-emotional matters.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, beyond the provision of after-school care and support to these students from less privileged or disadvantaged families, are there plans to uplift each of their families as well?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, these could be in the form of employment assistance or employability coaching for the parents, financial planning workshops for the parents, parenting workshops to enhance parent-child bonding, and educational enrichment programmes for the children to promote personal and character development as well as the development of lifeskills.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Countries or economies, such as Norway, Hong Kong and Iceland, are leading in the adoption of electric vehicles onto their roads, with generous incentives, such as waivers of import tax and value-added tax, reduced road tax and free parking in the city.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there plans to increase the import and use of electric vehicles on our roads with similar incentives, particularly when Dyson will be setting up its electric car plants in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One final segment of this year’s Budget I wish to speak on is in building a community of care and contribution, mainly through SG Cares.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I strongly support the focus on nurturing students in Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to give back to the community, do volunteer work and service learning, and to develop community leadership qualities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are necessary skills and values that our youths must possess as there is a need to feel, think and act beyond the self or based on personal aspirations only.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The community is ours to shape and develop, and each of us has a role to make our community one that cares for and loves all.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that community projects or programmes which demonstrate values-in-action will not merely be items to be ticked off on a checklist for our youths.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that our youths will take ownership and leadership in planning and implementing meaningful and impactful community projects that can help uplift the different segments of our community, not merely because it is an assessment or graduation requirement, but because it is something they truly believe in and want to do.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At this juncture, Mr Speaker, please allow me to speak in Malay.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that our entrepreneurs will seize this opportunity to explore new borders and opportunities and bring further glory to our nation.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the experience of working overseas and the opportunity to learn about and understand foreign cultures and markets is invaluable to our young Malays who are interested in broadening their experience, viewpoints and minds.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the Malay saying goes, "If you are afraid to get your oars wet, your sampan will never make it across".

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the effort by the Government and employers to help vulnerable groups, such as those with special needs as well as those with mental health challenges, each of us has an important contribution.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a society, each of us plays a role in ensuring that the vulnerable amongst us are not left behind.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our attitudes towards them, whether as employers, colleagues or neighbours, will determine the extent of their acceptance by society, how independent they can be and whether they will continue to have a chance to lead a normal life.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): In conclusion, Mr Speaker, this year's Budget is more than just dollars, incentives or programmes.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is about coming together and helping one another in ways beyond the immediate or the individual.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If I may end with a quote by Cesar Chavez: "We cannot seek achievement for ourselves and forget about progress and prosperity for our community... ...Our ambitions must be broad enough to include the aspirations and needs of others, for their sakes and for our own." I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Inequality has been a buzzword in recent years and it is a positive sign.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It shows that, as a society, we are not just concerned about ourselves but we are also concerned about those who have fallen behind, those who need our help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is the best way to reduce inequality?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The answer is ensuring social mobility and social mixing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this respect, I agree with what Prime Minister Lee said in October last year: "We must not allow social stratification to harden in Singapore." We have done well to ensure that there is less social stratification where we live.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Prime Minister gave the example of our HDB towns, which mix rental blocks with owned blocks, and have flats of all sizes within the same building.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Prime Minister said, "We want high- and low-income families to live together side by side, get along with one another, interact with one together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Not live apart and treat one another as aliens from a different world." But what about social stratification where we study, especially in our secondary schools?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Students spend perhaps half or even more of their time in schools.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In these environments, it is surely just as important that high- and low-income children learn together, play together and mix with one another.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The recent Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) report titled “Excellence and Equity in Education” similarly shared many positive aspects of our education system and about how disadvantaged students here do well compared with their peers around the world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But as MOE has acknowledged that the report also showed that more work needs to be done to ensure good social diversity and mixing in schools.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We introduced streaming in 1980, and I understand the rationale.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It caters to the different learning needs and pace of our students and it has helped to lower our attrition rate, which is now at less than 1%, compared to 30%-40% at the start of our education journey.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar also said in 2017 that streaming "helps teachers in being more focused in their teaching so that they are able to pitch their teaching content and pedagogy that are suitable for the students they teach." But the problem is that we are not just streaming our students based on their academic results.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We also know that the percentage of students living in public rental flats is higher in the Normal streams than those in the Express stream.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We all know that we hang out with our classmates much more than with our schoolmates.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What streaming has possibly done is to reduce social mixing and, again, harden social stratification.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I spent the last year researching for this speech, filing questions in Parliament and I spoke with parents, students and teachers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But quite a number of them gave pause and raised concerns when I suggested that streaming could be stratifying our schools and preventing our students from mixing across socio-economic backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure streaming was not meant to divide our nation by socio-economic status, but we now see that streaming does contribute to it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have tried so hard to prevent social stratification in our homes; we must try just as hard to do so in our schools.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The next logical question is whether students move between streams.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, if a Normal (Technical) student can move easily to the Express stream, we could all afford to be less worried about social stratification.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Each year, 530 Normal (Technical) students transfer to the Normal (Academic) stream.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Here is what it means: if you are a student from the Normal (Technical) stream, you have less than 1% chance to move to the Express stream.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is worse, the stratification continues further up the education ladder.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Most finish their studies in the Institute of Technical Education (ITE).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Data provided by MOE shows that ITE graduates earned a starting salary of $1,900 in the private sector in 2017.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By contrast, public university graduates earned a starting salary of $3,300.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why do students from the Normal stream struggle to move to the Express stream?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One reason could be the psychological barriers that streaming imposes on Normal stream students.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Ng Chee Meng last year acknowledged concerns that streaming could inadvertently discourage students.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar also said, "Academic streaming tends to pigeon-hole students and inadvertently places expectations about their intelligence or abilities according to the stream they are in." Indeed, for some students, there is a strong stigma associated with being in the Normal stream.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One 2006 research paper, titled "Building Teacher Capacity in Curriculum and Pedagogical Design in Normal Technical Classrooms," provided this summary: "Perhaps the most common and injurious perception associated with Normal (Technical) or English and Mother Tongue (EM3) students is stupidity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Other negative perceptions of people interviewed on the streets are: "attitude not good", "Ah Beng type", "hopeless", "can't do anything, can't go anywhere", "unmotivated", "lazy" and "ill-disciplined".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some students may have even internalised such negativities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not unusual for students in the Normal stream to blame themselves, leading to the worry that such students suffer from low self-esteem." The impact of this stigma was already raised in this House by Mdm Cynthia Phua nine years ago.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She said, "The present streaming of students in secondary schools has much psychological impact on the youths.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Normal stream is not normal, according to how the students and parents feel.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They feel that they are inferior to their academic-better fellow schoolmates.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And why do we have a system that makes our youths feel inferior at a young tender age?" There are, of course, students from the Normal (Technical) stream who have done well, and we have featured them regularly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I met David Hoe and am so inspired by his story.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: David is the poster child of a successful student from the Normal (Technical) stream who has made it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, he is an economics teacher at a Junior College.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: His parents divorced when he was young, and he lived with his mother who was visually impaired.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He went around selling tissue paper together with his mother to make ends meet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: His mother passed on when David was 12.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He did not do well for his PSLE and went into the Normal (Technical) stream.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He fell into bad company and took up drinking and smoking.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As he shared with the media, "I hung out with these people for a few months before I met the right ones." His new group of friends often hung out in the canteen to do their homework.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They also helped to coach him in his studies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He had a dream of becoming a teacher and worked hard for it for his GCE "N" level, in hopes of eventually doing his GCE "O" level.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He did well and was one of the top scorers for the Normal (Technical) "N" level.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But he was still not allowed to do his "O" level.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Desperate, this 16-year-old wrote an email to then Minister for Education, Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who intervened on his behalf.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It was only through this intervention that he was able to get past the system and eventually did his "O" level.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: David is a success story, and he worked hard to succeed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But, as he shared with me, his story is also about how social mixing made a difference for him.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While we share the success stories, we also need to remember that David is not representative of the majority of Normal (Technical) students.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While we celebrate the successes, we need to remember those who have been left behind.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe the debate we need to have has already happened.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The concerns I raise today are the same ones students, teachers, parents and Members of this House have previously raised about primary school streaming.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Minister Ong Ye Kung shared this month about the replacement of streaming with Subject-Based Banding in primary schools, "We believe that this has helped raise the confidence and motivation of students while customising education to their aptitudes and pace of learning." He also added, "there are also more opportunities for interaction among students across the different subject combinations, as a form class can have students of several subject combinations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Concerns about labelling and stigmatisation have diminished." Both teachers and parents have also expressed support for Subject-Based Banding.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, what is stopping us from abolishing streaming in secondary schools?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is stopping us from preventing this kind of social stratification?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Students there are grouped not based on their streams, but by co-curricular activities (CCA) groups.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means that students of different socio-economic backgrounds are more likely to mix with one another.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As a parent of young children, I am thankful for these changes and hope that we can do more.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But if you judge a fish by its ability to climb a tree, it will live its whole life believing that it is stupid." There will be inequality in our education system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The fact is that not everybody is the same.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But our students are not stupid and should not feel that they are or face that kind of stigma.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to make sure their future is not decided by one major examination.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to make sure that, like where we live, we do not have social stratification in where we study.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Now, let us make every class a good class.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This decline in support is not an irrational one.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is evidence that globalisation has so far produced winners as well as losers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This could offer a partial explanation for Britain voting to leave the European Union, and for the triumph of the United States (US) Presidential candidate Trump's election slogan: "America First".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Most analyses show that Asia is doing relatively well with the growth of the middle class, but Asia faces the challenge of growing domestic inequality.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, it is good to see the Minister for Finance acknowledging that Singapore's long-term challenges include social mobility and inequality, which will be stressors of our social unity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Much literature has been published about what governments should do to manage globalisation for their citizens.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some have argued that living standards of citizens should be equalised as much as possible, with particular attention paid to vulnerable groups, that financial markets and labour protection need to be regulated, and welfare policies implemented.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is suggested that taxation policies need to be progressive, with clampdowns on tax avoidance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the fiscal front, there should be increased spending on health, education and social safety nets.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Labour markets should be reformed to boost labour's share of income.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Coming back to Singapore, the direction of the Government in economic transformation and workforce reskilling for relevant industries is necessary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The other pillar that is equally necessary is to have compensatory policies in the form of social safety nets to cushion citizens who face disruption and are unable to fit into different industries immediately, or perhaps unable to catch up at all.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The theme of Budget 2019 is to "Build a Strong, United Singapore".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I wish to speak on the issue of disruptions to employment, under-employment and the vulnerable workforce.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We have heard a lot during this debate about the "Fourth Industrial Revolution".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Across the world, the impact of Industry 4.0 on jobs has generated intense interest.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Many predict major job losses due to automation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, in a 2013 Oxford University study of the impact of computerisation on employment, authors Frey and Osborne predicted that almost half of US workers would face risks of their jobs being automated by 2030.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Economist Tyler Cowen has argued that automation could produce profound inequality as a majority of people will find their jobs taken by robots and will be forced into low-paying service work.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Only a minority – those highly skilled, creative and lucky – will have lucrative jobs, and be wildly better paid than the rest.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Others are less pessimistic, with Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) economist Erik Brynjolfsson noting that automation will eventually create jobs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singapore, being one of the most open and connected economies, is readily open to job disruption.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, there have been significant efforts by the Government and the private sector to respond to disruption, as seen in the massive digitisation efforts, automation initiatives and PSPs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The message that workers need to adapt is clear.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The question is how well such initiatives are serving to give economic security to workers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the number seems impressive, it would be useful to know whether these jobseekers who switched industry had comparable remuneration or had pay cuts, and how many of them could not find new employment even though they tried to sign up for the initiative.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Underemployment arises, basically, when a person is working but below his or her capacity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is referred to by the International Labour Organisation as "labour under-utilisation".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today's labour market is much more diverse than when MG came out to work in the 1970s.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In those days, it was common to hear of employees spending their entire working lives with one employer, and "job hopping" was frowned upon.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, employees move more often, take on contract assignments and do gig economy work, including some university graduates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As far as underemployment is concerned, there was a recent interesting survey, published in 2017 by the Ong Teng Cheong Institute.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The study discussed the issue of how to measure underemployment properly and recognised that underemployment was too complex to measure with any single indicator.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It decided to adopt a multifactor definition of underemployment, namely, persons who were degree holders and above, in full-time work and earning less than $2,000 per month.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the survey, the profile of the underemployed showed that they tended to be female, have no children and stay in HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They were employed at businesses serving mainly the domestic market, with a median age of 35, and with 10 to 15 years of work experience.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As to the effects of underemployment, the study found that the underemployed reported facing challenges, such as having lower status than what they deserve, being underpaid, feeling insecure about their income and job, and lacking finances for daily expenses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This group indicated that they were in their current predicament involuntarily, as they were found to want to better their prospects by reskilling and upskilling, although they were unsure of what skills may be in demand and how to take the next step.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The rate was derived on a time-based definition of underemployment, that is, persons working part-time and would like to work full-time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This may suggest that if there may be a class dimension to this as well, with the less educated more prone to underemployment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In order to get a better handle on how underemployment is affecting our society, I ask the Government to continue to improve its measures of underemployment and to monitor the effects of underemployment on the well-being of different segments of society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I plan to talk more about this at the MOM Committee of Supply (COS) debate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Over the years, I have noticed that at the Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS), residents of lower income commonly report doing gig economy jobs, such as furniture movers and in food delivery.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some have told me that they have few options and need the flexibility of time to attend to family issues which crop up often.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The vulnerable workforce also has less ability to withstand the vicissitudes of life.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I recently encountered a young single mother who had three children.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She received no support from the children’s father whom she divorced.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Due to her need to work and care for her young children, she took on a gig job, delivering food on a motorcycle.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In a moment of inattention, she beat a red light and was duly notified by the Traffic Police to pay a composition fine of $200.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As she did not have the funds to make the payment, she came to the MPS for help.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I do not know whether the law enforcement agencies have ever allowed payment of composition fines by instalments, but I know that the clock is ticking to the deadline for payment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Failure to pay will result in the case going to Court and attracting higher fines.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I did not write in to the agency but instead found funds to assist her to pay.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledge that significant efforts have been made towards economic transformation and upskilling our workforce.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What we need to watch closely are the many stress points on our social solidarity, and address them, if we are to be a Strong and United Singapore.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Innovation in arts and culture, sounding the horn for digital arts.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: It is heartening to note that one of the key thrusts in this year’s Budget is to foster a caring and inclusive society and this is done by, "securing our home and growing our economy and to improve the lives of our current and future generations of Singaporeans".

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In fostering a caring and inclusive society for all Singaporeans, this is where the role of the arts and culture can come in.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The arts and culture are an important platform which contributes to the maturity of the populace.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Allowing us to reflect on our shared heritage and common identity while at the same time to understand our differences and to celebrate our diversity.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially relevant and important in our Bicentennial year.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In an ever-changing socio-economic landscape we live in, digitisation has become our way of life.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: We see it on the streets, hear it at the supermarkets.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: There have been campaigns encouraging Singaporeans to adopt digitisation as a way of life.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: There is also the MeshMinds Foundation which recently collaborated with students from LaSalle College of the Arts to present an exhibition on using art and tech for good.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: These are just a few of the many examples of how arts groups and organisations in Singapore are innovating and using digital technology to enhance the sustainability and relevance of arts to the greater audience, serving them well and wise.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Launching an exhibition at the ArtsScience Museum last year titled "All Possible Paths: Richard Feynman's Curious Life", Minister Heng Swee Keat said this, and I quote, "The best ideas emerge from the intersection of technology with the arts, when people from different disciplines collaborate to learn from one another".

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, as we have also heard in the Budget, partnering to win is also an important dimension in ensuring a skilled workforce and a vibrant economy.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: We can build more partnerships amongst the art and culture groups, technology companies and even within academia.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This would allow the arts and culture to innovate and create programmes, cutting down boundaries, enhancing audience and visitor experiences as we create new entry points for audiences.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to more research and development (R&D) efforts resulting in the above-mentioned partnerships which would both sustain the arts and culture by making it more accessible and inclusive in Singapore for the disadvantaged communities.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, from 5 to 17 March, our local theatre company, The Finger Players, will be presenting an inclusive theatre performance, which caters to the needs of audiences with disabilities, through usage of closed captioning and audio description.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I welcome Members of the House to support The Finger Players.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: More can and should be done through R&D efforts to promote inclusive arts.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, while the Government has invested significantly in cultural infrastructure, more funds could be allocated to improving and upgrading the existing hardware of the arts, allowing our arts and culture groups to stay relevant and enable them to truly execute digital arts, allowing us then to be able to grow our "heartware" of the arts.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, sounding the horn for digital arts.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In his 2019 Budget Statement, the Finance Minister talked about how Singapore should strive to become a Global-Asia node of technology.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: To lead in the future, Singapore must innovate, develop and cultivate more tech talent so that we can face the challenges of this fast-changing digital world.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The Government will also equip small and medium enterprises (SMEs) with capabilities to stay relevant and go towards digitalisation and automation.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore moves towards high-end technology development, arts and culture can play an important role in showcasing our inner world and are closely tied to our social life.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Various digital arts developments will not only provide people with rich mental nourishment but also allow arts and culture to captivate the public through more advanced technology and multiple channels.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This can be an effective tool to popularise and elevate arts and culture.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Digital technology has also spurred many artists to achieve breakthroughs into a new world, allowing them to create more influential works of art.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In this era of technology innovation, local arts groups are sparing no efforts to create surprises using digital technology.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The use of digital technology has made their shows and performances more attractive.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I firmly believe that the use of technology can not only improve efficiency in commercial field but also serve communities from different backgrounds better.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: We can do more for the vulnerable by the use of technology.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This will bring arts and culture closer to people and allow people with different backgrounds to have a chance to come into contact with the arts.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The concurrent development of the arts and culture in the digital age can enrich the soul of the nation and make Singapore more efficient.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2019 will lead us into the future and build a strong and united Singapore together.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):  	Mindset and progress of the Malay community.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is the engine that drives our motivations.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Mindset can determine the ebb and flow, the ups and downs in someone's life.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Mindset is related to how we shape our lives, our journey and our family with a vision.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This year, Singapore commemorates 200 years since Sir Stamford Raffles set foot on this island and 54 years since we achieved Independence.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What are the status and performance of our Malay/Muslim community?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What is the level of our achievement so far?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Over the years, various programmes had been implemented, new policies were crafted, and progressive and competitive schemes had been rolled out by the Government, self-help groups and other organisations.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In doing so, with this background, the principles of meritocracy, diligence and cooperation among the different races and religions have always been emphasised.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: All these are stepping stones and opportunities for us to improve and enhance ourselves and our families.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Although we are a minority group, our desire to achieve progress and excellence is strong.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The expectations of our younger generation, millennials and our descendants will continue to grow.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Each generation gets better, more successful, better educated and trained, more successful and more global, and we must not turn back again.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In order to determine the thrust of this future, we, and the next generation, must continue to strive, share a common vision, collaborate, possess a broad and progressive mind, and look ahead while exploring a new world order and a new economic landscape with new strategies.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In education, we must continue to inculcate the love for learning at every level, in every individual.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For workers, this kind of learning includes the upgrading of skills, capabilities and qualifications.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We must never get tired of seeking knowledge, broadening our minds and improving ourselves.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We have now begun to move away from a single-minded focus on academic qualifications and expanded capabilities in other fields.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This provides a good platform for our Malay/Muslim community to close the gap and level up with the other communities.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This also means that the criteria for educational assistance and the criteria that solely use academic benchmarks should be reviewed and revised.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This demonstrates an emphasis on education, because we know that education is the only factor that enables us to raise the standing and status of our family.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As they say, education is the greatest equaliser.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In healthcare, during Singapore's early years, we faced the challenges of malnutrition and infectious diseases.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: At the moment, our Malay/Muslim community is battling chronic diseases, such as diabetes and high blood pressure, and the rates of complications and risks are also high.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Now, the issue of ageing has gained prominence.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How do we plan ageing successfully and comfortably for ourselves and our families?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Certainly, culture and personality have something to do with one’s perception of ageing.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: A survey in Singapore found that factors seen as important in old age are good health, financial means, healthy lifestyle and strong social support.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: However, the most essential thing is that our preparations and plans for our golden years begin while we are still young.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
