text: Most importantly, we must have a roof over our heads, adequate funds for expenses, health insurance, a family that supports and cares for us, peace of mind and the ability to comfortably lead our lives and practise our faith.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The number of youths studying up to post-secondary level and those reaching university has risen.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The number of workers in the professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMET) category has also grown.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The number of entrepreneurs spreading their wings globally has also increased.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For our SME owners, there are many types of assistance and schemes available for business expansion and automation.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For our asatizahs, they are getting better qualifications and many are graduating from illustrious Islamic institutions, such Al Azhar.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We now have access to global developments and can gain a positive impact from this.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We live in a secular nation with religious diversity.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We lead our lives freely and we are not oppressed in Singapore.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We can pursue our religious activities with ease.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (MUIS) is also always available to issue advisories and rulings for us to follow.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In the US, 10 states have legislated Bills that are anti-Islam and promote Muslim-free businesses.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is an unhealthy, worrying and very grim situation.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In Singapore, we, the Malay/Muslim community, are fortunate that our rights are protected as a minority group.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, please do not squander the opportunities given to us, which are the same as the other communities.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But what about the next stage of our journey?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is up to us whether we can adapt to the modern world, the application of information technology (IT), e-learning and gain new skills in a fast-paced world.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I end my speech with a pantun: Values and principles of Singapore, Between the Government and the people Working together, hand-in-hand A community of excellence, a stable nation.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, they say a stable world order is a rare thing.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Governing nations will require skillful statecraft because we will have to wake up to something new every day.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Governance must be robust and, at the same time, nimble, subjected to frequent changes and disruptions, which we have to adapt to.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The 21st century is a different world we live in.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is a complex, multi-polar era in world politics that we live in with all these tectonic shifts.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore is vigilant, well-placed and can adapt, if we keep on this trajectory that we are on.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Any instability, any major shifts in the way we work, our little red dot will get left behind.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We must surmount the challenges of the day together and retain our core values and principles for a cohesive and stable Singapore.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thus, my focus on "Partnerships to Prosper", or P to P.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Old partnerships, existing partnerships, new partnerships and yet-to-be-formed partnerships.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Only through deepening our partnerships, understanding and collaborations can we have a better grasp of issues, things and phenomena.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I always say that partnerships are about "building bridges and managing our egos".

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is about respect, honesty and cross-cultural understanding.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: These include partnerships and collaborations at the global level, with foreign affairs.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How we collaborate and befriend other nations is critical, some more than others, but it must all work in a rules-based world order.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our principles must prevail and Singapore's interest must prevail.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For example, at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) level, Singapore is looked to as a model Asian society and we must strive to demonstrate and model this.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore relies also on foreign workforce and new immigrants.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: These partnerships with them must be two ways: for them to understand us and for us, them.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our own global platform for deepening our learning process is also deepened through our interaction and work with these people.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: On diplomacy and defence, as mentioned by the Finance Minister, this, too, needs formation of partnerships.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our interaction and relationships with nations and neighbours are just as crucial as building up our Singapore Armed Forces (SAF).

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Ask any business person and it will be evident that good partnerships and communications are the basic fundamentals of joint ventures, business networks and economic collaborations.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: At the community level, with ground-up initiatives, partnerships can make the difference as well.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We see the positive corporate social responsibility (CSR) by many organisations and companies.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We also see their help and support evolve and change according to the needs of the times.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: These are all examples of useful and meaningful partnerships and they are also customised partnerships.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They have to stay relevant and they have to be relevant in the world of not just today but also moving forward to tomorrow.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thus, there is also one more partnership that I just want to mention, which is the disruption in partnerships.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Partnerships are, indeed, an invitation to engage, and engaged ones are critical in the formation of meaningful networks.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: With disruption and transformation in our partnerships, the impact is certainly wider, greater and deeper.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Disruption is already affecting our local and global relations.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Every business and society entity now has greater potential to expand their mission and work.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The outreach through disruption and transformation can be tremendous.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There are even funds provided by the Government to support this.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Digital disruption has coloured our partnerships and relationships.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Even our VWOs and non-government organisations (NGOs) are forming partnerships with clients, supporters and sponsors through disruption and disruptive techniques.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For example, counselling can even now be done through videoconferencing and through electronic partnership portals.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Of course, a word of caution is on the maintenance of confidentiality on such platforms.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: My views are that national Budgets do not just represent the governments handing out to the population unilaterally.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is about the partnership between the people and the Government.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is about how people understand the Budget and tap on the schemes and programmes, and that is where we come in as well where we have to do simplified explanation because there is really a lot of sophistication in simplicity.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is also about how specific groups utilise the resources made available through the Budget.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is thus important to have a proper and deep understanding of why each scheme and each subsidy is proposed and not be swayed by superficial, emotional interpretations of the Budget.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I would also like to thank the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and lend my support for their strong commitment to Worker 4.0, to do our best for every worker, including freelancers, older workers and low-wage workers, which is both the necessary thing to do for Singapore's economy and the right thing to do for society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I would also like to recognise Member Ms Sylvia Lim's acknowledgement of the Government's efforts to help our workers adapt and grow literally for the future economy and also her concerns over the vulnerable segment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: My colleagues and I will speak more on these areas in MOM's COS segment next week.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Yesterday, Members, including Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Jessica Tan, Ms Denise Phua and Mr Chong Kee Hiong, have spoken of their support as well as their concerns with the high S Pass growth, the unsustainability of foreign worker growth, and the need to push on with economic restructuring.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I am glad that they have also recognised the Government's efforts to smoothen the transition through various initiatives and schemes with the industry, trade associations and the Labour Movement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Our foreign workforce policies are an integral part of our broader workforce strategy to improve the quality of jobs and employment outcomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We want Singaporeans to be able to participate in Singapore's economic growth and prosperity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Therefore, we want to give our workers the opportunity to access quality jobs, as long as they are prepared to work hard, be productive and gain the necessary skills required to become competitive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: These are contingent on a vibrant economy and strong job creation as well as a sufficiently tight labour market.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Our foreign workforce policies are, therefore, calibrated to support economic growth and enhance complementarity between the local and foreign workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The profile of our local workforce is changing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, we need to keep improving the quality of our jobs to meet the highest aspirations of our people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Having come from the commercial sector, I also recognise that companies, large and small, also want access to human capital with relevant skills to grow their business.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And for companies that use Singapore as an international hub, I recognise that access to international manpower is also crucial to be able to address the regional and global markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: As we restructure, it is important to assure companies that Singapore remains open to foreign professionals or specialists with experience in emerging growth areas or skills that are in demand globally and in short supply in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This allows employers to assemble the best possible international teams in Singapore in order to compete globally which, in turn, create more quality jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: However, our short-term needs must not become our long-term dependency, lest we become over-reliant on foreign manpower and risk hurting local employment outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: That is why we have made a series of adjustments at the Employment Pass (EP) level which many PMETs have also asked about.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In 2017, we increased the EP qualifying salary to keep pace with rising local wages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This ensures that foreign professionals do not compete with local PMETs by undercutting wages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This has led to a moderation of the number of EP holders, with the exit of lower-quality EPs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: As local wages rise, we will have to adjust the EP criteria from time to time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: For employers suspected of unfair hiring practices, we place them on the FCF Watchlist.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Beyond PMETs, we aim to uplift all segments of our local workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: As Singaporeans live longer, we want to do more to support our older workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We want to help those who still want to work so that they have the opportunity to enjoy good employment outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We also want to help low-wage workers upgrade their skills and uplift their wages as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And we also want to foster an inclusive society, one that enables all workers, including ex-offenders, persons with special needs, to thrive and find meaningful employment, and for women to be able to fulfil both career and family aspirations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The reality is that many ITE and polytechnic graduates also work in the Services sector, alongside S Pass and Work Permit holders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We want our ITE and polytechnic graduates to be able to access opportunities in these sectors, too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In particular, by keeping the labour market tight, employers will have the incentive to develop the local workforce and to redesign and transform jobs to attract locals and to invest in training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Ms Denise Phua raised concerns about the manpower shortage in the Services sector yesterday, where locals may not be willing to take up Services jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: However, this does not mean that firms will never be able to attract locals into these jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We must put in the effort to redesign jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I have met employers who have gone out of their way to redesign jobs and create more flexible working arrangements (FWAs) for mature workers, persons who are disabled and others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Certainly, there is scope to make this happen for many of our common jobs, too, if we put our minds to it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We should recognise that there are already many Singaporeans working in the Services sector, alongside S Pass holders and Work Permit holders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In fact, the majority of locals are employed in the Services sector, including in food services and retail jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We should avoid reinforcing the view that these are jobs that only foreigners want to take up.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: There are good jobs for our Singaporean workers, and we should and can do more.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We will spare no effort to help businesses transform and transit.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: To help companies grow and achieve sustained productivity improvements, we will work closely with the industry to support businesses in developing more efficient techniques and service models so that they can grow and transform in a tight labour market.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Mr Douglas Foo shared his concerns that some Services sub-sectors will not be able to cope.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Firms will also take time for workers to be trained before they can contribute meaningfully to the company.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I recognise some of these challenges that firms are facing, particularly SMEs, which may be too bogged down with day-to-day operations to think about change, especially deep systemic changes that would really allow firms to reduce reliance on foreign manpower.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We did not want a situation where firms continue using existing operating models and simply pay higher levy costs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Restructuring will not be easy and I acknowledge that.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We are also enhancing our enterprise support by subsidising qualifying project costs, training costs, among other measures, as the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) mentioned yesterday.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: For those who are looking to grow their local workforce, I encourage employers to participate in the Earn-and-Learn programmes under the SkillsFuture movement to bring in fresh polytechnic and ITE graduates and take up Adapt and Grow programmes through Workforce Singapore (WSG) and its partners to recruit suitable mid-career workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We provide generous funding for employers to hire and train Singaporeans through our Place-and-Train Programme, CSP and Career Trial.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In particular, Career Trial will be useful for employers who have redesigned jobs and want to engage local workers to try them out.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I encourage businesses to pay more attention to the work environment, remuneration and skills upgrading, and even consider FWAs to be able to attract, develop and retain local workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This is to help firms which are serious about growing sustainably within the new DRCs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I hope this gives assurance to Mr Douglas Foo who advocated for a more flexible labour policy to meet the needs of individual businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Depending on the transformation plan of businesses, we can calibrate the extent of transitional manpower support to firms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Government recognises that essential sectors, such as healthcare, will need to ensure day-to-day operations are not affected as firms adjust.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We want our companies to transform so that they can grow in a sustainable manner and create quality jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We want our workers, on the other hand, to be able to access these opportunities – quality jobs, good salaries – and participate in Singapore’s economic growth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We cannot have an outcome where workers win and employers lose, or employers win and workers lose.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We want a win-win for both workers and employers, supported by the Government and the Labour Movement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: (In Malay):  	The essence of this year's Budget clearly centres on the commitment to build a stronger and more united Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: But at the same time, it focuses on the well-being and welfare of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This Budget is comprehensive and takes into account current and future needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Not many countries have the luxury of presenting a budget that prioritises future needs, year after year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: For the Malay community, I urge that they take full advantage of the opportunities and available schemes for upgrading, especially in skills training, so that they are not left behind in our economic transformation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Our workers may already be affected by the economic transformation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In fact, those who have undergone skills training must continue to increase their knowledge in order to fulfil the needs of the current and the future economies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Education and lifelong learning are the best avenue for upgrading.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: However, the recipe for success will still depend on the attitude of our people and their desire to want to succeed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: As the saying goes: when there is a will, there is a way.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Government's move to further reduce employers' DRC for S-Pass and Work Permit holders should be seen as a good opportunity for our ITE and polytechnic graduates because their contributions and skills are much needed in this sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Our foreign manpower policies are designed to spur better employment outcomes for our people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This can be done by creating a balance whereby employers are allowed to take in foreign workers so that their companies can stay competitive and continue to grow, but at the same time, ensuring that the number of foreign workers does not compromise our objectives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We must manage the inflow of foreign manpower in the service sector in order to encourage our firms and businesses to innovate and improve their operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: At the same time, we also focus on improving our local workforce through education and skills upgrading.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It is hoped that this will encourage employers to redesign and transform their work processes and invest in training so that the job opportunities and the career prospects are more attractive to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This also provides better job opportunities for mature workers or those who are seniors, as well as women who wish to return to the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: For instance, Career Trial is very useful for employers who have redesigned their jobs and wish to take Singaporeans who want to try out those jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: After spending eight years building a career in the banking sector and the Public Service, Ms Norfazillah Shariff, 32 years old, made the courageous move to try a new career outside her comfort zone by becoming a social worker.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Ms Norfazillah seized the opportunity to join the PCP for Social Workers in July 2017.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: She has a Post-Graduate Diploma in Social Work from the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS).

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Mr Muhammad Rusydi Md Norr, 31 years old, was previously a convenience store manager.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: He is now a nurse, after joining the PCP for Registered Nurses (Degree).

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: He entered the 2-year Bachelor of Science (Nursing) programme at the Alice Lee Centre for Nursing Studies at the National University of Singapore (NUS).

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This is because, as we transform our economy and help businesses become more resilient, we also do not wish to see Malay/Muslim workers and students get left behind.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The same goes for businesses affected by the economic transformation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Their worries and concerns are understandable, especially in the context of today's fast-changing and unpredictable economic and global situation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Workers are worried about their future, whether their jobs and their income can be maintained.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Businesses are also worried about their future with regard to business costs, competition and other factors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: They certainly feel quite worried and anxious about their future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: For firms and businessmen, we understand the challenges they face, especially Malay/Muslim entrepreneurs from SMEs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We are committed to helping companies and businesses undergo transformation and implement new and effective operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: If more time is needed, these companies can make use of the transitional manpower support under the Lean Enterprise Development (LED) scheme.All these programmes and support are readily available to help every group, including workers, businessmen and employers, to progress together with Singapore now and in the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The overall thrust of this Budget is comprehensive enough to assure all Singaporeans that their future in Singapore is the Government's priority.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: On the whole, while the Government invests in these programmes, Singaporeans, all of us, businesses, must make use of all the opportunities available.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It was not an easy decision, a tough one which I have laid out the considerations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: But it is a measured one that will be good for Singapore in the long term.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I know that the Workers' Party has been quiet on where it stands on our DRC announcement this Budget.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Does the Workers' Party support the Government's policy on the DRC changes?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Over the years that I serve as their Member of Parliament, I see more and more of them using wheelchairs and relying on walking sticks to aid their mobility.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As they age, they also require more medical care.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The PGP introduced in 2014 provided great financial relief for many of these senior citizens as it helped reduce their healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Over these past years, I have met Singaporeans who have expressed appreciation for the healthcare-related subsidies which they received due to their PG status.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some of them may not realise it when they receive the PG card.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, when they are hospitalised, the benefits of being a PG is much clearer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Healthcare costs will always be a concern for our citizens regardless of home types, and the MGP would provide greater assurance to our citizens.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It also shows the appreciation of this Government for the generation of Singaporeans who have helped build Singapore up.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As with every Budget, we would never be able to please everyone.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There will always be economists, academics and other well-meaning Singaporeans who will call for the Government to spend more on other things.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The challenge is who will pay for all these extras?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And will all these extras be sustainable in the long term?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Will Singapore end up like some other countries which are struggling to balance their budget or are on the brink of bankruptcy?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What should be the core business of the Government?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: To me, it must be to provide all Singaporeans a safe living environment; to ensure that healthcare remains affordable, that every Singaporean has access to good quality education, that we continue to grow the economy and create good jobs for Singaporeans; that our public transport system allows our citizens to travel within the country in a convenient and reliable manner and that public housing is accessible and affordable; that every Singaporean, regardless of our starting point, should have equal opportunities to do well in life.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Although there are areas where we can improve upon, I support the efforts of this Government to ensure that the basic needs of all citizens are met.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This includes the need to spend more on defence and security as we need to be able to stand up to unfriendly forces.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In fact, a strong defence force will be the main deterrent to any hostile activities.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also support the increase in spending to deal with different security threats.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The state-sponsored cyberattack on the SingHealth IT system is a strong reminder to all of us on the need to strengthen our IT security measures against those who wish Singapore to fail.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Even countries like Germany and Australia were recently subject to attacks on their IT network system.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I have three points for the Government's consideration.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If a citizen is a retiree with no income but staying in a private property, why should he get less GST Vouchers than someone who earns a lot more but stays in a 3- or 4-room HDB flat?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Why should someone without any income not enjoy the benefits of the Bicentennial Bonus simply because his home has an annual value of more than $21,000?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is unfair to the Singaporeans who had contributed to Singapore but had pursued their dreams of staying in a better home when they were younger.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also call on the Government to consider a change in its policies to allow elderly singles to rent a flat alone.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: During my MPS, I regularly receive requests from elderly seniors who, for some reason, cannot get along with their family members or their children.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They quarrel frequently and want to shift out so that they can preserve their dignity and not stay in an unhappy home.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Much as we wish to encourage the families to look after their seniors, the reality is that relationship issues are not easily resolved.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am of the view that we should not compel an elderly person to stay with the family when he or she is clearly estranged from the family.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This would allow some of them to live in dignity in their retirement years instead of living in a hostile environment.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Last month, I filed a question to ask whether the Government can waive stamp duty for sellers in an en bloc sale if they did not agree to the sale of the property.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Government declined to do so, and, with respect, I feel that this is unfair.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Government should not impose a tax on owners of properties when they are unwilling sellers of their property during an en bloc sale.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They are forced to sell their property due to the nature of the en bloc sale.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: A review of this policy should be considered.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the Budget, the Government plans for the future of Singapore, and I am grateful for the many considered decisions of the Government.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We frequently hear residents complain about the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And although official data does not show high inflation, I am sure many of us here in the House have our residents telling us that the cost of living keeps going up but their income cannot keep up.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have met residents who are struggling to cope.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And these are young couples who are just trying to start a family, the elderly or needy families and they are squeezed because basic costs, such as food, healthcare and education, keep rising.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I feel it is not fair to dismiss their concerns as purely the result of unrealistic expectations because they are certainly not benchmarking themselves to the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) survey, which is mostly crafted for expatriates.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On the contrary, they visit Johor Bahru and often wonder how come prices in Singapore are so high.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have also met residents who are able to cope but they are unhappy because they are running harder than ever just to stand still.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They feel they cannot even achieve what their parents had.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They lament, "We are university graduates, but our standard of living does not seem to be better than our non-graduate parents who could afford bigger houses and more luxuries when we were growing up".

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For them, every generation doing better than the previous generation is not happening. "一代好过一代" is not happening for them, but "一代好过一代" must be the objective of every government.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This allows us to keep money in our pockets and decide how to spend it rather than him deciding how to spend it for us.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When I was working in Japan, in an ironic way, I was unhappy.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Every month, when I got my paycheck, it was painful because 50% of it would automatically be deducted for taxes.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It was the same in the US when I first started working.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: More than 40% of it went to taxes and paying rent and keeping the lights on, and I had little to show for it.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, I would like to focus specifically on young families starting out.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: First, their costs are going up; and second, their income is getting very volatile.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On the cost side, they face intense pressure at this stage of their lives.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They have to cope with wedding expenses, paying for the house, planning for kids, trying very hard to afford a car, but on the income side, there seem to be fewer stable jobs as more companies move towards contract and freelance work.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many workers in the private sector not only compete against Singaporeans in what we know as meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They also compete against nationalism as practised in some foreign-owned or foreign-run companies and they are fighting forces beyond their control and they might not be doing well not because they are not trying hard enough.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must put ourselves in the shoes of such workers and not just simply dismiss their concerns.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, in such a situation, to delay or avoid having children would be altogether a very rational response.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Children are expensive, they raise the minimum income any household needs each month.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And from my conversations with residents in Marsiling-Yew Tee, this is the main contributing factor towards our low TFR.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There have been countries that have been successful in reversing a low TFR.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Their experience suggests that addressing the cost of living issues, particularly the cost of raising children, is important.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Policies in Sweden and Norway make it easier for mothers to both work and have children.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Research shows that Swedish mothers are the least conflicted and the most contented.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Childcare is affordable and of an acceptable quality, and lower income inequality puts parents under less pressure to spend on enrichment and tuition to push their kids to succeed.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Singapore, awareness of income inequality has risen and this has given recent attention to this topic.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Ms Teo Yeo Yenn pointed that out in her book "This is What Inequality Looks Like", and this topic has become coffee shop talk.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Parents are forced to spend on tuition and enrichment in an arms race to bring up the ultimate student.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While we cannot fix inequality and TFR with a magic wand, we need to help parents to stop feeling like they are not being good parents just because they are not spending thousands of dollars every month.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, Mr Speaker, I would like to make several suggestions in this debate for the Government to consider.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Residents complain that the current structure is too complicated.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Instead of a working mother’s subsidy, they would rather pay less upfront.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, instead of paying the gross and then claiming a subsidy, can they just pay net?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Government has said that different providers of preschool services is essential to safeguard consumer choice.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But many cynics would also point out that the only provider of primary school services is MOE.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is not much choice although there are many schools.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is a growing awareness that preschool affects our future performance and, hence, is important.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, let us put our money where our mouth is and make this truly affordable.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are cheaper alternatives, but quality is often not up to expectations.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some couples are lucky and may have able grandparents to help them out.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But for those who do not, it is very difficult to have kids.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is amazing to me that we are able to read a story in The Straits Times about exorbitant bus fares, and highlighting the need for better regulation.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While some might say that this is a small amount, I would say that each straw adds up until the camel’s back breaks.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Fourth, make it easier for mothers to choose between work and motherhood.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At a minimum, mothers would benefit from being allowed to work remotely and to have flexible hours.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But how many employers are enlightened, or do they need a bit of Government nudging in the right direction to do so?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have to ask ourselves: what is the value of each additional child to Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Would we consider this to be a worthwhile investment for our national resources?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If low fertility is an existential threat to the nation, then it should be given the highest priority.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore has thrown everything but the kitchen sink at this problem.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Perhaps, it is time to throw the kitchen sink!

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In terms of Government subsidy, it is only fair that the less well-off receive more and the more well-off receive less.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: For this debate, I would like to focus on the healthcare budget.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Rising healthcare cost and expenditure on the elderly are critical issues affecting our overall healthcare system and are highlighted in the recent Budget speech by Minister Heng Swee Keat last week.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: As a healthcare professional working in the public sector for the last 20 years, I can see the transformational change in our healthcare system, especially in the last eight years.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: From a previous healthcare system designed to tackle acute medical condition for a much younger population to new models of care and financial assistance schemes implemented to cater for the ageing tsunami, we have seen many changes.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I will highlight some I consider to be especially significant to acknowledge the hard work and foresightedness put in by MOH and the various health and community partners.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, I would like to salute MOH for taking on the nation’s future health challenges but, at the same time, would like to share my grave concerns for the escalating healthcare cost.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: With the increasing burden of an ageing population, and the steep and continuous increase in incidence of chronic diseases, coupled with increasing complexity in the management of chronic diseases, more can be done to promote a team-based model of care.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This model encourages healthcare professionals – doctors, pharmacists, nurses, allied health professionals – to work in synergy to provide cost-effective but holistic care to achieve positive health outcomes.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This is in line with MOH's Beyond 2020 master plan.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: We have to focus our resources to upskill and empower our allied health professionals and pharmacists in the community to take on greater roles to provide value-based care at a sustainable cost.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In my current role, I see a huge potential for allied health professionals to be engaged in the team-based collaborative practice framework where practitioners can practise at the top of their licence to be the first touchpoint for the management of certain physical, psychological, podiatry or speech-related disorders.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: One example is paediatric patients with only speech delay but without other medical conditions are seen and evaluated by doctors in polyclinics.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: However, they have to be seen by another doctor in KKH before they can be referred to our speech therapy department.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I am concerned that this leads to additional consultation costs as well as delay in seeking proper speech intervention.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Similar examples are in adult restructured hospitals as well as patients who need outpatient rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Is it not possible to streamline the process even for doctors who work within the same healthcare cluster?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Empowering allied health professionals as the first contact point under a defined criterion of a collaborative framework, coupled with the right financial subsidy framework, can free up our doctors to focus on more complex medical conditions.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This will allow our healthcare system to extend their reach to a greater population and improve accessibility to appropriate care in a more financially sustainable manner.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Take, for example, in the Queensland Health system in Australia, physiotherapists treating patients from Emergency Department (ED) triage Categories 3, 4 and 5 with a range of agreed musculoskeletal presentations.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: These roles typically involve assessment, intervention, referral for further treatment and assessment, and discharge when appropriate.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Allied health first-contact ED services assist the Hospital and Health Services to meet their National Emergency Access Targets (NEAT).

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This will, in turn, improve accessibility and affordability of medications in the community, enhance the provision of health information, improve health literacy in the community, and reduce overall healthcare expenditure.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: A 2017 systematic review published in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health looked at studies that calculated the return on investment for public health interventions.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The researchers identified 52 studies that looked at interventions at a local and national level.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: We need a holistic system to keep patients in the community.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: One example I can relate to is to provide training support to upskill our allied health professionals and pharmacists in the community setting, focusing on communication skills with the geriatric population and other health literacy skills.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Residents screened under the CHAS programme can also be referred to the community pharmacist for continued follow-up and reinforcement of a healthy and active lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that the above proposals can be considered and resources be allocated to support this new model of care through mainstream funding.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: These proposals will reduce inefficiencies, make our access and processes in healthcare leaner and reduce healthcare costs.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: For now, we have FY2018 surplus to draw on, but we need to remain prudent and constantly look for ways to remove waste in our healthcare system so as to ensure long-term sustainability.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding the above, I stand to support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.55 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.31 pm until 3.55 pm.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat had me at, quote, "Building a Strong, United Singapore" because it is a confident narrative that acknowledges our resources and strengths, alongside our challenges, as a nation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: He also had me at, quote, "We are using our financial resources to help realise our strategies for a strong, united Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But financial resources alone do not get us there." And if I may state the obvious, neither should financial well-being alone be our aim.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, "Building a Strong, United Singapore" can only be possible with a people that is mentally resilient across all ages and segments of our society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat mentioned "resilience" and "confidence" repeatedly throughout his Budget Statement.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Resilience and confidence are a result of a mentally healthy society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, mental well-being must be an ongoing national and whole-of-Government priority with the recognition that our quality of life is defined not only by markers of economic growth and our material well-being but also our subjective well-being.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must constantly question if our national policies and spending empower, beyond just enabling, our people to be ready for challenges ahead and confident of our future.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Given that, should mental health be one of the longer-term domestic challenges alongside those highlighted in the Budget speech, namely, ageing, social mobility, inequality, economic transformation and climate change?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Please allow me to share my personal experience and ground observations with the different communities I am involved with to substantiate my claim.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: My incredibly bright nephew was first diagnosed with anxiety disorder in 2017 at just 15, and later with depression last year.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: He is currently out of the school system at the promising age of 17.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The young man who works with me at one of my community projects called "A Good Space" also almost jumped off from the 15th floor of an HDB block a few years ago when he was just 19, even whilst he was on treatment for depression.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There is also the old uncle living in my block at Marine Crescent who was depressed from the death of his wife and started sleeping on the bench in the void deck at night.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Just the other day, a young taxi driver shared with me about his 87-year-old grandfather jumping to his death by climbing up the flowerpot racks along his HDB corridor after his breakfast.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: His whole family was still having their breakfast inside the flat when they heard the loud thud.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Then, there is my own close shave with depression over 12 years ago when my world collapsed at the height of professional and economic success.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: My nephew, unfortunately, is not alone in his struggle.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As our young progress to adulthood, they continue to be most at risk of suffering from mental disorders, according to the latest Singapore Mental Health Study just published in December 2018.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: My cousin is not an odd statistic either with his experience at the workplace that resulted in the deterioration of his mental health.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The mental well-being of working adults in Singapore is 13% lower than the general population according to HPB.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Further, 90% of psychological conditions with adults in Singapore have their root cause in workplace stress.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, studies have shown that an overwhelming 86.5% of those employed do not seek help for their mental health difficulties.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: My elderly neighbour and the taxi driver's grandfather are also sadly not alone in their plight.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: One in five elderly persons in Singapore aged 75 and above show signs of depression.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The number of elderly aged 60 and above who took their own lives peaked in 2017, the highest since suicide tracking started in 1991.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: An estimated one in 10 people aged 60 and above has dementia, whilst half of those aged 85 and older have it.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: One in five elderly caregivers in Singapore suffer from depression.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Six in 10 migrant workers with an injury or salary claim are likely to suffer from a serious mental illness.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Single-person-headed households struggle to seek state support, and it is generally accepted that individuals with physical and learning disabilities are at higher risk of suffering from mental health conditions although no study has been made.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Globally, this number is one in four persons.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: By way of comparison, the US is one in five and the UK is one in four.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, I would like to remind the House that the prevalence of diabetes, which we have waged a war against, is one in nine people in 2017, versus one in seven for people with mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Ageing has been rightly prominent in our national policymaking narrative and was cited as the first longer-term domestic challenge in the Budget Statement because by 2030, one in four Singaporeans will be aged 65 and above.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, there is clear and present danger that the invisible yet mounting challenge of mental health could be headed that way with the escalating prevalence.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must, therefore, make mental health a deafening priority now rather than languishing it in the shadows because mental health affects the lives of Singaporeans across all ages and all segments.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While a direct causative link cannot be drawn so simplistically, the question nonetheless stands: how does 10 out of 1,000 or one in 100 students receiving counselling become one in seven adults experiencing a mental health condition in their lifetime?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must normalise mental health and bring it out to the open.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Government and community have to learn to value mental health as a basic need, and to then reduce stigma and improve help-seeking and recovery.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We have made much progress moving from a predominantly medical approach of the past on mental health to one that is aspiring to involve every member of society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Primary care providers like polyclinics and GPs are being trained to support mental health services in non-stigmatising environments.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This year, the President’s Challenge is focusing on mental health.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, mental health is not and must not be the responsibility of MOH and the social sector alone.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: All Ministries should recognise their role in protecting Singapore’s mental health.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The impact on the mental health of any group of stakeholders, whether it be citizens, service users, staff or other, should be considered consistently and robustly in all key Government decisions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Cross-Ministerial policymaking will be required to address the burden of mental health in our society, from interventions in education, reforms in employment practices and community initiatives.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Despite the escalating prevalence among our children and youths, mental health condition programmes, such as the Holistic Health Framework by HPB, are still optional, placing the onus on schools to adopt and implement these programmes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Peer support programmes in schools and IHLs are also optional.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Mandating mental health education in our schools and IHLs is the surest signal to normalise mental health, together with providing support structures for parents and families to be equipped with emotional management skills, coping mechanisms and problem-solving skills to help our children and youths better navigate stress.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: IMH studies have clearly demonstrated that mental disorders have significant consequences on the workforce in terms of lost work productivity in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must update our employment policies to recognise and promote employee well-being by enacting clear and deliberate provisions that are upstream and preventive in nature.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Our employment laws, including the Workplace Health and Safety Act, must also explicitly include and provide for psychosocial health and safety, beyond physical health and safety.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Our social policies must place mental health as a priority for the underserved and vulnerable communities alongside basic needs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Quality of Life Standards by NCSS is a great start.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, we can and must do more in partnering these communities to design solutions that take into account their mental well-being and dignity, beyond merely fixing problems or providing services for them.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There are many ground efforts in mental health and support services, including VWOs, informal groups and social enterprises.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A group of 25 C-suite leaders and I came together to form the WorkWell Leaders Workgroup last year as a national ground-up leaders' initiative to share, discuss and co-create inclusive practices for workplace well-being.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The first-ever mental health insurance product was also launched early this year by one commercial insurer which augurs well for the surging destigmatisation efforts and also providing much needed support for those with mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: How much Singapore shares in this, we are not sure because no study has been done by the Government to date.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We could, however, surmise, with the wide-ranging impact mental health disorders have on innovation, productivity, economy and social cohesion as well as rising medical services and infrastructure needs, it might not be too far from the $2.5 billion that we expect diabetes to cost Singapore by 2050. "No other health condition in humankind has been neglected as much as mental health has", said the same Lancet Commission Report.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The way we look at mental health reminds me of climate change, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is invisible and so it gets parked mindlessly and incorrectly in the "important but not urgent" quadrant of our awareness.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, like climate change, it is our future, our young ones, that we are jeopardising most if we continue with a transactional approach in addressing this challenge.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The clarion call made by Budget 2019 to build a Strong, United Singapore is, as I read it, to bring our attention back to our biggest asset – our people.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Because "strong" and "united" are finite in concept if we merely rely on our financial resources, economic growth and pre-existing institutions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Our social cohesion cannot be taken for granted; resilient communities follow from resilient citizens.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Government must ensure its policies are underpinned by a drive to help our people thrive mentally and confidently as empowered citizens.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I strongly doubt one-off and indiscriminate bonus payouts will yield this outcome.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Neither do they engender a caring and inclusive societal attitude.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is time to redefine our values as a nation as we cherish every individual’s subjective well-being, dreams and aspirations beyond just their material and economic achievements.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It can be done and it must be done because mental health is what makes us human.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And this, surely, is what a strong, united Singapore must first and foremost always be.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am heartened by this move to show our gratitude and care for these seniors’ contributions to our nation in their silver years.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The feedback from the seniors have been very positive.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They appreciate the benefits which provide them with greater peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The reasons to reduce our reliance on foreign manpower and to accelerate adoption of automation to boost productivity are well understood.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, we must take note that there are categories of the services sector where innovative transformation is not yet ready.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For all the excitement over robotics and automation, the stage of technological development in the care sector is not yet so advanced that we can replace human caregivers and nursing aides with CP30s and R2D2s.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The six basic Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) take on various levels of complexity for the elderly at different stages of health decline.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Not all seniors have family members and foreign domestic workers (FDWs) to care for them full-time.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For those who do, caregivers need to work, study and upgrade their skills, look after children and take regular occasional breaks to avoid burnout.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Foreign manpower in the care sector, mostly Work Permit and S Pass holders, help to fill the gaps for full-time and part-time care, complementing family members and local workers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I agree with the Minister that we should not be too dependent on foreign workers, in this particular case, we have limited options.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the one hand, it would be ideal to attract more Singaporeans and Permanent Residents (PRs) to this sector.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, we just have to match care provision fees.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If we have a higher proportion of Singaporeans in the care sector, overall fees for therapies, long- and short-term care need to increase.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the other hand, will we be able to get enough Singaporeans to join this sector?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We face a double whammy – a fast-ageing population and low fertility rates.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On top of this, the younger generations are better educated and drawn to new opportunities, many in high-tech sectors, in our restructured economy.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Presently, we have access to affordable foreign workers to assist us with the care of an increasing number of elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should tap on this valuable manpower resource until the tech revolution reaches a stage where we can realistically start the transition to robotic assistants.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In their capacities as nursing assistants and aids, nurses, therapists and caregivers, they make immense contributions to our care sector, enabling family members of our seniors to contribute to other areas of our economy and nation building.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singaporeans are keenly aware of these foreigners' role in our care sector and do welcome their assistance.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Going forward, we will face competition for this pool of workers and professionals in the care sector.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is hard to say how long we can continue to attract them at our current rates of remuneration.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Japan adopted new measures last December to attract foreign workers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Other countries, such as Australia, are also beckoning.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The other issue which I am deeply concerned about is the mental health of our elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mental well-being is very important and, as part of preventive mental health, we need to help them stay active and engaged in the community through volunteering, arts and sports participation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government and private sector support and the community have to come together to make the effort to involve and integrate our elderly in our events, programmes and activities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The interaction will also help us with early detection, whether a senior is absent, not looking well or behaving differently than usual.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such observations are not possible if they are isolated or detached from their communities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When a senior shows signs of weakening mental health, including depression, dementia, Obsessive-Compulsive Disorders (OCD) and Alzheimer's, getting help for him can be very challenging.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The senior himself and the family may be in denial and resist medical assessments.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With more seniors living longer, the number of cases is expected to increase significantly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Do we have enough qualified professionals for assessments and treatment?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And where treatments do not work and seniors start to have behavourial problems, cause disturbances or pose a danger to themselves and others, what systems do we have in place to cope?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would MOH consider assigning a suitable VWO in each constituency to address this pressing need?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This VWO should already be involved in this field.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If there is no VWO involved in this area, the Government may wish to consider collaborating with an existing VWO to provide this service.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Once these seniors are identified, we can refer them to this VWO which should be within walking distance of their flats instead of requiring them to go to IMH or waiting for officers to visit these seniors to render help.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With such an infrastructure in each estate, seniors with or at risk of mental health issues will be able to age in place with support from family members, volunteers and mental health professionals.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Only when their conditions deteriorate further or pose a hazard to their communities would they need to be enrolled in institutional care.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I look forward to addressing this issue together with the Government.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Although technology is advancing by leaps and bounds, this sector’s technological advancement has not reached such an advanced stage that robots can replace nurses and caregivers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Nursing and caregiving remain a very labour-intensive sector.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Due to the less attractive job nature and remuneration, Singapore has always relied on foreign workers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Most of them are Work Permit and S Pass holders.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With a rapidly ageing population, the number of elderly who need care will only increase.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If we want to attract more Singaporeans to this sector, the salary must be increased, and seniors and their families will have to pay correspondingly higher care fees.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As Members can see, fee increase will become a problem.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To date, foreign caregiving workers are willing to work in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another topic which I am very concerned about is the mental health of the elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To maintain physical and mental health, seniors need to participate in community activities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This way, friends from the social clubs and neighbours can help monitor their physical and mental conditions.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: There is support for almost every segment of our society, from families to workers and our elderly.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Of interest to me and my generation is the MGP.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I am thankful that the Government recognises a generation that grew up in relative poverty but who had put in so much hard work to build this new nation.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Support has also been given our SMEs to help them flourish in a changing economy.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, with your indulgence, I would like to share my views on two issues, namely, on growing the economy and on the Bicentennial commemoration.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: This is important as it will mean the continued survival of our nation and I do not pretend it is an easy thing to do, something which Minister Heng Swee Keat acknowledged in his speech.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Having been involved in this process in my previous incarnation, I can see the necessity of transformation.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I have been meeting these businesses to share with them the benefits of the digital revolution.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Our SMEs can grasp that the world is changing and that their businesses must change, too.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Nevertheless, our SMEs face a myriad of challenges.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: For some, it is a matter of survival, making just enough sales to get by, while others hesitate to spend resources on something they are not sure will benefit their businesses.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: To me, transforming an economy is not just about economics.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: It is also about transforming our society, from business owners to workers, so that all levels of society embrace the spirit of change.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: My hope, Sir, is that Government agencies will continue to listen and problem-solve with us, so that we can remove roadblocks to progress and remove misconceptions that prevent businesses from embarking on change.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I am actively involved with several startups as advisor.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I am also involved with several networking sessions involving Malay/Muslim startups and entrepreneurs.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I meet many new entrepreneurs regularly, some young, some not so young.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: It is heartening to meet mid-career professionals who have decided to give entrepreneurship a go.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: And I hope that some, if not all, will succeed in making it big, thereby bringing some sense of achievement for our country as a whole.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: My concern, however, Sir, is whether such a vibrancy is felt in our heartlands.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I support the Ministry of National Development (MND) and HDB's efforts to refresh our towns, inject new businesses, and introduce new ways of encouraging interaction.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: In this regard, I would like to suggest a fresh approach to instilling innovation and entrepreneurship.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Many Singaporeans may remember replicating the exploits of Maradona or Ronaldo at the void decks, though they will also remember, too, how many at a time they incurred the anger of the immediate neighbours staying on the second floor or of the Town Council officials.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Many also may recall seeing Malay boys stripping their motorcycles to clean and make minor repairs at the void decks.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: These days, we see groups of professionals offering free repair services in the heartlands who are continuing that tradition of tinkering.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
