text: Calling themselves Repair Kopitiam, they encourage home owners to bring the broken appliances to the void decks for them to help home owners learn how to repair the appliances.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Our ability to repair things when they are broken is an important skillset that can help to reduce waste.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: These gardens have attracted residents whom we may not otherwise see in some of our grassroots events.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Some have used the produce of the gardens to raise funds for their welfare committee, while others have used the gardens as venues to conduct healthy cooking classes with HPB.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Another example I can compare this to, Sir, is the Active, Beautiful and Clean (ABC Waters) programme which I initiated as Minister for the Environment and Water Resources.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Before the ABC Waters programme came about, there used to be many signs across our reservoirs warning the public not to do a variety of things near or in the reservoir.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: But to the credit of PUB, they accepted my idea and created new recreational spaces out of our drains and reservoirs.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: More importantly, our reservoirs and water bodies are now full of life and activities.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I am hopeful that if we do this right, we can turn our void decks into places of energy, life and creativity.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: It requires, of course, our authorities to move away from an attitude of so strictly regulating these spaces that they have become sterile, void of life.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: We want to strike a balance so that some messiness is possible, but, in return, the neighbourhoods of our heartlands can become the birthplaces of mutual support, practical ingenuity and great ideas.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Interestingly enough, these measures are parked under the pillar of building a caring and inclusive society.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The Prime Minister in his 2018 New Year's Day message called for us to use the Bicentennial "to reflect on how our nation came into being, how we have come this far since, and how we can go forward together".

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Since then, there have been several exhibitions, events, talks and opinion pieces about this occasion.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: While there is broad-based support for the commemoration, there are also voices of concern and unease.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: A certain Mr Osman Sidek wrote to the Straits Times and his letter was published in the 4 February 2019 issue.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: In it, he raised the insightful point that colonialism cannot just be presented from one community's perspective.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The impact of colonialism on the indigenous population and their sense of loss and justice need also to be acknowledged.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: But he cautioned that the unhappiness is not directed at history, but at the very idea of colonialism or, specifically, how one could lose one’s own country to colonisers.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: He appealed for us to reflect on how such a historical event could have happened and that Singaporeans must endeavour never again to lose our own country to another.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: And he ended by asking us, having experienced colonial rule, to empathise with those societies "whose lands are occupied against their will, even in this day and age".

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: If we are to build an inclusive society, as mentioned by the Minister for Finance, then we need to ensure that inclusivity applies not just to how we view the here and now, but also how we view our history as a people.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to acknowledge that different communities have different historical experiences and memories.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to recognise both the good and the bad.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The coming of the British and the start of colonial rule in this region is an important event for all of us to reflect upon.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: After all, the very language we use today in education, commerce and many other facets of our life is a colonial heritage.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: But we need also to be cognisant that there are winners and losers in history.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: And history is written by the winners for the winners.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Eighteen nineteen is marked as a turning point in our history.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: And yet the sacking of a once-vibrant Malacca Sultanate in 1511 by the Portuguese has also been highlighted by some historians as a turning point for this region.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Some have speculated that it marked the death of the indigenous mercantile class, leaving the region more vulnerable to conquest by succeeding waves of European colonisers.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The first myth is that Singapore was a fishing village waiting to be discovered and transformed into a modern metropolis.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: And I quote here from the historian Peter Borschberg from his article "Singapore as a Port City, 1290-1819: Evidence, Frameworks and Challenges".

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I quote, "There is an enduring perception in our historical consciousness that before the arrival of Raffles, Singapore remained unrecognised and underappreciated fallow land.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: However, as we dig deeper into the past, the mirror of history unabashedly refutes the belief that Singapore was a sleepy backwater kampung, forgotten or neglected by the powers that trawled these waters for centuries.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Similarly, it is also a misguided notion that no one had envisaged the presence of a port in Singapore before 1819.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The impetus here is a larger one, not only for the history of the port but also for Singapore's history as a whole – one cannot remain obstinate in only thinking about Singapore in terms of an East India Company (EIC) settlement.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: While the transformative hand of the EIC and the British on Singapore is beyond doubt, there is a history of a port, settlement and island that runs far deeper than historians had surmised until about the beginning of the third millennium.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore was also far more intimately connected to its historical predecessors as well as its locational context."  Sir, this is an important point.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: It is right that we acknowledge every event for what it is worth.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The coming of the colonialists changed the region forever.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: As it turns out, Singapore today is a thriving metropolis.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: But to overly ascribe this success to the coming of the British is to ignore larger forces at work well before the arrival of the British.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: This myth has been studied and debunked extensively, for instance, by the late Prof Syed Hussein Alatas in his famous book entitled "The Myth of the Lazy Native", which tore apart the colonial ideology behind labelling the indigenous population as lazy for not wanting to work in the mines and plantations.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Nevertheless, that still lingers in the minds of some people.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: When I was growing up in modern Singapore, my own teachers dismissed my community as being lazy and unable to study hard.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: I would also add that our history is intertwined with the history of the region.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Our history points to certain truths about this region and Singapore.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: That I think is a point that needs to be stressed more by this commemoration.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: In this way, more, especially our young, will understand how Singapore has been and will continue to be a part of the larger region, tapping on its good location and the talent of our diverse peoples to provide a peaceful hub for mutually beneficial trade and commerce.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: The diversity that we see here in Singapore reflects the diversity of the region and beyond.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: When I walk the corridors of the HDB flats in my constituency, I can hear different voices, dialects and languages.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: My friends who hail from Bugis or Minang ancestry are proud of their heritage.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: We should use this commemoration to celebrate the diversity that defines who we are and to promote a better understanding and appreciation for the long and rich history of Singapore and this region.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, I hope that this will not just be a one-off commemoration.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: National education at the higher primary and lower secondary levels can be expanded so that Singaporeans better understand the colonial experiences of our ASEAN neighbours.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Talk about both the good and the bad so that we know ourselves better and will never again be divided or colonised.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: Being part of this region, I strongly believe that we should have a good understanding and appreciation of the region’s history.

speaker: Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, acknowledging how that history has impinged on our own history and the myriad strands of diversity of ideas, lifestyle, food, religions that have come together to enrich our own experience as both Singaporeans and Southeast Asians.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It became clear that it could not be business as usual for Singapore and there was a need for the Government to chart out a transformation plan for our economy and our people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This came amidst addressing all the daily challenges of Singaporeans, like increasing cost of living, an ageing population, healthcare costs, concern over social inequality and struggles of the sandwich class.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The daily struggles are real, and support needed to be given.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But there was also a real need to nudge our people and our businesses to evolve so as to be prepared for the changing times and ensure a sustainable economy for the nation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This year's Budget has built on the past efforts to transform the economy and support Singaporeans through the changes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are clearly different views on the Budget, but the general sense was that it was generous in many ways, leading many to ask if it is an Election Budget.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe that this Budget is a comprehensive one, which seeks to address current concerns that have been raised by Singaporeans but yet stay on track with the economic transformation which Singapore needs to undergo.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The approach taken by the Government in giving social support has always been a targeted one, seeking to focus attention where support is really needed and to provide a solution that is sustainable.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Often, it is a calibration, and it is sometimes hard to say if the help given is sufficient.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Over time, after implementation, upon assessment of whether the support given has achieved its desired outcomes, and upon review of changing circumstances, there may be a need to adjust policies and schemes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is imperative to ensure that the implementation of the various policies and schemes translates into effective solutions for people and there is always room for improvements.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am, therefore, glad to see the willingness of the Government to make the appropriate changes when necessary.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many Members and I have highlighted the challenges faced by the elderly and the concern about recurring healthcare costs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: CHAS was one scheme which could alleviate some of these issues.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For the Budget to completely achieve its desired outcomes, everyone needs to play a part.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This sense of responsibility and ownership is necessary if Singapore is to survive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The community needs to come together and do its part.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have many schemes and programmes in place, but there will always be gaps and those who fall through the cracks.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The community plays an important role to complete the support network and close the gaps.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are many examples of people who have stepped up and took ownership by being the change that they want to see.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat spoke about the SG Cares movement, and I am happy to hear that there will be efforts to continue building on this movement.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is common knowledge that there are many examples of everyday heroes who also contribute towards our growth as a community of care and contribution.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One of these heroes is Magdalene Ong, the mother of 14-year-old Chalmers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Chalmers was diagnosed with mild to moderate autism when he was 18 months old.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Magdalene was relentless in sending Chalmers for therapies and treatments, with the desire to find out his interests and gifts so that she could support him.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Chalmers turned out to be a talented artist.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Empowered by this experience, she felt the need to do something for special needs children from underprivileged families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She started organising sessions for many families with special needs children to expose them to art, music and sports.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I was introduced to Magdalene by one of my residents, Anita, who told me that the group needed a space.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I was more than happy to offer a room at the Bukit Batok East Community Club.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The best part of the story is that the group has since formed a choir called the Singapore Special Voices.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Since last year, they have been going to places like Alexandra Hospital and Bright Hill Evergreen Home for Dementia to spread cheer to patients and the elderly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Magdalene believes that the children can give back to society in their own way and is taking the effort to make that path for them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Another example of someone who has stepped up is Coco Oan Jia Xuan.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Coco is a young environmentalist who is a resident of Bukit Batok East.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In 2016, she started Project bECOme which aims to reduce single-use waste by engaging with businesses, organisations and members of the public.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One of the programmes under this project is the CNY Container Donation Drive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Coco and her volunteers collected plastic cookie bottles from the public, washed them and donated them to various beneficiaries for reuse.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The beneficiaries included bakers, eco-enzyme makers, gardeners, handicraft makers and zero-waste stores.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In 2013, she started a non-profit group Back2Basic which delivers free groceries to beneficiaries, such as home-bound elderly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Noor is also a co-founder of Interfaith Youth Circle, which seeks to promote a better understanding of the role that faith can play in an increasingly divided world.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Do you see the common thread in the stories I have shared?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: That is not to say that there are no male heroes, but I would like to take this opportunity to celebrate the efforts made by our women activists and volunteers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They have defied traditional expectations and made great strides to change society’s preconceived notions and habits.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On this note, I would like to touch on the status of women in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: While women here have access to education and jobs and we have representation of women in many key positions in leadership, there is still much that we can do.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In doing all these, beyond setting numerical goals, it is important to get the whole community, men and women, on board to change cultural mindsets and progress together.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   We have witnessed many changes globally over the past few years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These changes will transform world economies and have an impact on our way of life.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Government is aware of this and has to transform our economy so that we can stay resilient and be able to compete globally and, at the same time, prepare to help our people during this challenging period of transformation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This year's Budget builds on past efforts in order to prepare our country and Singaporeans for the future.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Singaporeans count on a Government that is sincere and cares for the people's well-being.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is undoubtedly the responsibility of any government.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, developing the nation and helping Singaporeans are a collective responsibility.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, it is important that we all come together and work hand-in-hand in efforts that can be beneficial to society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This combination of three important agencies within our community – the Council for the Development of the Singapore Malay/Muslim Community (MENDAKI), the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (MUIS) and the People’s Association Malay Activity Executive Committees Council (MESRA) – with the support of other Government agencies, local Malay/Muslim bodies, professionals, academics, entrepreneurs and other individuals, it is hoped to produce efforts that can assist and support more members of our community so that they can progress further.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am aware that much is being done.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I hope that more information can be shared so that we know more about the M3 efforts and the type of community involvement that is required.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): Singaporeans are intelligent and discerning people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Having one Budget with some perks will not necessarily sway people at elections.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At the end of the day, the Government will be judged on how it has performed throughout the term and whether it has taken the effort to make life better for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The people want a Government that is responsible, cares, works hard and is transparent.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, nation-building and making lives better for Singaporeans require a collective effort.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For us to breathe life into the various policies and schemes, we all need to take ownership.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We can give constructive feedback to improve policies and their implementation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We can take action to close the gaps and be the change we want to see.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I hope for a whole-of-Government, whole-of-community approach in its implementation so as achieve the best for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But several announcements this year have particular significance to women which I wish to highlight.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It happens that this is our Bicentennial year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When we look back at history, it is clear that women contributed as much as men to building up modern Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Not many of us would have heard the name.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But Mdm Hajjah was a tradeswoman and philanthropist who came to Singapore in the 1800s.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Just eight years after starting her career as a librarian in 1952, Mdm Anuar became the first Singaporean to be appointed as the Director of the National Library.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Her leadership laid solid foundations for the modern library system that Singaporeans still enjoy and it benefited generations of avid readers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is also Mdm Mary Quintal, one of the first 10 women in Singapore to begin police training in 1949.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: She excelled in a field which was traditionally dominated by men.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, our Criminal Investigation Department (CID) is headed by a woman.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Then, there is Mdm Gloria Lim, an expert on fungi, who became the first woman to be named Dean of the Faculty of Science at the University of Singapore, and later on, as the first Foundation Director at the National Institute of Education when it was set up in 1991.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our women Pioneers set solid foundations for the generations after them, so that we can all advance and progress in society.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over the next few months, the Singapore Bicentennial Office will be working with our community partners to breathe these stories and many more to life.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Their stories serve to remind us that, we too, should strive to continue laying strong foundations for our children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren, so that when they look back in history in time to come, they will be able to see how women have continued to progress and played a pivotal role in our country's development.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: During the COS debate, MOM will outline measures to further support women in our workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Besides these outstanding women and many others who contributed in the workforce or through their involvement in the social sectors, there is one particular group which is not often mentioned and I would like to talk about them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These are the many housewives and homemakers who toil to care for their families so that their husbands can work, comforted in the knowledge that someone is tending to the needs at home, caring for elderly parents and other relatives and raising the children to be upright citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Being a housewife was the default choice for many women long ago.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There were few other options until after Independence, when girls were given good access to education and women could also advance in the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, even today, when women have more choices, many dedicate their lives to their families by staying home to personally care for them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some of our homemakers left the workforce years ago and are now in their 50s and 60s.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We do not say it often enough, but their sacrifices did not just make a difference to their families, they also made a difference to our nation-building.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It recognises that they had fewer years to build up their retirement savings.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is why I welcome the Bicentennial Bonus.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But it is also worth noting that the Government's care and support for older women go well beyond one-time gestures like top-ups.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, the life expectancy of women in Singapore is 85 years old.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is a fact that we live longer and will possibly outlive our loved ones.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many schemes introduced by the Government do, in fact, benefit women more.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Similarly, in time to come, more of the benefits of the PGP will be enjoyed by women.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For Budget 2019, further measures, such as the MGP and CareShield Life Incentive, will help to ensure that older women are taken care of.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many initiatives like CHAS enhancements and new nursing homes will help older women as we age – ourselves, our mothers, our sisters and everyone we, as women, very often and are now having to care for.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many programmes in the community, too, benefit older women, such as health screenings organised by the grassroots volunteers in partnership with other VWOs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We do not usually apply the gender lens when debating our Budget, but when we do, it is clear that every Budget benefits women in significant ways.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And they all add up to a lot of support for women.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (In Mandarin):   As the saying goes, "Women play a very important role as the other pillar of the world".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many women in their 50s and 60s helped their husbands to support their families when they were younger, so that their husbands were able to work with peace of mind.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These women made great contributions to our economy and social development during the early post-Independence period.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many of these senior women chose to leave the workforce in order to care for their children and also their elderly parents.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a result, they sacrificed the opportunities to save for their retirement needs and, compared to other citizens, their savings are relatively lower.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This one-off Bicentennial Bonus clearly acknowledges the contributions and sacrifices that these women have made for society.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, Singapore is commemorating our Bicentennial this year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As we reflect on the modern development of our country, we should also draw on precious lessons from the past so that we can progress to greater heights.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: During the early years of nation-building, our mothers, grandmothers and mothers-in-law went through a lot of hardship.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Most of them were not able to complete their education.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Instead, they had to enter the workforce or shouldered the huge responsibilities of looking after their families.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The sacrifices and commitments they made laid a solid foundation for Singapore to achieve great success so that we can enjoy the great opportunities that we enjoy now.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Moving forward, we need to think about the foundations that we would be laying for our children, our grandchildren and the next generations, so that when they look back in history, they, too, will be able to see that women in Singapore continue to have great opportunities for progress.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (In English): Deputy Speaker, I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In this year's Budget, he added a fourth trend – the decline in support for globalisation and rising geopolitical uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Put together, the world we live in today is much more volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous (VUCA) for short.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Adapting to a VUCA world, VUCA is a term developed by the US Army War College at the end of the Cold War, but it has been most recently adopted by the millennial generation as a description of the unstable world that we are inheriting.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The young are not unaware of the challenges that face us today and in the future.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In this VUCA world, we think about how much the nationalist and anti-globalisation trends will affect our economy in Singapore and, in particular, our jobs.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: We worry about whether we can afford the increasing cost of living and supporting our elders and providing for our children.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: While we are familiar with technology, we also see how technological progress can overtake us in some of our jobs.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: And with technology, we also see how countries have taken to cyber warfare, where attacks can come silently and unpredictably.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: But we young Singaporeans also know that it is in our Singaporean DNA to adapt, overcome and excel.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I am confident that we can strengthen our Singapore DNA to weather this VUCA world and prepare ourselves for the future.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: That is why it is heartening to see this year's Budget address these challenges head on.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to focus on a few themes from this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: For a small state like Singapore, survival and success are two sides of the same coin.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Innovation is becoming a driving force in our economy and globally.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In order to realise the vision of becoming the Global-Asia node of technology, innovation and enterprise, we have to continually reinvent ourselves to stay ahead of the curve.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Speaking at a Ministerial forum at the Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) last year, Prime Minister Lee said that good design thinking was a key reason for Singapore's successful journey from Third World to First, and it will be critical in the country's future transformation for it to remain an outstanding city in the world.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: He further explained that design is a core element of Singapore's nation-building.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Increasingly, organisations in Singapore are seeing the value of design thinking and are starting to adopt it as part of their operational strategy.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Global institutions like DesignThinkers Academy are also setting roots in Singapore to develop a fresh pool of design thinkers to cope with the increased demand for design thinking professionals in these dynamic and trying times.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The basic building blocks of a vibrant economy are strong, competitive companies that maximise value creation.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Design thinking is not just a niche brand.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is critical that all our companies, especially SMEs, adopt this innovation strategy.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The question is: how do we make sure design thinking and innovation become mainstream for all our companies?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened by this year's Budget focus on investing in our people, including young Singaporeans, to provide them with opportunities to gain working experience abroad.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Our youths are ready to venture abroad and to gain valuable work experience and contribute back to our economy.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: However, the Global Ready Talent Programme alone is not enough.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: We have to also transform our IHLs to prepare our youths to be ready for the future.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: One such programme that does that is SMU-X.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Pioneered at Singapore Management University (SMU) in 2015, the SMU-X is an experiential learning framework where students tackle real-world challenges by taking on projects from corporate, non-profit and Government sector organisations both locally and internationally.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: SMU-X has been lauded by global accreditation body Association to Advance Collegiate Schools of Business (AACSB) as an "innovation that inspires".

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I strongly urge the hon Minister to look into expanding such programmes across all IHLs to prepare our youths for the future workforce.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Another area I would like to highlight in my speech is the WIS programme, which is a key pillar of our social security system to mitigate inequality in the working years.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is said that low-wage workers receive annual WIS payouts of up to $4,000.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Based on Annex D-1 in the Budget Statement, if Members look at the 35-44 age group, the maximum annual WIS payout for employees is only $1,700 and $1,133 for self-employed persons.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, these individuals receive just 40% in cash, with the remaining 60% going to their CPF.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: If you work out the monthly cash component, it is a mere $56.70 and $37.80 for employees and the self-employed respectively.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Increasingly, I am seeing more young people entering the gig economy just to make ends meet, often taking on two or three jobs and scraping by monthly.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Government considers this proposal and perhaps the inevitable GST hike can help to offset the spending.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Having said that, the Bicentennial Budget has clearly signalled its commitment to build a caring and inclusive Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: As a youth, I welcome the announcement of MGP that is set to benefit about half a million Singaporeans covering their healthcare subsidies for life.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: At the end of the day, they are Singaporeans and they have contributed to our nation over the years.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The other slew of measures aimed at helping Singaporeans is also much appreciated.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: As part of the Government's commitment to address climate change and reduce emissions, and in line with Budget 2017 and Budget 2018 announcements, the Carbon Pricing Act (CPA) and its accompanying Regulations came into operation on 1 January 2019.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: While the carbon tax will not apply directly to households, the implementation of such a tax on industries will see a cascading effect on end consumers.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Although the impact is expected to be minimal in the short term, any subsequent increase in the carbon tax rate may have a more significant impact on end consumers.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Can the hon Minister share more on the cost and effects of the carbon tax in the long run?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is a result of human effort and imagination.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: As we mark the Bicentennial year, we have to reflect on what has made Singapore succeed in the past and, more critically, what would be important for its continued survival and success in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: A national Budget is a strategic plan to allocate resources across competing needs – be it defence, economic, human, social or environmental.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Some of these needs are current, others involve investing for and securing the future.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat has struck a fine balance in addressing these varying demands, with an eye on maintaining fiscal prudence.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe this year's Budget seeks to shape the country's competitiveness and continuing relevance on the world stage in times of increasing uncertainty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to start by commending the Government for crafting a Budget that is inclusive and which addresses many important challenges facing Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We are devoting considerable resources to economic restructuring, ageing and public infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But let us consider why are these ongoing MediSave top-ups necessary, why are operating expenditures on healthcare increasing significantly, and why have operating expenditures on transport risen sharply?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We have a rapidly ageing population and many of our Pioneers do not have substantial retirement savings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We have an ageing public transport system, and we have been catching up on maintenance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We need to fulfill our commitment to the public to deliver the high quality of services they deserve.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the unasked question is: why are operating expenditures needed now when many of these systems were designed to be prefunded?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This Government has always expected and planned for the population to age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, the question is: to what extent were our lifecycle costs anticipated and prefunded versus unanticipated and, therefore, requiring new expenditure today?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Let us consider MediSave, although a similar story exists for rail infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I note that in 1983, the Government’s operating subsidy was 90% for Class C wards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But MediSave projections were made based on a 50% subsidy only.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, MediSave was part of a broader prefunding strategy to not only cover the majority of hospitalisation expenses but also, if finances allow, to gradually rebalance the distribution of medical costs towards prefunding and away from operating subsidies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: To what extent and why has MediSave not worked out completely as planned?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The pace of medical advances, and hence costs, have been rapid.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Some of these factors were expected, others were not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I say this not to bury MediSave but to praise it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is the hallmark of a good government to plan ahead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We can certainly disagree about the best way to distribute the burden of medical costs between different segments of society, or even different generations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The broader point I want to make is that given the complex long-term challenges facing Singapore, we should not expect any one institution, including the Government, to have perfect foresight and knowledge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I will touch on three institutions that each could be strengthened in specific ways and where each has a role to play in policymaking: Parliament, Civil Society and Academia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Parliament must hold the Executive to account and must have the expertise and resources to discharge this function well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, in all parliamentary systems, including ours, there is a natural imbalance of power.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Executive is supported by our highly qualified and well-resourced Civil Service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But Members of Parliament, in performing their duties, must rely on their own knowledge and networks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, all hon Members make valuable contributions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Hon Members from Law and Medicine are experts in their profession.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Hon Members from the Labour Movement have Union support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And all elected Members reflect the views of their constituents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But Members do not enjoy automatic access to the relevant professional expertise to contribute to complex policy debates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are already Parliamentary institutions that play an important role in holding the Executive to account.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Under the Standing Orders, Parliament has formed the Public Accounts Committee and the Estimates Committee to provide independent oversight on how the Executive manages public funds and expenditure policies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These Select Committees have been diligent in following up on Government lapses and in examining the implementation of policies enacted in each year’s Budget.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But, Sir, our Parliamentary system is largely inquisitorial.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It relies on our Parliamentarians asking hard questions of the Executive, and having the Civil Service respond.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Hon Members do not shy away from asking critical questions when needed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But there is no formal capacity to assist Parliament in coming up with independent answers to the policy problems that face Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I suggest that we strengthen our Parliamentary Committees by commissioning expert secretariat staff that answer to the Committees and not the Ministries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are examples elsewhere of professional institutions that support elected representatives in their role of overseeing the Executive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: At the level of the individual Member of Parliament, I believe more support for Legislative and Secretarial Assistants could be useful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I understand we want a lean and cost-conscious Parliament.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But, Sir, in recognition of the increasing complexities of policymaking, this support should be reviewed and enhanced, particularly for Members serving on Committees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If I may add a point of personal interest, Nominated Members of Parliament also would benefit from engaging Parliamentary Assistants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This would help ensure that personal wealth and career considerations do not stand in the way of being able to serve fully.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Next, let me turn to strengthening civil society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our NGOs and think tanks have shown both policy expertise and, crucially, a passion to make a difference for Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For civil society and academia to engage the Government in providing meaningful collaboration and debate on the issues that matter, we must have more access to information outside Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is not helpful to talk about the problems of retirement adequacy or the barriers facing women in the labour force unless we have a common understanding on what the facts actually are.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While there have been great efforts to publish Government data through sources, such as data.gov.sg, more can be done in key social areas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are, of course, legitimate concerns that Government has about releasing more information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Information could be exploited to sow sectarian divisions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are privacy and legal concerns, especially for commercially sensitive data, personal finances, and healthcare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is the simple problem of limited resources to organise and publish the data, and nearly unlimited wants for information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The displayed chart shows the top Ministries with a PQ requesting data.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: With the help of research assistants, we coded whether a question requests data, and whether that data was provided in the answer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The top five Ministries with data requests are MOM, MND, MOH, the Ministry of Transport and the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Now, we are still studying PQs before 2018, whether the answers given are complete, and what are the reasons for not providing data.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: These answers show that much information held by the Government is of public interest, is readily available, and by releasing them, poses no significant sensitivities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Therefore, I propose that information released in response to PQs be prioritised for permanent regular statistical release.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Since most data today is already collected through administrative and ongoing sources, the marginal costs are low and consist largely of setting up the system to enable release.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The Transparency Fund could further provide for research that provides interpretation and guidance on how to use these data.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Indeed, the problem of fake news often is not that the information itself is fake, it is rather that it is taken grossly out of context and used to sow divisions in society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But that is why the Government must take the lead in providing information, in providing guidance and education on how to use and understand it, and to accept that there will be honest disagreements from time to time on what the facts mean.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The Government has agreed that we must build a strong local core in academia, especially in the areas of social sciences and humanities, which are not only relevant as sources of expertise for Government policy, but also help us understand who we are.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Indeed, many of the problems this Budget addresses are topics that academics in Singapore have devoted their careers to studying.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: However, the data on our local core is more sobering.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: However, Singaporean representation is much stronger among teaching staff rather than faculty, and among older staff aged 50 and above.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: There are several schemes underway to encourage promising young Singaporeans to join academia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But I think it is too early to say what progress will be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: We want and must have Singaporeans in academia and in research, not to protect their jobs, not to allow for lower standards in teaching and research, but because Singaporeans must be in charge of asking the critical questions about who we are, what the problems in society are and how to solve them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: We have always said that no one owes us a living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But no one owes us an answer either, about the key questions of our society and economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: We are frankly too small for experts from elsewhere to want to study us thoroughly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: In any case, we should never depend on them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The first barrier is that the academic will find it difficult to study Singapore questions without the active cooperation of the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Academic credibility depends on being able to publish independent research findings based on high-quality data or observations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Much of this data is held by the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Hence, research and publication often depend on Government agreement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The same principles of information disclosure I have outlined earlier for civil society will likewise help local academics contribute and build their careers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But because the Government often works closely with Singapore academics in research, I also urge the Government to be more accepting of research results that may be inconsistent with official narratives or policies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Many local academics supported the Government’s rebuttal of the Oxfam study last year which ranks Singapore in the bottom 10 globally on tackling inequality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But the Government must be cognisant that it has much more power than a mere academic has, and there should be room for even disagreeable academics to contribute to Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Second, our autonomous universities must recognise that local research that contributes to policy and our understanding of society is valuable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: There is a structural problem with prestige in academia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: We all want high quality and internationally renowned research institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But university rankings are based on publications and citations in top ranked international journals, and there is simply little international interest in Singapore questions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Therefore, research on Singapore is less likely to be published in the prestigious journals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Much Government work has benefited from the quiet contributions of local academics, through research collaborations, consultancies and advisory panels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But these contributions are quiet, and simply do not count, compared to the loud signals that journal publications provide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: To address this, I urge the Government and the autonomous universities to systematically document and acknowledge the contributions of local academics to policy and society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Third, careers in academia are based presently on the prevailing international model that an academic must get on the tenure track as soon as possible and devote their best years to publishing internationally relevant research.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But policy and public work are not just a side line to academic work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Instead, I believe it actually enhances and strengthens research and teaching.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Anecdotally, in the early days of Singapore, it seems it was more common for academics to devote time outside the academy to building up Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I believe this practice should be continued today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I wish to address my friends in Government directly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Your party may well be in power, but it may be a different party with less integrity and less ability than today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Or it may not be in power at all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I know that hon Members who serve in this Government firmly believe that Singapore's best chance of success lies with the continued governance of their party.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Voters agree and that is why this Government has enjoyed an uninterrupted mandate since Independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: If and when that happens, to set and keep Singapore on the right path, let us invest today to have institutions in place that allow Singaporeans to speak from a position of strength on the issues of the day and challenge any future Government they feel is not acting in the best interests of Singaporeans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are so many factors he has to address to keep our economy vibrant and society inclusive.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Out of these factors, one of the trickiest is the transformation of our economy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For the past few years and past few Budgets, we have been tackling it, but there are still many challenges ahead.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This year, the companies, especially SMEs, are really feeling the pinch.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I will reflect some of their opinions and suggestions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As a result, many service providers have lost money overnight.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They have contracts signed with the old price and they are not allowed to claim for material price fluctuation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some of them even asked me, "Is it because the Government needs money badly?" This tax increase might have a domino effect on other prices.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This has eaten into the take-home pay of taxi drivers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But since Comfort made over $400 million in profit last year, I feel they missed an opportunity to show some magnanimity.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At least, absorb part of the price hike.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Taxi drivers already toil day and night, and they earn just enough to support their family.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should not be adding to their burden.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He was ready to give back the Carbon Tax collection to businesses as grants for companies to implement measures to reduce their carbon footprint.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will he do the same for this collection from diesel price hike?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If the Government cannot do this, then I would like to appeal to large corporations not to transfer the full price hike to their workers and customers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This could set off a domino effect of rising prices across the economy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many in the service sector are already crying.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They are facing problems like higher rental, no local workers and so on.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With the tightening of S Pass quotas by one-third over two years, many businesses, especially the smaller ones, feel that their operation will be greatly affected.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They have invested a lot in training their current workers and it would be a waste to send them back.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Because local workers generally do not want to work on evenings and weekends, businesses might even have to scale down operations.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The new reduced quota will apply only when they apply for S Pass or when they reduce the local workforce.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In this way, the impact on the operations of our businesses, especially the smaller SMEs, will be minimised.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They will not lose foreign workers who have already been trained.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As Lianhe Zaobao reported, in restaurants, people look forward to chatting with the waitress and hearing her off-menu recommendations.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One resident also wrote to me saying that when she went shopping in Taiwan, the sales lady made recommendations and even took extra care when wrapping.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It was the best service she had ever encountered in her life.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She said if the foreign worker quota goes down further and Singaporeans will not do such jobs full-time, then the staff turnover rate will be high.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Staff will not have time to learn how to provide proper service.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Since Singapore is already more expensive to shop in, we need good service to draw locals and tourists to spend in Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Minister can consider my proposal of letting the businesses retain their current foreign workers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, can the Government help to rebrand the service sector to make it more "sexy", more appealing to our local workers, especially the younger ones?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We used to have great shortages in local school teachers, nurses, security guards.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Now, we have overcome it to a certain extent.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure our Government can do it one more time for our service sector.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many agree that we need to catch up on many fronts if we want to be a Smart Nation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The SMEs and Government agencies are opening up their system for exchange of data.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Admittedly, the SMEs' systems would never be as robust as those of the Government agencies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope these agencies can develop a standard protocol for exchange of data, which will maintain data security while being manageable for the SMEs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For example, IRAS and MOM have established Application Programming Interface (API) platforms which do not require SMEs to test their servers separately.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These systems also should not impose exorbitant compliance costs for the SMEs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For example, the Energy Market Authority (EMA) exchanges consumption and household data with open electricity market providers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore Power (SP) has been managing the data for electricity.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It demanded that the companies' servers for data transfer must be tested annually and this costs over $10,000 every year!

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To enter the electricity market, these companies already had to set up a new Accounting System which costs about $100,000 with billing.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some of them thought of asking SP to do the billing, which will be more convenient for residents as SP still bills them for water.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I ask the EMA to keep a close eye on this, because if the providers cannot handle the costs and go bust, it will cause great inconvenience to citizens.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Enterprise Singapore (ESG) should help with such compliance costs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, ESG states that if it is Government requirements, no help can be extended.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The help to our SMEs has to be more coordinated and focused.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In a similar vein, some practices by agencies are very unproductive.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This afternoon, my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Ang Wei Neng, had mentioned some.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For building contractors, agencies require long processes of applying for service diversion, power, water and so on, and require lots of manpower just to watch other people do work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I will share more details in the COS debate on MND.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have a 62-year-old resident, after working for 24 years in an international airline company, was asked if he would like to have re-employment up to age 67.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As he is still healthy, obviously, he said yes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He was then asked whether he was willing to take on extra job scope from his younger colleagues.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Later on, the company told him he has to take a 40% pay cut.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government can relook this issue.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is not the first time I have heard from my residents on such unfair treatment from their employers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I move on to measures that directly impact families.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The MGP is very welcome, especially the help on medical expenses.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope MG Singaporeans will take advantage of the $4,000 incentive to join CareShield Life.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It will give them and their family some peace of mind, that they will be taken care of if they unfortunately become severely disabled.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Just like when MediShield Life was launched, we should conduct CareShield Life consultations at all CCs, too.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This will help middle-aged and senior Singaporeans figure out how much they have to pay for CareShield Life and encourage them to sign up.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I was also struck by the CPF top-ups for Singaporeans aged between 50 and 64 who do not have sufficient CPF savings.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many of those who would benefit would be women who have been housewives for most of their lives.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is a great way to help this group achieve retirement adequacy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is also a way to show our appreciation to all of them for their sacrifices.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I urge families to take the chance to top up more for your mums and wives.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: You will get a tax relief of up to $7,000 for doing this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But more importantly, it is to show her how much you appreciate her sacrifices.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On the Bicentennial Bonus, what is interesting about the bonus is that it favours the middle- and lower-income.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Although almost everyone gets something, the lower-income get more in the form of GST Cash Vouchers and WIS top-ups.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This reflects that our society is, indeed, doing its utmost to help those in need.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Malay):   The diesel tax imposed was too abrupt and it surprised many SMEs, taxi drivers and delivery workers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Government help those affected so that they can use this assistance to buy fuel that is more environmentally friendly?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Assistance provided can be similar to the one for the carbon tax.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to appeal to the bigger companies to avoid taking advantage by transferring this tax to workers and customers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This may cause a domino effect and affect our nation's economy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   The diesel tax increase announced in the Budget took effect immediately.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This has upset many SMEs, taxi drivers and delivery drivers who saw their costs increase overnight.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The purpose of diesel tax is to promote more eco-friendly fuels.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Would it be like last year's carbon tax, which would be returned to the people in the form of grants so that they can use more eco-friendly fuels?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This could set off a domino effect of rising prices across the economy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I would like to conclude with a story.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He has an Ah Gong who loves him very much.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Ah Gong scrimps and saves, always mending his clothes over and over, trying to save every penny he could.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Every three to five years, Ah Gong would give a sum of money to his grandson.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For example, when Ah Seng went to university, Ah Gong would give him some money.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When Ah Seng went overseas to attend immersion programmes, Ah Gong would also give him some money.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When Ah Seng got married, Ah Gong also gave him some money.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When Ah Seng and his friends want to start a business, Ah Gong also gave him some money.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One day, Ah Seng asked Ah Gong, "Ah Gong, why do you give me money every three to five years?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why don't you give me money every year?" After Ah Gong heard this, he was very upset and also very angry.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Ah Gong burst out in Hokkien, "You terrible child!

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: You have such a great grandfather and you don't know it.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I scrimped and saved all because of you.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are all the other grandfathers as good as I am?" Mr Deputy Speaker, my residents all know we have a very good Government that is very conscientious in taking care of us, taking care of our Reserves.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is because of this that we are able to enjoy a Budget surplus, and therefore, we can have this MGP, we can have the PGP.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Not every Government in the world can achieve that.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, on behalf of my Nee Soon South residents, I would like to thank our Finance Minister and our Government.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Budget Statement 2019 outlines the Government's strategic plans to build a strong and united Singapore – a nation that is safe and secure, powered by a vibrant economy and inclusive society, prepared for the future through sound fiscal policies and, above all, a global city we can call home.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: While the Government takes the lead in creating useful policies, systems and platforms for businesses and individuals to succeed, every one of us can and must do our part to build Singapore together.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Budget 2019 is an inclusive Budget that highlights our commitment to ensuring that all Singaporeans, particularly the most vulnerable groups, have universal access to healthcare.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I urge all seniors to continue to take good care of their health, and also keep themselves socially active through sports, arts, volunteerism and lifelong learning.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Make good use of your senior concession travel passes to catch up with your relatives and friends, and explore various parts of Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Remember, senior citizens 60 years and above, which include all MG members, can make a journey on the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) and public bus to anywhere within two hours, which is more than enough time to travel between any two places in Singapore; senior citizens just pay a maximum of 88 cents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: A greener environment means cleaner air and thus healthier living.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Today, the land transport sector is the second largest source of emissions in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: As our land transport sector grows, we have to address emissions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This will be done by promoting public, active and shared mobility and managing the growth and use of vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We also encourage the adoption of cleaner and more carbon-efficient vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The additional diesel tax will help to discourage diesel consumption and create a better and healthier living environment for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I am very glad that taxi companies have stepped forward with concrete measures.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: While this may not fully cover the cost increase faced by some drivers, it does go some way in reducing their overheads while nudging drivers to be more conscious of the impact of diesel consumption on the environment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I also note that taxi companies which operate diesel pumps are already offering lower prices than retail pumps.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, I do echo Er Dr Lee Bee Wah's call to taxi companies to do more by absorbing part of the diesel tax.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Second, I am happy to note that for cabbies who are driving a diesel taxi which is five years and above, ComfortDelGro is offering a $100 voucher if they convert to a hybrid taxi by end of March this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The rental rates of such hybrid vehicles may be slightly higher, but they are more environmentally friendly and fuel-efficient, which could lead to savings for taxi drivers overall.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
