text: About 30% of the entire taxi fleet in Singapore is non-diesel.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I urge taxi companies to play their part towards a cleaner environment and add more non-diesel vehicles as they renew their fleet.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Learn from ComfortDelGro, offer more incentives to encourage drivers to switch from diesel taxis.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: First, all diesel buses will receive a new road tax rebate for three years from 1 August 2019.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This new rebate will start at 100% for the first year, 75% for the second year, and 50% for the third year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Diesel private hire or excursion buses used to ferry school children can continue to apply for a further 50% rebate on their road tax.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Second, all diesel school buses, diesel private hire buses and excursion buses ferrying school children will get an additional cash rebate for a three-year period from 1 August 2019.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The additional cash rebate for the first year is $1,600 for school buses, and up to $1,800 for diesel private hire or excursion buses ferrying school children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Third, school buses continue to enjoy Certificates of Entitlement (COE) exemption, on top of the offset measures shared earlier.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Taken together, these measures will help school bus operators maintain financial sustainability and keep costs down for parents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Even if it may not be possible for school bus operators to transfer all these savings to every single student or parent, they can look at ways to improve service delivery.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For our public bus industry, the Land Transport Authority (LTA) is already shifting from pure diesel public buses, with the introduction of 50 diesel-hybrid buses and 60 electric buses to our fleet.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Some commercial vehicle fleet owners have also expressed their intentions to progressively convert their fleets to electric or hybrid vehicles, as part of their fleet renewal plans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We are encouraged by these industry-led efforts as we make the transition towards cleaner vehicles together.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Such efforts cannot be solely achieved by the Government.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The costs of adopting and using cleaner technologies may also have to be borne by consumers, too, alongside businesses and the Government.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: (In Mandarin):  	Singapore's clean and green environment is our source of pride.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To ensure that our future generations enjoy a quality living environment, we must continue to do our part for the environment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To encourage more companies to use cleaner technologies, the Government can provide incentives or subsidies and implement measures, such as regulations and taxes, to address environmental pollution.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In the process, costs will inevitably increase and must be borne by all stakeholders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Taxi rental and diesel make up the bulk of taxi drivers' operating costs, while their income is determined by the taxi fare structure, all of which are factors beyond their control, and they are caught in the middle.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This will go some way in reducing their burden.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Consumers, too, have to play their part in shouldering the cost of cleaner air.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Within our communities, all of us can do our part to show care for one another.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Even coffee shops can play a significant role.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To cite an example: under "Project 215" in Tampines, seniors get to enjoy 50-cent coffee every Tuesday morning.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The scheme is now into its third year and the promotional price of each cup of coffee remains at 50 cents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The original price of each cup is at least $1, which means the participating stallholders have contributed more than $22,000 to the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These piping hot cups of coffee warm the hearts of our seniors and allow them to feel the close-knit community spirit of Tampines.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The Finance Minister faced the difficult task of allocating resources but did not forget the Government's responsibility to the people, from meeting our basic needs to following the latest trends from Raffles' arrival to the One Belt, One Road plan.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Our population is ageing but agile as we shape a uniquely Singaporean culture and voice and continue to do our part for the environment.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Like Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, I have also come across many people like the Ah Kong that she mentioned.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many parents want their children and future generations to live better lives than their generation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, they work hard in the hope that their next generation would have a good life, scrimping and saving to leave savings for the next generation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some say that we already have very good savings and no longer have to work as hard as our forefathers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As these values begin to weaken, we may fall into the situation akin to a boat going upstream whereby it will fall behind so long as it is not moving ahead.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is a saying that one can deplete a mountain’s worth of assets.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we do not cherish what we have and become complacent, fail to improve, we may face the risk of a national decline.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Being mindful in times of peace is key to our self-reliance.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We cannot relax nor let our guard down.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Once we are complacent, we will gradually lose our competitiveness, investors will also hesitate to invest in us.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many parents told me that they were worried that their children would abandon our traditional values.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, it is very important to maintain sustainable and stable economic growth.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will enable Singaporeans to enjoy a better quality of life while a strong Reserve will enable our people to enjoy the benefits of a strong and stable Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We all know that Singapore passports have international prestige and convenient access, due to our country's prudent, healthy finances and abundant Reserves.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, it is necessary for the Government to continue to exercise prudent and sustainable financial management to plan and take care of our long-term interests.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They have to be realistic and avoid short-sighted measures.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have nothing, but we can "create something out of nothing" and have what others cannot have.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of our MG had to start work at a young age to supplement the family's income and care for their younger siblings.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, many of them did not get to enjoy the comprehensive benefit of CPF, especially after the CPF was amended and enhanced to bring better safeguards for our members.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, the measures to assist MG are quite popular and welcomed by many older residents, which leads to the next question: what about subsequent generations?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The future is unpredictable and there may be changes beyond our control down the road, leading to certain batches of future seniors facing difficulties in their retirement years.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, there are usually some seniors in every cohort who would need some form of Government support.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, we must continue to search for more engines of economic growth and revenue resources to finance not just elder expenditures but all necessary expenses.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Government continue to encourage investment of private hospitals here and to promote medical tourism?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Government ride on our achievement in education to encourage more investments in international schools and established private universities to encourage foreigners to send their children here for further studies?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Revenue can also be collected from travellers, while no effort is spared to attract tourist arrival and spending in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should also consider reviewing our immigration policy to draw ultra-high and high net worth individuals who can invest substantial amounts in Singapore to create quality jobs and income for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have been focusing a lot on restructuring our economy and transforming our industries.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us have a concerted effort to uplift families which are struggling to cope.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of these families need money, quite often after an illness or death tips their finances over the edge.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They need befrienders and professional counsellors to help them navigate the various assistance schemes available to them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For families struggling to get by from day to day, seeking help in the maze of many-helping-hands may be a real challenge.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we improve our present assistance delivery system?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do we have an evaluation framework to assess how productive and efficient we are in getting help to those who need it?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For other families with challenges, their problems are compounded by unconstructive family cultures in the way the members behave towards one another or manage their finances and resources.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Investing time and resources, particularly manpower resources in the form of counsellors/guidance with a hand-holding approach, on such families will help them to break out of poverty cycles and ensure that the children live up to their highest potential.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Going forward, the increase in diesel tax and the implementation of carbon tax will make more hardship in sectors where there are limited energy choices.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should continue to build the infrastructure for businesses to switch to natural gas, electricity or solar and so on and so forth as soon as possible prior to the introduction of such a tax.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Every Budget Statement, I reach first for the Budget numbers for the financial year (FY) and compare them with previous years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I do so, not because Minister Heng Swee Keat’s annual Budget Statements are unimportant – they are always enlightening.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But because, like many of my generation and those before me, fiscal sustainability and financial prudence are foremost on my mind.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Numbers, I have found, give me the clearest indication of both.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I rise today to speak on these trends and decisions.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our expenditure has increased significantly over the years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This, in and of itself, is no surprise.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat raised in his Budget Statement several domestic demographic issues that confront us – an ageing population, social mobility, inequality, economic transformation and climate change.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I would add the need for infrastructure expansion and renewal.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: To address these issues, monies need to be spent.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is about a three-fold increase in 10 years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This, in part, is due to our ageing population.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In my constituency of Potong Pasir, more than 40% of my residents are above 50 years old, one in five above 65.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Even as I speak, we are building one nursing home and one senior day care centre within our constituency.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There is a genuine need for these healthcare facilities.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: An ageing population is the reality on the ground.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The Government needs to look after our seniors and, therefore, we expect national healthcare expenditure to continue to increase in the future.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The trend on expenditure is, therefore, quite clear.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Increased spending is also likely required in Defence, Education and Transport, just to name three other sectors.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The question is, how do we pay for these expected increases in expenditure?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: For FY2009, overall expenditure was approximately $57 billion.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The fact is that, without the NIR, our Budgets will be substantially in deficit every year.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Of the total NIR every year, 50% is used to contribute to the Budget and the other 50% reinvested as part of our Reserves to ensure continued sustainable contribution to Budgets of the future.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There are those who advocate for more NIR to be used for the present, but I think the current arrangement is fair.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As they say in Hokkein: "jit lang jit pua" (一人一半), half for this generation and half saved for future generations.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In business, when expenses exceed income, we balance our budgets either by increasing revenue or reducing expenditure.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But, Sir, expenditure is unlikely to decrease in the short term.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our domestic demographic dictates this and the need for infrastructure expansion and renewal is a pressing one.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There are also no "magic bullets" to significantly increase revenue.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Some argue that the projected increase in GST by 2% is about increasing taxes on Singaporeans to return the same to them.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As stated earlier, our estimated expenditure for 2019 is $80.3 billion.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This does not even include Special Transfers, which covers items, such as, CPF and MediSave top-ups, GST Vouchers, S&CC rebates, Wage Credit Scheme and so on, which are estimated at $15.3 billion for FY2019.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The projected GST increase is, therefore, simply only one measure to mitigate the trend of rising expenditure but, clearly, is unable to meet it in full.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: One approach raised by Minister Heng Swee Keat in the Budget Statement is to pay for major infrastructure investments by borrowing.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As the Minister explained, this has been done before, for example, in the building of our MRT lines in the 1980s.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Other Statutory Boards and Government-owned companies continue to borrow to finance major infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The Changi Airport Group is expected to take up loans to finance the development of Terminal 5.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Singapore is in a better position now to dictate favourable borrowing terms than in the past as our Government's credit rating is now amongst the world’s best.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If the Government provides a guarantee, presumably with the President's concurrence, we are likely to obtain even better terms.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We have seen enough examples around the world of countries mired in debt arising from careless borrowings and reckless funding of projects.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is, therefore, imperative that decision makers are prudent and that proper due diligence is carried out.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Careful judgement needs to be applied to ascertain the financial sustainability and viability of each major infrastructure project funded by borrowing.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Will the Government consider measures, such as an independent panel or body, to provide oversight over major infrastructure projects funded through borrowings?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I am supportive of the strategy of borrowing for our major infrastructure projects and agree with the Finance Minister that it will achieve fairer and more equitable outcomes in the allocation of resources on expenditure.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I invite the Minister for Finance to elaborate on his Ministry's plans to ensure long-term fiscal sustainability in light of the expected increasing expenditure as well as the measures that MOF intends to take in order to protect our Reserves in the light of the Government's decision to borrow to finance major infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This year, we celebrate our Bicentennial, 200 years from the arrival of Sir Thomas Stamford Raffles, and rather fittingly, the Budget has made provision for this important milestone.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the time, the British were probably the most powerful nation in the world, overseeing an empire stretching from North America to Australia, covering vast portions in Asia and Africa.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The British Empire, at its peak, held sway over 23% of the world’s population and covered 24% of the Earth's total land area.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It was called the empire on which the sun never set because the sun would literally be shining on some part of the British Empire at any given point in time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore was part of an immense global empire and was a hub for merchants, traders and workers from around the region to make a home.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It was around this time that many immigrants came here, including the Chinese, Indians and Malays from other parts of the archipelago.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many of the founding fathers of independent Singapore were born during this period, including Mr Lee Kuan Yew, as were my grandparents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore was the impregnable fortress of the British Empire in the east.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At this time, it would have been unthinkable that the British Empire might end, or that anything might happen to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, the fall of Singapore in 1942 changed just about every assumption that the people of that era held about the British Empire.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The atrocities that followed in the Japanese Occupation left an indelible mark on that generation on what it feels like to be helpless in the face of aggression and our Pioneer Generation (PG) recognised that security was a prerequisite for prosperity and acted accordingly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Today, Singapore is more prosperous than many of our forefathers would have dared imagine.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have a gross domestic product (GDP) per capita that is higher than most developed countries, including the old colonial powers, and our people are well-educated and enjoy amongst the longest life expectancies in the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singaporeans have high expectations, of course, but happily, we have a leadership that is ever ready to try and meet this challenge.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In particular, this Budget focuses on helping people and businesses in a wide variety of targeted areas to better equip our workers and the population for the challenges ahead.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As one of the last speakers in this debate, I would like to emphasise that I think it is important for us to remain committed to our security needs and to anticipate and deal with the new threats we face.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Multilateralism is under unprecedented challenge and nationalism is on the rise.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the post-World War II era, institutions, such as the United Nations (UN), the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and, subsequently, the World Trade Organization, were set up to facilitate multilateral cooperation on the most important matters for countries, namely, security, trade and financial systems.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Regional alliances for security and trade continued to develop during this period and Singapore is involved in many of these alliances.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These provided important opportunities for Singaporeans and Singapore businesses to thrive.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, in recent years, multilateralism is starting to lose its support amongst the developed world who set up these institutions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The European Union (EU) is under threat with Brexit, and the pro-Europe leaders, such as Chancellor Merkel and President Macron, are facing unprecedented threats at home.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A corollary of this is rising nationalism, and nationalist parties are getting increasingly popular.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the absence of a strong multilateral threat against the use of force, countries may be more inclined to take unilateral action against one another or against non-state actors in another state’s territory, which is a tinderbox.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is particularly dangerous as more and more nations militarise and even develop nuclear capabilities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One wrong move and damage on an unprecedented scale could be unleashed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Militarised non-state actors are also becoming an increasing threat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The threat of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) is pervasive, not just in the Middle East where it holds territory, but also in our part of the world where it has terror cells and, most worryingly, online.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many countries, including Singapore, has self-radicalised individuals who may plan or take part in terror activities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The events that have taken place over the past few nights between Pakistan and India – two nuclear powers – show how these dangerous trends may collide.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The sequence started when an Indian military base was subject to attack from a terror group Jaish-e-Mohammed operating from within Pakistan and 40 people were killed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Closer to home, I am grateful that matters seemed to have cooled down with Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are also more insidious threats to our country lurking beneath the surface.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The cyberhacking on SingHealth by a foreign state actor still leaves me with a feeling of unease as it is clear there are sophisticated, well-funded entities out there operating against us.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is also growing evidence of foreign interference in elections, with particularly startling reports that both during the last US presidential election and the United Kingdom's (UK's) Brexit vote may have been influenced by fake news originating from sources outside both those countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For most Singaporeans, these threats are not foremost on their mind, probably the same way none of our forefathers could have imagined how the world may have changed 100 years ago.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Yet, I think it will be important for us to imagine these scenarios and to be able to deal with them, both as a Government and as a people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Without security and preparation for the threats of the future, all our prosperity may end up being meaningless.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am grateful this Budget has provided well for our security needs and I look forward to addressing these matters in more detail during the Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I am glad the Minister for Finance also emphasised Singapore's unique social compact – how the Government is partnering people to build a caring and inclusive society and encouraging people to volunteer and give back to society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because the social compact of any society impacts how citizens cooperate with one another.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Within a pluralistic society, people will have different views about what the social compact should be.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because it is important that there continues to be a broad slate of policy options for consideration for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What used to work in the past may not work in the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore has had to adapt her economic strategies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: According to the book Dynamic Governance, in the 1970s, as change was more gradual and predictable, planning and predetermining what needed to be done was important for Singapore's survival.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But when things changed more rapidly because of globalisation and instantaneous communication, Singapore needed to go beyond that to sensing and responding to emerging opportunities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When that happened, the role of the Government shifted from directing and allocating resources to facilitating the exploitation of opportunities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a small island city-state, Singapore faces unique challenges.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What worked in other countries may not be suitable or may need to be adapted before being applied to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As Mr Lim Siong Guan wrote, "Singapore is unique in its demographics, its small size and its lack of natural resources.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We cannot become a first-world economy simply by following what others are doing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we look at the successes elsewhere, the critical questions we continuously have to ask are not what they are doing, or how they are doing it, but why they are doing it and why they are doing it that way." Because of the rapidly changing world and our unique challenges, it is critical that we be able to draw from a broad slate of policies and avoid strict adherence to theories.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Theories can be assistive, but they are just that – theories.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Theories have limitations and thus cannot be overly, rigidly adhered to.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Dogmatic adherence to theories or rigid ideology also lacks the ability to capture the multifaceted complexities of democracies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Financial Times article entitled, "Capitalism and Democracy: the strain is showing" pointed out tensions between liberal democracy and global capitalism, citing Harvard University Prof Dani Rodrik as stating, "democracy, national sovereignty and global economic integration are mutually incompatible: we can combine any two of the three but never have all three simultaneously and in full." If he is correct, then balancing the tensions among these concepts – democracy, national sovereignty and global economic integration – cannot be achieved through strict adherence to dogma.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, aiming for theoretical purism is not the goal; rather, aiming to do what is best for Singapore is, drawing from a broad slate of possibilities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe that this is what the governing party in Singapore must continue to do.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Different perspectives make us reflect on things from a different angle.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, during the recent debate on the National Parks Board (Amendment) Bill, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah raised concerns of safety and that of a hygienic living environment for her residents, citing multiple unsupervised cat feeding episodes as attracting big rats and the need for relevant authorities to be trained in handling snake sightings near residences.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Louis Ng took a different view on the matter, suggesting that the removal of snakes which eat rats contributed to the problem of a rising number of rats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such an exchange is a real plus; a real advantage.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such an exchange sheds light on the same issue through different perspectives, sparking new ideas and increasing the range of possible solutions to be explored.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a win-win, provided, of course, those involved in the debate want what is best for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The need to compromise for the sake of political dividend does not necessarily lead to the best policies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The focus, one can argue, is not on the effectiveness or efficiency of the final product but on the political compromise.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A New York Times article entitled "A Tax Code of Politics, Not Reason", says that "This compromise has left us with a loophole-riddled code that isn't very good at raising money." Compared to other developed countries, the US does not collect much tax at all.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At least that was the state of things in April 2012 – but such is compromise.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my humble view, the better way is to focus on possibilities and persuasion rather than loose compromises.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In order to do this, we should not label a person as "right" or "left", "liberal" or "conservative".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A person can have different views on different issues and should not be limited to representing the "right" or "left" view.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If we label people in this manner, the focus shifts from what is best for Singapore to whether or not a view conforms to a certain ideological view.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because there is no such pressure to fit or not fit a certain label in Singapore, I feel the freedom to decide based on what I think is the best course for Singapore on the issues that came before this House.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In some matters, my view could be categorised as more "right".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, my hard stance against recreational drug use because of its harm to society could be characterised as right-leaning.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On a different issue, my view could be characterised as being more "left".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, advocating for the Prevention of Human Trafficking Bill in order to protect vulnerable workers in Singapore from being exploited in a capitalist market.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, what is important is not whether my views are ideologically right or left, but rather, I have the freedom within the government party to act or voice a view in accordance with what I thought was best for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This has strengthened my humble belief that, in Singapore, those elected must possess "political ambidexterity" – they must deploy right- or left-leaning policies in accordance with what Singapore needs for the long term based on a defensible and robust system of values and ethics.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A person should not be pigeon-holed left or right.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the course of the debates, there will be times when we debate morality and our interpretation of it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That is important and we should not shy away from it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Nevertheless, it is important that politics in Singapore does not move into single-issue politics.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yes, the issues have wide-ranging impact on many different sectors.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the running of a country cannot be reduced to a single issue.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Worse still, examples from jurisdictions around the world have shown that some of those who push single-issue politics focus on polarising fault lines, exploiting them for a political purpose and deepening divisions in society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, some pockets in the political spheres in Germany and the United Kingdom (UK) and other countries have stoked interracial and inter-religious tensions by running on racial supremacy or anti-religion lines.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The AfD quite arguably ran elections on an anti-immigration, anti-Islam ticket.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the UK, the Britain First party ran on an anti-immigration and openly nationalist agenda.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2016, Jayda Fransen, the deputy leader, was convicted for religiously aggravated harassment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The answer is this: irreconcilable division breeds an environment of politics of extremes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Policies become political bargains that compromise on effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would not want this to happen in Singapore for the sake of our social compact.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the US, partisan brinkmanship causes shutdowns of government, and it impacts the lives of many.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An October 2018 article in the Asia News Monitor about Bosnia-Herzegovina, reported that the country faced a collapsing healthcare system, struggling public infrastructure, regressing education, catastrophic and accelerating brain drain.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead of meaningfully engaging these issues, the political discourse centred on nationalist brinkmanship and paranoia.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Main campaign issues among nationalist parties were "either 'we're going to kill the other side or we're going to keep you from getting killed by the other side.'" In Britain, some think that the fear of a disorderly Brexit might be used to squeeze the deal through in Parliament or to help Britain in its negotiations with the EU.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, Sir, from what the world has shown us, we need, in Singapore, to refrain from the politics of brinkmanship.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Further, we need to be able to collect a collage of differing views under the umbrella of a single party, thereby avoiding sole-issue politics.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This way, even hard issues and issues touching on morality and ethics can be debated in a respectful and productive way.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It avoids the need for politics by referendum, since differing views are already represented in the legislature.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) Radio recently aired an excellent programme just last weekend, entitled "The Real Story: Are Referendums ever a good idea?" In that programme, a quote on Brexit from the expert being interviewed caught my attention.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Caroline Vernaillen from Democracy International explained: "I think what is definitely never a good idea... is putting a general programme to a vote if it contains multiple questions... the way Brexit was actually a broad reform programme." As representatives of the constituents we serve, we are entrusted with the mandate to make difficult decisions on policy or morality for our country.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A valuable ingredient for an effective social compact is to ensure cooperation within society by reflecting and giving voice to differing views in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is healthy and avoids the politics of extremes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Undergirding this must be an openness to different views and new evidence, even as one holds strong positions on certain subjects and issues.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is because all of us here in this Chamber owe it to the Singaporeans we serve to form the most accurate conclusion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On that topic, I respectfully seek to persuade this House that politics in Singapore should remain about possibilities and persuasion, always with a view on what is best for Singapore's long term; it should be carried out under a broad umbrella where differing views can flourish and consensus built on a foundation of ethics, stewardship and values.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It should never lead to brinkmanship, single issue politics or hollow short-term compromise.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a place where policy and societal morality is charted.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If we can all do it right, then unity will prevail.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If we can all do it right, our social compact – as a people – will be robustly defended and protected.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Speaker, Sir, thank you for the opportunity to speak in this debate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My colleagues have put forth their earnest opinions and excellent ideas covering many aspects of the Budget in the past two days.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, as the last backbencher to speak in this debate, I will keep my speech relatively brief, or at least I try to.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Budget is an important business of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This House must decide not only how we allocate resources to address immediate needs, but also how we can find resources to invest for the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Budget is a means to implement the Government’s strategies and realise Singaporeans' collective vision for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, what we spend on and how much we spend on are important.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This significant package will make a tangible difference to the lives of the Merdeka Generation (MG).

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It shows our gratitude to seniors who had given so much of themselves to build the Singapore we are proud of today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The package will clearly address the top-of-mind concern and alleviate the healthcare cost burden on this group of seniors, while encouraging them to age actively.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So far, feedback on the package from my residents has been positive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Seniors who missed out on the Pioneer Generation Package (PGP) are happy and appreciative.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The younger ones, who are children of the PG and MG, are supportive as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is because these packages relieve their parents' medical expenses, indirectly benefiting them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To the others, the fact that there is such a package is an assurance that the Government cares about the more vulnerable and understands what worries our people most.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Taken together with the many other schemes and programmes for our seniors, it is apparent that the Government is working hard to enable Singaporeans to age with dignity.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, one of the highlights of this Budget is the MGP.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is a concrete manifestation of our sense of gratitude.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The package has focused on healthcare, and it shows that the Government empathises with the elderly's concern over healthcare costs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They have, therefore, addressed the problem directly, with the aim of lightening senior citizens' burden in terms of healthcare costs, so that they can enjoy their golden years and have less to worry about.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Actually, the Government has always looked after the elderly and the disadvantaged.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In recent years, our social and public healthcare expenditure has increased significantly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the youngest Member of Parliament, I am very grateful that the Government has made these efforts, as policies rolled out by a government that cares for the people would definitely prioritise the long-term interests of the nation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, besides dealing with current problems, a responsible government with foresight must also plan for the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, I am glad to see that this Budget continues to prioritise economic transformation and talent development.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Faced with ever-changing conditions, Singapore must continue to strive relentlessly and strengthen our capabilities both externally and domestically to maintain our position.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I hope that the Government will continue to give strong support to manpower training, urban development, building resilient and cohesive communities, and the aspirations of our youths.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In English): Speaker, Sir, I fully support MGP and the other social initiatives announced in this Budget.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But it is also important that we strike a balance between spending to benefit the current generation and directing a good part of our financial muscle towards investing in the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A significant portion of this year's Budget is dedicated to strengthening our economic competitiveness and building deeper enterprise and people capabilities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I hope we will also think about the following.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Through the annual Formula One night race, last year's Trump-Kim Summit and the movie Crazy Rich Asians, Singapore showcased our beautiful city to the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But in 10, 20 years to come, when our infrastructure has aged and as other cities catch up, will we still have anything to show and be excited over?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What is the next big attraction after Marina Bay, the new financial district and Gardens by the Bay?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What is the next iconic public housing project after the Pinnacle and Kampong Admiralty?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is important that we continually upgrade and rejuvenate our city.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is equally important to find ways to create new "space" where new developments can take place.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, we should retain some parts of old Singapore so that our people can remain connected to our heritage.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But Singapore should not be an old city.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is important that Singaporeans continue to regard Singapore as a city of possibilities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our size may be small, but our imagination must be big.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Despite our land constraints, we must somehow find ways to reinvent and remake what we have; develop new buildings, new districts and new gardens that delight our citizens and amaze the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A beautiful Singapore must be underpinned by strong and united communities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore's community-building efforts have come a long way since our Independence.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have a harmonious society united for progress.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The consequences are serious if we do not actively address these challenges.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They will lead Singapore into our next bound.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is important that they see Singapore as the place where they can achieve their dreams, whatever they may be.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our youths want to make Singapore and the world a better place.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They have their own idea of what this means and they are taking steps to do this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many believe in environmental causes and have mobilised and pushed on various projects, for example, promoting renewable energy sources and getting rid of straws and other one-use plastics.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must remember to invest to benefit Singaporeans of tomorrow, just as we have benefited from the investments made by our PG and MG.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe our constant effort to imagine our future, to find the next big thing in Singapore that will excite our people, to strengthen communities for a strong and united nation and to support our young in their development and endeavours will have far reaching effects.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These will require our constant attention and consistent investment by our Government.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To be sure, the Government plays a critical role in improving the lives of our people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It keeps Singapore secure and the economy humming along.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But the Government does not have the sole responsibility or the best ideas all the time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Nor can the Government alone solve all the challenges that we face.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We face macroeconomic uncertainties, geopolitical instability, rapid social change and game-changing technological innovations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Government action alone is inadequate to the task of navigating a safe journey for all Singaporeans into the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In our daily lives, we see many examples in our community of how different people, different organisations and different parties coming together to support our people, our residents, our seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Recently, her sister passed away and so she is staying alone in a rental flat.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But with the help from the Government, monthly financial assistance, as well as support from the Sallim Mattar Mosque where she goes for her Koran studies periodically every week, she is very meaningfully engaged in our community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, even as she lives alone, there are many helping hands available to help her.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs), the mosque, our grassroots leaders, through our programmes, outreach and befriending, she is now a very happy senior living in Macpherson.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Sometimes, help need not be in a big way.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It could be as simple as a neighbour running to a senior's house to help fix that remote control that he or she failed to operate to switch on their favourite television (TV) show.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have so many people, so much resources within the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If we are all able to come together to work hand-in-hand, we can multiply our efforts and do so much more to make our community and Singapore a better place for everyone.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In fact, I would say that regardless of whether it is just the Government working alone or together as a community, regardless of what role we are playing, at the end of the day, it is about the people we feel for.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is about the bonds that we forge, the hearts we touch and the lives we make a difference to.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I hope that Singaporeans will see this and Budgets past and future not just as Government or Parliamentary business, but as collective, decisive moves to prepare ourselves for the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I hope Singaporeans will step up and contribute as well with our ideas, voices and energies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Let us, together, ensure that Singapore continues to thrive and be truly inclusive and caring.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Over the last two weeks, I have also noted thoughtful views from fellow Singaporeans, academics, journalists and business owners.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As we celebrate the Bicentennial, let us take a step back to reflect on how we got here today and how we would like to move forward.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some Members have provided good and useful overviews of the Budget and how they benefit various parties, such as Mr Liang Eng Hwa.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some have delivered vivid speeches during the Budget Debate, such as the one about Ah Kong and Ah Seng.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: My speech will not be as poetic as Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng's.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And as Members can see, I, too, have two files like on Budget Day.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, Mr Speaker, Sir, with your permission, may I use some slides so that it is easier for the Chamber to follow my speech, please?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These principles reinforce one another and have allowed us to do more with less.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For instance, in the area of education – I showed this slide at last year's debate – we did not spend the most, but you look at the outcome that our students achieved in this Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) score.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: On healthcare, again, we did not spend the most, but we have the second highest life expectancy, next to Japan.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And Members can see the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries’ averages on the right-hand side.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For policing, good outcomes in policing where, again, with the spending that we have of just slightly above 0.6% of GDP, we are ranked one of the safest in the world.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, these are all very credible outcomes despite spending less than what other countries do.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I will now elaborate on each of these principles.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The first principle of the Singapore way is putting Singaporeans at the centre of what we do.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We empower people through education, create a good environment for families, help Singaporeans to earn and save more for retirement and support ageing with assurance.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Er Dr Lee Bee Wah put it so eloquently, all that we do "完全是为了你", that is, "It is all for you".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Many Members, including Mr Louis Ng, Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Gan Thiam Poh, have given suggestions on addressing class divisions, inequality and helping all Singaporeans do well, including the less privileged.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The question is, how best to do so?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Saktiandi Supaat put it, it cannot just be through a Robin Hood style of social transfers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We believe that the best way to take care of our people is to build capacity, that is: (a) For our young, we give them a strong foundation in terms of a good education and exposure, so that they have the knowledge, skills and values necessary to chase their dreams.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: (b) For our workers, we invest in increasing their capacity through upgrading and reskilling.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Crucially, we also build an economy that provides them with opportunities.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: (c) For those who have fallen behind and who need help to access opportunities, we provide stronger support systems.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is with the ultimate objective to give them the confidence and dignity to succeed for themselves as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: (d) For our seniors, we support them in their desire to age successfully.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have been providing significant support and will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our young get a high-quality education which provides a solid grounding to chase their dreams.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We make sure this is available to all our people, regardless of background.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is possible due to the significant subsidies provided to every child.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: On average, every child entering Primary 1 in 2018 would have received over $130,000 in education subsidies by the time he or she completes secondary school.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Those who go on to post-secondary education receive another $15,000 to $22,000 for every year they remain in school.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And beyond just making sure that everyone can afford education, we make sure that there is good quality for everyone, not just the top achievers or better off.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In 2018, we provided at least 60% more resourcing for primary school students with a weaker foundation in literacy and numeracy through learning support programmes in schools.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our commitment to maximising pathways to success is clear.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have specialised schools catering to the needs of Normal (Technical) students, those with interests in science and technology, or the arts or sports.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Most visitors to our country are very impressed with what we have done for our Institutes of Technical Education (ITEs), sometimes better designed and resourced than their universities.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Several Members in this House and myself have been bringing visitors to ITE and they have been surprised to see what we have in the ITEs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Ministry of Education (MOE) will elaborate more on our plans to Uplifting Pupils in Life and Inspiring Families Taskforce (UPLIFT) our students at the COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What we do is not necessarily the case worldwide.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In the United States (US), public funding per student varies widely across states and within states.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For example, within the state of New York, one school district can get three times that of another school district, based on how well-off each school district is.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I agree with what Prof Lim Sun Sun said about the need to help our students develop cross-cultural, digital and ethical (CDE) competencies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is on top of the ABCs and 123s we teach them.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Prof Fatimah Lateef also called on Singaporeans to develop strong networks to thrive in an age of change and disruption.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our schools provide this holistic education by making available co-curricular activities (CCAs), Applied Learning Programmes and Learning for Life Programmes, all of which are heavily funded by MOE.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And you never know where the path will lead you.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Take the example of Mr Wong Kah Chun whom the Prime Minister spoke about at the National Day Rally last year.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: He grew up in a Chinese-speaking family but, through his school band, discovered a love for Western classical music and is now the first Singaporean to conduct the New York Philharmonic Orchestra.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We also support our young people to build their cross-cultural competencies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I was at the groundbreaking ceremony of Razer last week.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I was excited that with Razer's expansion, we will be able to have many more opportunities for young Singaporeans, both here and overseas.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will continue to do more for our young.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have been investing more in preschool to make preschool education better, more accessible and affordable, especially for the lower-income.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This will help our children build a solid foundation from an even younger age.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I agree with the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) Secretary-General Ng Chee Meng and Mr Seah Kian Peng that for the Fourth Industrial Revolution, or Industry 4.0, to work for us, we need Worker 4.0 as well, meaning, we need our workers to transform and build capacity in tandem.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Desmond Choo mentioned, learning and building capacity do not stop after formal education.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The workplace is a good place for our workers to learn.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Patrick Tay has mentioned, we provide support for our workers to reskill and upskill, to seize opportunities and do well for themselves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The SkillsFuture movement provides support for our workers to develop skills and pursue lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For those who are displaced, we help them find a new job, and reskill where necessary, through programmes, such as Adapt and Grow.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Labour Movement plays a key role in this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Senior Minister of State Heng Chee How spoke on putting workers at the heart of all we do.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And I am glad that they recognise, in Mr Zainal Sapari and Mr Ang Hin Kee's words, that this year's Budget is pro-worker.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Labour Members of Parliament and Ms Sylvia Lim have spoken about various segments of our workforce – young workers, older workers, mid-career professionals, low-income workers, self-employed workers and those with caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and MOE will address some of their suggestions in greater detail during the COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A common thread in the comments, as Mr Arasu Duraisamy has noted, was how employers have a key role to play in helping their workers upgrade.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Melvin Yong commented that workers who go for training need to pull "double shifts" – training in the day and working at night.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As workers put in the effort to train, I urge all employers to give them full support.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I would also like to explain how we support our low-wage workers, in line with concerns raised by Dr Intan Mokhtar and others.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Where possible, we want them to build capacity through upskilling, so that they can move up the wage ladder.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Through WIS and the Progressive Wage Model (PWM), we help lower-income workers upskill and reskill, earn more and save more.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am heartened to hear that Singaporeans, both within and outside the House, are concerned about whether families of lower-wage workers can make ends meet.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some, like Mr Mohamed Irshad, have suggested that the way to address this is to allow younger Singaporeans to be given WIS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: At this point, I would like to explain the design of WIS and why we provide more support to older lower-income workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Much as we wish to help those who earn less, how we do it is important.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Permanently increasing their capacity to earn more is the most sustainable way to improving their lot in life and helping them support their family members.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is best done by upgrading their skills and improving their chances of getting better paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What they learn today will be useful for many years down the road, and build a foundation for further learning.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In the meantime, we help them take care of their families' needs, such as bursaries for their children or MediFund for their parents' hospitalisation bills.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Where there are challenges with accessing skills training, I am confident that NTUC and our unions can come in to support.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Education and employment support are part of the comprehensive system of social support which benefit our less well-off.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This structure tilts the benefits in support of members with lower balances.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is in the spirit of what Mr Saktiandi Supaat mentioned, of helping small savers grow their income.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We also help Singaporeans own their homes, with more housing subsidies for the lower-income.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There are few countries where young couples buy a home before they get married.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, in many cities, there is a huge gulf between those who can own properties and those who do not.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We continually rejuvenate our estates and upgrade our flats, so that they remain vibrant and liveable homes for our people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These flats could also provide an additional source of income in retirement.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: At the same time, we provide other targeted support for those from less advantaged backgrounds, in different forms.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: ComCare is available for those with greater needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There is always room to do even better, as many Members of Parliament have mentioned.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But overall, it is a good system which gives Singaporeans a good foundation in life.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That we still find the occasional cases which fall through the cracks does not behoove us to knock down the system.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It gives us policymakers, public officers, social workers, community volunteers the motivation to do better, through action.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Singapore is ageing quickly, quicker than many other developed countries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We made the transition from an ageing to an aged society in an exceptionally short span of 19 years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In comparison, Japan, the world's most aged country, took 26 years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Other countries like France took more than a century or 115 years, and Sweden took 85!

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Furthermore, by 2025, Singapore will become a super-aged country, with 21% of our citizen population aged 65 and older.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But this should not be viewed in a negative light.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our $3 billion Action Plan for Successful Ageing was launched in 2016, taking in feedback from thousands of Singaporeans, both young and old, on what they saw successful ageing to be.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Compare the title of this latest action plan with the title of the first committee on ageing we set up in 1982, namely, the Committee on the Problems of the Aged.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And learning from the many seniors I have met who inspire me, let me share how they are redefining ageing, by staying active, healthy and connected.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If we help all our seniors to make the transition, it will benefit them and also inspire all our younger generations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our seniors want to stay active, be it through work, volunteering, learning something new, or keeping up with their grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And we want to support them in doing so.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Opportunities to learn, grow and achieve do not stop at the retirement age.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, the National Silver Academy, which was part of the Action Plan for Successful Ageing, came about because our seniors told us that they wanted to keep learning and contributing to society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Academy now provides a range of courses for senior learners, and supports inter-generational learning programmes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am glad that we have support for this on both sides of the House.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh and Mr Faisal Manap have also made a strong pitch for our seniors to be active and continue to be the best they can be.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Having the second highest healthy life expectancy in the world, we are in a good place.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I recently met Ms Peng Lee Er, one of our MG, at a TV forum.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: She told me that she appreciated the MGP benefits as they provided assurance that her healthcare expenses would be taken care of.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Even better, the benefits would be there but not used or what she called "备而不用", meaning that it was best if she could stay healthy, and do not have to seek treatment in the first instance.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The intention is for our seniors to focus on staying well.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The MGP is there as an added assurance.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I am glad to hear Ms Joan Pereira and Ms Irene Quay expressing support for this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am always very happy to see groups of seniors coming together regularly in parks or other public spaces to exercise, like doing line dancing or Zumba Gold together.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, I understand that many of our seniors are exercising regularly in over 400 locations across the island.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is a good sign, and I hope there will be even more of such groups in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And last but not least, our seniors want to stay connected with one another and with those around them.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am encouraged by the progress made through the Community Networks for Seniors, which brings together Government agencies and community partners to help us have the "ABCs" where seniors stay active, befriend and care for one another.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some 1,500 seniors have come forward as volunteers to befriend and help other seniors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Take the example of Mr Bernard Lai, who is a member of our MG.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Besides juggling his work commitments, he is an active grassroots leader, a member of various sports clubs and a Silver Generation Ambassador!

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: At the MG tribute event hosted by the Prime Minister early this month, Dick Lee, Jacintha Abisheganaden, Mel Ferdinands and Rahimah Rahim – all MGs – gave a spirited rendition of Merdeka Sayang, I quote, "With our silver hair, we still contribute", and another quote "we work hard, but still young at heart".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, these lyrics reflect the spirit with which we approach ageing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, "Fried Rice Paradise" just got better with age!

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our Pioneers were the first generation of Singaporeans who were living and working in Singapore after we became independent.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our MG is the next younger generation, better educated and healthier.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, we look to you to redefine ageing and forge a new path on what it means to be the independence generation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have spoken on how we take care of our people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In essence, it is through building capacity in everyone – our young, working adults, seniors – to be the best that they can be, while giving those who need help even more support and help in a targeted way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Members of Parliament have also brought up other important issues.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Ms Anthea Ong spoke of the importance of support for those with mental health conditions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This will be taken up at the Ministry of Health's (MOH's) COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Joan Pereira, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh and Ms Rahayu Mahzam have also spoken on how to better support women, especially those who are caregivers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Minister Josephine Teo shared, many of our existing schemes do benefit women more.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is a fitting recognition of their contribution.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We build capacity and adopt a long-term orientation in our planning.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is the second principle of the Singapore way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We plan for the long term, because we plan for Singapore to be here in the long term.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We look ahead, often tapping on the knowledge of experts here and overseas, so that we can prepare for the future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ageing, climate change and changing economic trends are just some of the issues that we have been preparing for.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Given the long-term horizon, it is difficult to project these spending needs now.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Nonetheless, we are planning early, seeing what we can do, and will work out the resourcing accordingly.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our plans span many years, putting in place the right infrastructure, charting the course of our economy and steadily building up our capabilities.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Given the long gestation of these projects, such as the airport and port projects, it is inevitable that they are subject to risks and uncertainties in the operating environment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I share Mr Dennis Tan's concerns on this issue.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: However, these uncertainties should not prevent us from making "exciting investments".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Rather, they are impetus for bold but deliberate planning.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Operating in challenging environments has always been our lot in life, which has taught us to plan carefully.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Back in the 1980s, when we were building Changi Terminal 2, we also faced regional and economic uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We do not shy away from making difficult decisions if they are necessary for the long run.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is why we have been pushing hard on economic restructuring and have taken further steps this year to drive deeper restructuring.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
