text: As Mr Darryl David and Ms Jessica Tan pointed out, there are significant shifts in the global economy, which means that we will be stuck if we stick to business as usual.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are fortunate to be in Asia where the growth is.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: However, the rapid growth of Asian economies will result in shifting comparative and competitive advantages in the region, which we will need to adapt to in order to benefit from this growth.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is driven by new technologies, the shift of global demand to emerging markets, and the consolidation of supply chains within manufacturing powerhouses in the region.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: At the same time, global value chains are becoming more knowledge-intensive, with research and development (R&D), software, design and other intangibles forming a greater share of value created.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are well-placed to ride on these changes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As a regional hub in many areas, such as finance, professional services and logistics, we are well-positioned as a base for businesses to capture the growing regional demand for such services.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will continue investing in research, innovation and enterprise development, and support our entrepreneurs and businesses to boldly venture into new markets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This will bring new opportunities to our people and firms.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: However, the window to achieve deeper economic restructuring, to help more of our firms capitalise on this opportunity, is narrow.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have achieved strong macroeconomic fundamentals through policies introduced over the years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Several Members, including Mr Chong Kee Hiong, gave feedback that some firms from the services sector find it difficult to automate their processes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But the reality, as Senior Minister of State Heng Chee How pointed out, is that our resident labour force growth will continue to slow.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If we do not move decisively on improving productivity and building up a skilled Singaporean Core in industries which are currently lagging, firms will find it harder to adjust in the future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat described it, the DRC cuts are like 苦口良药, bitter medicine that makes us better off in the long run.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Even as we cut the DRC levels, we will help our firms in the transition, as Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad has outlined.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As we take a long-term view in our planning, we must also consistently review our policies to take into account new trends, new feedback and new evidence.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Christopher de Souza just mentioned, because of the rapidly changing world and our unique challenges, it is critical that we be able to draw from a broad slate of policies and avoid strict adherence to theories.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must be prepared to experiment and take calculated risks.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If we do not succeed at first, we learn from our experience and try again.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is how we become better as a people and as a country.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I encourage all Ministries to adopt this entrepreneurial mindset, and to continue to keep trying out different solutions for the issues that we face.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must be focused on exploring what works, discard what does not, and execute effectively, so as to achieve better outcomes for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Hence, we adjust and calibrate our approach as we go along, to take in feedback and learn from outcomes, to make our schemes more useful and effective for firms and workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For example, a common feedback from SMEs was that it was difficult to navigate Government schemes and get support for business transformation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To help firms identify the support available to them, we launched one-stop portals like the Business Grants Portal and Startup SG.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our policies have been gradually adapted to help Singaporeans better prepare for retirement as we live longer.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: CPF LIFE, Silver Support and the Lease Buyback Scheme were introduced to boost the retirement savings of our seniors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: MediShield Life, which started as MediShield, and CareShield Life, which will replace ElderShield for younger cohorts, will provide universal and lifetime coverage for healthcare needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This last move, as Ms Rahayu Mahzam noted, shows the willingness of the Government to make changes when necessary.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, as Dr Lim Wee Kiak said, "we do have a universal healthcare system".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As a pre-funding scheme, MediSave, too, has to evolve as medical technology advances, as more options become available, and as the population ages.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will remain flexible and adaptive to deliver the best outcomes for our people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There have been questions, in and outside of this House, on whether we will or should have packages like the PGP or MGP for future generations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some asked in anticipation; others asked because they were worried about who pays.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Policymaking in real life does not assume that we start with perfection.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: My earlier examples show that we do not let the perfect be the enemy of the good.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We do what is good, learn by doing, and adapt and improve continually.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: During Singapore's journey from Third World to First, our MG, and our Pioneers especially, did not benefit from the social safety nets we have today and the investments we can now make.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The CPF contribution rates started out very much lower.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, a cohort-based approach to support them in their silver years is appropriate.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: You can say that we custom-made the packages to better meet their needs, and to honour them for what they have done for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For the younger cohorts, they, too, will have needs, but they are not of the same nature as the Pioneers or MGs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is compared to less than two in 10 among our youngest MGs, and about one in 10 for our Pioneers when they were at the same age.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The schemes we have put in place over the years – MediSave, MediShield Life, CareShield Life – enjoyed over their full working lives, will make sure that, by the time they reach retirement, they will be in a much better position than the Pioneers or MGs to look after their own healthcare needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Of course, some among us will still need more help.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Government will look at the needs of each group, and tailor our policies and programmes in the future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat has summarised this well.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The MGP is not linked to the election cycle, nor is it linked to the unexpected surpluses this term.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is a plan that has been carefully studied over a significant period of time.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Not many countries in the world had gone through a similarly compressed period of accelerated growth, leading to relatively wide divergences between the older and younger generations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have outlined two aspects of the Singapore way – putting people at the centre of what we do and planning long term.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The third principle of the Singapore way that I would like to highlight is partnership.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have consistently been advocating this partnership for years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Murali Pillai pointed out, it is not just this Budget, but also past Budgets which had partnership as a key element.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In Budget 2016, our theme was "Partnering for the Future".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In 2017, it was "Moving Forward Together", and in 2018, it was "Together a Better Future".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Previous Finance Ministers have had different ways of titling their Budget speeches, but partnership – working together – has always been key to our policies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Prof Fatimah Lateef put it, "Partnerships to Prosper" involves partnerships at all levels – globally, regionally and in Singapore – in our businesses and in the community.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Partnerships are also important for the arts community, as Mr Terence Ho shared.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We seek to be friends to all and build strong international partnerships for mutually beneficial outcomes and we have been steadily strengthening our partnerships.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Free Trade Agreements allow our businessmen access to other markets, and this is particularly important in this period where there are significant trade tensions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Defence agreements allow militaries to build mutual understanding.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Collaborations between officials and businesses build goodwill and better people-to-people connections.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Examples are Suzhou, Kendal, the Chongqing Connectivity Initiative, Iskandar Malaysia and the new state capital city of Andhra Pradesh.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But of all the partnerships that we build, the most foundational ones are the partnerships within Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A strong and united Singapore enables us, both Government and our people, to build strong partnerships elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A strong and united Singapore assures our partners around the world that we can be taken at our word and will not cycle back on our commitments due to domestic divisions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A strong and united Singapore also sends a clear signal of our will and resolve to defend our sovereignty and safeguard our vital interests.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: One key partnership within Singapore is our tripartite arrangement, which is a unique strength for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must build on this and strengthen partnerships between the Government, firms and unions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Firms must build deeper capabilities together with their workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The workers benefit from better jobs and better pay.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A skilled, committed workforce gives firms a competitive edge, and this is the smart thing to do.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will continue to provide support to firms which more directly link their companies' growth and transformation with capability building for their workers, such as in changes we made to EDG and PSG.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am glad to hear about the Singapore National Employers Federation's (SNEF's) efforts to help employers implement responsible employment practices as a means to enhance competitiveness and sustain business growth.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I was pleased to hear NTUC's Secretary-General Ng Chee Meng and Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon talk about the NTUC's plans, such as the setting up of training committees and partnering companies to build worker capabilities.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our unions take concrete and meaningful action which makes a difference to our firms and workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And we will continue to support our unions in this effort.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: One example of how the tripartite partnership can lead to positive outcomes is PSA.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When I visited PSA earlier this month on the first day of Chinese New Year together with Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon, I was glad to see them adopting new technologies, such as the automated crane system.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: PSA has worked closely with the Singapore Port Workers Union and Port Officers' Union in engaging and facilitating the change for the large pool of staff involved in this transition.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some of the crane operators I met had worked with PSA for over 20 years and commented that the changes led to better working conditions as they could work from a remote air-conditioned office, rather than in the crane cabin, high on top of the crane.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Another example is ST Engineering's aerospace sector, which I visited earlier this week.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To ride on the wave of Industry 4.0, ST Engineering has been investing in smart maintenance, repair and operations (MRO) initiatives at its hangars to adopt data analytics, additive manufacturing and automation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I was encouraged to hear that its union-management Training Council worked closely with NTUC Learning Hub to customise the SkillsFuture Digital Workplace course for the workers, to familiarise the workers with digital technologies, new work processes and automation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Over 200 staff attended the course in 2018, with another 600 staff expected to attend the course in 2019.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I am glad to see ST Engineering building enterprise capabilities and deepening worker skillsets in tandem.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is the type of positive outcomes for workers, businesses and the Government, which we all strive to achieve.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our Trade Associations and Chambers (TACs), as representatives of firms, have an important role to play in this effort.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I am glad to see more stepping up over the last few years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For example, through its networks with the global water community, the Singapore Water Association (SWA) introduced Imagine H2O, a leading water innovation accelerator in San Francisco, to local industry players.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And this led to exchanges of ideas on commercialising innovative water technologies between our firms and Imagine H2O's startups.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This Association is also working with Enterprise Singapore to immerse Imagine H2O into the local water ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As an outcome from this exchange, Imagine H2O has assessed Singapore to be a strategic location to set up its presence for the Asian market, and it is in the midst of establishing a presence here.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I was glad to hear Mr Douglas Foo's affirmation that the TACs remain committed to enhancing the business community’s capabilities and collaborating with member firms, the Government and the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And I support his call for, I quote, "TACs to further break down individual walls, and work with one another to accelerate our common national interests".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We invest in building an environment to help firms with the capabilities thrive, through steady investments in R&D, and strengthening economic linkages to the region.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This builds on our comparative advantages to help us, as an economy, to excel.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To do so in a way which works for each sector, we bring relevant stakeholders together to drive transformation through Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) and ITM cluster strategies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We also take an enterprise-centric approach, which focuses on issues faced by firms at each stage of growth.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This tailored and targeted approach allows our economic schemes to yield better results.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For firms which are ready to scale up and compete on a global scale, we provide more customised support.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked if the customised approach of the Scale-up SG programme meant that the Government is picking winners.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The customised support that we provide is available to companies that show ambition and are willing to take the effort to transform themselves to scale up quickly.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This support comes on top of many schemes which are accessible to firms, small or micro, for example, schemes which help firms adopt digital technology solutions, such as Start Digital Pack under SMEs Go Digital.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And where there are market gaps, we provide support, such as through the Enterprise Financing Scheme, to provide financing for younger and smaller firms.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These schemes, together with a wide range of schemes under the Startup SG branding, provide a strong base of support for startups, which Ms Denise Phua asked about.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As pointed out by Ms Rahayu Mahzam, many Singaporeans and businesses have demonstrated their care and concern for fellow Singaporeans through their good work over the years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In addition to providing pro bono legal services for the disadvantaged, the firm also regularly partners VWOs to contribute time and dollars to a broad range of causes and activities.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: VWOs, like Ang Mo Kio Family Service Centre (AMK FSC), Society for the Physically Disabled (SPD) and Empower Ageing, have also done an excellent job in serving a broad range of needs in the community.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And as Ms Denise Phua said, their reach extends beyond what the Government can do.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I thank them for their efforts, their hard work, and more importantly, heart work, in reaching out.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To help them to continue deepening their capability, and increase the impact of the good work they do, for instance, we started the VWO-Charities Capability Fund (VCF) in 2002 to help VWOs train their staff, expand their reach and serve people better.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Jurisdictions like Hong Kong, the US and Australia provide only 100% tax deductions for corporate and individual donations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Matching grant schemes like the new Bicentennial Community Fund which I announced will also catalyse more funding to our Institutions of Public Character (IPCs).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Together with the 250% tax deduction, effectively, every dollar donated can draw a Government contribution of up to $3.50.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth will elaborate on our efforts to support philanthropy and volunteerism at the COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will keep Singapore safe and secure together.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is another important part of our partnership.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I am heartened that Members of Parliament, like Mr Henry Kwek, Mr Darryl David, Mr Dennis Tan, Mr Mohamed Irshad and Mr Vikram Nair appreciate the geopolitical situation that Singapore is in, and support our commitment to make sustained investments in our security and defence capabilities.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have good men and women in our security forces and diplomatic corps.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But they cannot be everywhere, or protect every flank.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Every Singaporean has a part to play through national movements like SGSecure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must stay alert, stay united and stay strong against threats, be it terrorism or cyber warfare.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Everyone must play a part in Total Defence.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And we will find the best way forward together.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But no one – not you, not me, not the Government – has all the answers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, we consult, engage and partner relevant stakeholders when formulating policy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I am glad Assoc Prof Walter Theseira and Mr Ang Wei Neng have spoken on the importance of feedback for more inclusive policymaking for the better of our society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There is always room for improvement, and Mr Ang Wei Neng has given robust feedback, which our agencies will take seriously.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But we must not stop at just making criticism, but reach out to one another, recognise that we may have different views, but we can work together and find the middle ground, find the right way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will tackle our challenges and construct better solutions, together.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And as Mr Christopher de Souza has just reminded us, our political dialogues must not degenerate into political brinkmanship, as we are seeing in many developed countries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have spoken about the Singapore way – our way – with people at the heart of our policies, planning for the long term while adapting to near-term circumstances, and doing it together, working in partnership.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our Budget reflects these principles, not just in the way we spend, as I had explained, but also in the way we fund our spending.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Many Members of Parliament in this House have called for more "M&Ms", not the sweet chocolate candy, but "more and more".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I, too, like M&Ms, but our resources are finite, but our needs are growing and diverse.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To square the circle, we need to use the right tools for the right needs, with these principles in mind.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And we need all of these tools, to balance our Budget in the medium term.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As individuals, we can all accept that we should pay for what we use.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Similarly, each generation should pay for their own needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We had debated this at last year’s Budget, and I am glad that many Members agreed with this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Nevertheless, there have been some reservations raised over the approach and timing of our plans to raise taxes going forward.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Foo Mee Har urged the Government to postpone the Goods and Services Tax (GST) hike for as long as possible.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: She suggested that the funds that we have set aside this term for various future expenditures like the MGP and the use of borrowing for future infrastructure expenditures could provide sufficient fiscal space to postpone the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I appreciate Ms Foo’s suggestion to delay this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As the Government, it is our responsibility to anticipate and plan ahead for future needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: While doing so, we also need to distinguish between one-off factors and underlying structural increases.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Such healthcare spending is of a completely different scale and nature from the cohort-based package set aside for MG or PG.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As mentioned earlier, the Government has systematically laid the foundation of a broad-based healthcare system that supports not only seniors, but all Singaporeans, regardless of their age and income.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They support not only seniors but all Singaporeans, regardless of their age and income.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We now provide significant subsidies in all care settings of up to 80% in our public hospitals and for long-term care services, up to 70% for specialist outpatient services, and up to 75% for polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This does not even include spending to enhance our healthcare facilities and to research more effective treatments.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As our population ages, spending on permanent healthcare schemes and other parts of the healthcare system will continue to increase structurally.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Funding this requires a structural increase in our operating revenues.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In other words, the base of our healthcare spending is rising.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Over and above this rising base, we have special packages set aside for our PG and MG.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Every ageing society faces similar structural spending pressures.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A recent OECD paper highlighted that in the median OECD country, public health expenditure is projected to increase by almost five percentage points of GDP between 2018 and 2060.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The OECD’s recommended approach is no different from ours.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To address the growing fiscal burden from higher healthcare spending and demographic change without further ballooning of public debt, there is a need for these governments to raise primary revenues.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What does 6.5 percentage points of GDP mean?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, you compare 6.5 percentage points to the 0.7 percentage point of GDP that we have, and you see the scale of the issues in many places.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have yet to decide on the exact timing of the GST increase and we will exercise care when doing so.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will continue to monitor the prevailing economic conditions, trends in expenditure and the buoyancy of our revenues carefully.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And as I said in the Budget speech, we have also been preparing a transitional package when this comes in.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Next, related to the issue that Ms Foo Mee Har and other Members raised, I should also put into perspective the surpluses accumulated so far in this term of Government.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some revenue items are volatile, especially those dependent on sentiment-driven markets, such as Stamp Duty or Vehicle Quota Premiums.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For instance, in FY2018, we had estimated that Stamp Duty collections would be lower because of property market cooling measures.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There can also be surprises on the expenditure side.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The two-year suspension of the Kuala Lumpur-Singapore High Speed Rail Project is a case in point.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The unexpected surpluses over the last few years are not due to the introduction of Temasek into the Net Investment Returns (NIR) framework, as suggested by Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The volatilities and uncertainties in revenues and expenditures, as I had just explained, account for most of this surplus.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: While the Government’s approach is to look ahead, plan ahead, and prepare for the unexpected, it seems that Mr Singh would prefer to look backwards to find unexpected revenue surprises, and count on them to keep happening.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am afraid such an approach of hoping for the best is not how we will secure Singapore's future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: While there is room for improvement, the accuracy of our revenue and expenditure projections has been reasonable and respectable by international standards.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Ministry of Finance (MOF) is constantly looking for ways to improve our forecasts.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But the experience of other countries also shows that this is not easy to do.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Nonetheless, we will see how we can continue to improve.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa also asked how the Government intends to use the accumulated surplus.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, let me clarify that any surpluses we have do not simply “disappear” at the end of the term.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They become part of our Reserves which are invested to generate returns, part of which will form the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Murali Pillai explained, when our economy grows, we have an obligation to contribute to the Reserves to be used for the uncertainties of the future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We should also bear in mind that the business cycle can turn, and having some surpluses on hand can allow us to provide targeted support to segments that need help to tide over the downturn.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For a major crisis, we can turn to the past Reserves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, $15.6 billion, out of $20.5 billion, were from current Reserves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In 2017, to support the construction industry to tide over a period of cyclical weakness, the Government brought forward about $1.4 billion of public sector infrastructure projects to start in financial year (FY) 2017 and FY2018.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In planning for FY2019, we were also faced with the global economic outlook being downgraded by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), as global trade tensions grew.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: More fundamentally, we should not have the mentality of trying to spend everything that we have before the end of each term of Government.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As part of our long-term approach, we continue to review our plans for the long term and will deploy financial resources where necessary.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: On this note, let me briefly reiterate the role of our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, NIRC is already the largest single contributor of our revenues, larger than any category of the taxes we collect.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If we did not have the NIR framework, we would have had to double our personal income tax collection or our GST collection to raise the same amount of revenues.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, we would not even be able to raise the same amount of revenue because it is now the largest category and doubling all the rest does not give you that same amount.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are a small country, exposed to global forces beyond our control.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our Reserves will allow us to tide over a crisis, without being reliant on others.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We should not underestimate the need for a rainy-day fund.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Singapore faces particular vulnerabilities, given our lack of natural resources.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: With an economy worth nearly $500 billion a year, we should set aside enough to protect it and our people’s livelihoods and future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, we take up to 50% of the expected returns for spending, and plough back at least 50% to grow the principal and generate more returns.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In this way, both the current and future generations benefit from the Reserves, and we can be confident of our future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Pritam Singh referred to a Business Times article and asked for more data on our Reserves so that I quote, "Singaporeans can crunch the numbers themselves, and better understand Budget policy tradeoffs".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: He has also filed a cut on transparency on the Government of Singapore Investment Corporation's (GIC’s) performance, which will be answered at MOF's COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But let me explain why the Member is misinformed.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our Reserves comprise assets invested by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), GIC and Temasek.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The size of MAS and Temasek's assets is public information.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Only the GIC portion is not disclosed, and that is because with the GIC figure, you get the complete picture of our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I was running the Monetary Authority of Singapore during the Global Financial Crisis, with Emeritus Senior Minister Goh Chok Tong as our Chairman.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We not only rode through the crisis well but emerged stronger.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Having our Reserves as a strategic asset played a key role in this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, let us not squander this strategic advantage that we have.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our Reserves also serve as a strategic defence, to deter parties who wish to undermine the interests of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Such moves go beyond currency speculation attacks, to other types of threats.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Mohamed Irshad noted, we live in a volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous (VUCA) world.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our Reserves, like our investments in defence and security, give us the confidence to plan long term, knowing that we will have the ability to take care of our people and to defend our sovereignty.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Over the next decade, we are making significant investments in our infrastructure to enhance connectivity and create new growth opportunities for tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In my round-up speech last year, I mentioned a number of infrastructure projects which our Statutory Boards and Government-owned companies are looking to borrow to finance.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This included the Integrated Waste Management Facility by the National Environment Agency (NEA), and the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System Link by the Land Transport Authority (LTA).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In this year’s Budget speech, I mentioned our long-term infrastructure needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And as Ms Tin Pei Ling has noted, we also have to plan ahead for our ageing infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: All these are long-term needs that have to be studied carefully.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In this regard, there is a simple answer to Mr Pritam Singh’s question about how borrowing will impact revenues available for future recurrent spending.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked how borrowing would impact revenues available for future recurrent spending.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And we must have every intention to pay back what we borrow.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, it is irresponsible for a government to borrow to spend on recurrent needs, such as healthcare and security.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Such borrowing shifts the burden of paying for today’s needs onto future generations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This goes against the same principles of inter-generational equity that Mr Pritam Singh said he stands for.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin has rightfully cautioned against this and has called for further safeguards to prevent excessive borrowing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If we proceed to use Government debt, we will make sure it is done in a disciplined and prudent manner.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Safeguards will be put in place to ensure that the debt, its interest and repayment are sustainable and in line with the Reserves Protection Framework.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Borrowing or not, it does not change the fact that all Government projects should be cost-efficient, well-managed and must yield economic or social benefits.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What do we have to show in 10, 20 years’ time?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: An important question raised by Ms Tin Pei Ling.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If used sustainably, it allows us to build a better living environment for our people and to make Singapore a dynamic and liveable city.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is not just a question about growth, but also one of sustainability, as emphasised by Dr Teo Ho Pin.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked if building Singapore will come at the expense of our green spaces.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Member should not take the word "building" so literally, not just in bricks and mortars.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have always incorporated greenery in our urban plans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is not only part of our climate change resilience efforts; it is part of Singapore’s identity as a City in a Garden.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Ministry of National Development (MND) will share more details on their greening efforts at the COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As we calibrate our fiscal tools, the ultimate goal is three-fold, that is, to remain pro-growth; ensure that our overall system of taxes and transfers remain fair and equitable; and keep the tax burden on the middle-income low.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There have been calls for the Government to do more in redistribution through the tax system, to address income and wealth inequality.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat suggested if we could tier GST for different goods to lower the tax burden on the lower-income.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This has been raised multiple times in Budget Debates over the years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But let me briefly reiterate the key arguments why a multi-rate GST is a less efficient way to help the lower-income.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, it is difficult to define a "necessity".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There are the white, and wholemeal loaves that you can find at supermarkets, but there are also loaves sold at artisan bakeries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: On top of that, there are so many other types of bread – floss buns, baguettes, kaya toast at your coffee shop.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, better-off households tend to spend more in absolute terms and thus benefit more from these reduced GST rates.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our approach is to have a flat GST rate, while providing structural offsets through the GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is a permanent scheme to provide more help to lower-income households and seniors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is also more targeted, as those who need help most get it most directly.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is in addition to other schemes and programmes to help the less well-off.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing spoke about whether car ownership can be taken into account when means-testing, while Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked if the Annual Value (AV) criterion can be removed.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: No criterion is perfect, but if we put all our different schemes together, we have a system that is progressive and, as Mr Yee Chia Hsing said, fair.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If we use vehicle ownership, for example, should we distinguish among the make and model, and what the vehicle is used for?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For those who have specific needs, the best approach is to appeal to the relevant authorities which will consider each appeal based on its own merits.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Miss Cheryl Chan has argued for a number of other measures to address growing wealth inequality, such as the introduction of a net-wealth tax, or an inheritance tax.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I spoke briefly about this during the Budget Debates last year.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What works best depends on the country’s overall tax system and broader economic and social circumstances.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our approach has been to tax fixed assets which, as the name suggests, are fixed and less mobile.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, a large portion of total Singapore household wealth is held in the form of housing assets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have two types of taxes on property, that is, Stamp Duty and Property Tax.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have been making them more progressive over the years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Owner-occupied properties enjoy a concessionary property tax rate, with the rate being higher for higher-end homes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The property tax rates are also higher for non-owner-occupied residential properties, such as those left vacant or rented out.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will continue to monitor developments in this space.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: At this point, let me address the concerns arising from the increase in diesel tax.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Dennis Tan acknowledged that the increase in diesel tax makes our environment more resilient, but asked if this is worth the price of potentially higher business costs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must go beyond framing this as a simple tradeoff, to a broader understanding of the longer-term approach we are taking to address the increasingly urgent issue of vehicular emissions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Diesel exhaust contains substantial amounts of particulate matter and nitrogen oxides which are associated with an increased risk of lung cancer and respiratory infection.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The long-term impact of excessive diesel use on the health of our family and children is significant.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is thus necessary to use a price signal to nudge diesel users towards cleaner and more sustainable alternatives.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Diesel tax is only one part of a larger roadmap to discourage diesel consumption.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In 2018, we introduced the Vehicular Emissions Scheme (VES) to further incentivise the purchase of cleaner vehicles and discourage the purchase of pollutive vehicles.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is encouraging to note that there were no new diesel taxis registered in 2018.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh suggested exempting vehicles and machinery from diesel tax if there are currently no non-diesel alternatives.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But this works against what we are trying to do.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The increase in diesel tax will help nudge businesses which are heavy diesel users towards greater efficiency.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For example, companies can consider adopting consolidated logistics and use better routing applications to optimise their deliveries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In the interim, we have provided a transitionary offset package to cushion the cost impact till 2022, as businesses adapt to reduce their diesel consumption.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, spoke about the impact of diesel duty on taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We recognise the cost impact faced by taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng said, all taxi companies have pledged to step forward to pass the entire savings from the Special Tax reductions to their drivers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There are also incentives being offered to encourage taxi drivers to switch to petrol hybrid taxis, as we strive for lower emissions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This year, I had several good conversations with people about this Budget at various forums.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There did not seem to be anything in this Budget for me".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Even if there is nothing new for you this year, you and your family have certainly benefited from every one of our Budgets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As I said, we must not look at the Budget in isolation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, let me outline how this Budget benefits different groups.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our young people have benefited from stronger support in education, housing and parenthood.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They also benefit from the opportunities that a vibrant economy brings, as I explained earlier.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We provide up to $80,000 in grants for new Build-To-Order (BTO) flats, and $120,000 for resale flats, and invest even more later on when estates undergo upgrading.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Parents can receive a maximum of between $18,000 and $32,000 in marriage and parenthood benefits for each eligible child, on top of paid maternity and paternity leave, tax benefits and preschool subsidies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our middle-income families, especially those feeling "sandwiched" supporting retiree parents and school-going children, would benefit from many schemes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For example, their children receive significant education subsidies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some middle-income and upper-income families also commented that the tax rebate of $200 is insignificant and of not much benefit to them.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But we must not forget that overall, income taxes are kept low, so that they can keep a large part of what they earn.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is, as Mr Ong Teng Koon mentioned, one of the key things that help with keeping expenses manageable.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I should share a story of a recent encounter with a Singaporean who came back from a very developed country.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And he told me, "Mr Heng, I am very happy to be back in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, I am very happy to be back with my parents and family.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But I am also very happy that I got a 32% pay rise." I said, "Wow!

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Your new employer has been most generous." He said, "No.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: My employer who sent me back from the headquarters kept my salary at the same salary.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But when I added up all the taxes that I have paid in that country – at the city level, at the state level, at the federal level – it added up to 32% of my pay." So, I thought that was a very powerful story.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: You can look up the tax rates of many of the countries that have extremely generous welfare systems but, as some of you shared, the moment you take your paycheck, more than half has gone.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Miss Cheryl Chan put it, we must not see the Budget as simply a "bag of benefits that serves some people in one year or the other".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is our strategic financial plan for the future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And because we take a long-term approach, we cannot see each year's Budget in isolation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our Budget builds on the foundation of earlier Budgets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have a multi-year plan, which tackles the priorities as systemically as we can.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We plan ahead by setting out the strategy for mitigating and adapting the impacts of climate change.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We look at the needs of different groups of people, as needs evolve and grow.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We invest in growing our economy and in our people so that we have the resources to do more for our people and their children, and their children later.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I am glad that many Members have asked the question, "What is in it for us, for Singapore?", rather than "What is in it for me?" Budget 2019 and our previous Budgets are to build a better Singapore for all of us.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: All of us benefit from a Singapore which is strong and united.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: With a strong defence, to protect our way of life; a clean and green environment, a liveable city and endearing home; a vibrant economy, where opportunities abound; and a strong community, where no one is left behind.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: My colleagues will share more on what the Government will be doing along these lines during the COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Prof Yaacob Ibrahim, Mr Darryl David and Miss Cheng Li Hui have mentioned, our Bicentennial is an opportune time for us to reflect on how we have come so far, on what we have built together, and what more we can do, as individuals and in our organisations, to strengthen our society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I look forward to our VWOs, clan associations and religious groups continuing to step forward regardless of race, language or religion to uplift the disadvantaged amongst us.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I look forward to more people – academics, professionals and, indeed, all citizens – providing constructive suggestions on how best to tackle critical issues confronting Singapore, as Mr Christopher de Souza mentioned, on strengthening our social compact.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Bicentennial is also a good time to reflect on what being an independent, sovereign state means.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It means fiercely protecting the precious freedom that we have to chart our own destiny, even as our relationships with our neighbours and the world change.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It means appreciating that we have our own unique way of solving our problems the Singapore way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And, indeed, not to be pressured to conform to theories which sound fashionable but do not work for us.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It means committing to give our best, building on what past generations have done.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Together, we can advance and make this little red dot shine even more brightly.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, let us work together to build a strong and united Singapore.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I have a clarification for the Minister for Finance.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I understand that the increase is largely due to the ageing population.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The biggest ageing generation is my generation, the MG.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I would expect that we will diminish in number over time.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: So, how much exactly is the projection and expenditure?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am glad that he is in the MG.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And as I said in my speech, I hope that our MG will redefine ageing and that the Member continues to stay healthy, active and connected and live longer.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, as to Mr Low Thia Khiang's question on how long this structural increase in our healthcare expenditure will last, in my speech, I mentioned that what we have been doing, for instance, is studying the OECD's experience.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I mentioned about the experience of a number of countries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Last year, I was in Japan to look at what they were doing to deal with the problem of an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And I must say that there are many variables that go into the long-term care costs and the long-term support that is needed.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, the one Minister that I spent a lot of time with is Minister Gan Kim Yong because, each time I see him, he comes up with a higher set of figures.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, if you ask me how long this will last, I would not want to mislead this House.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are continuing to study this very carefully.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As I said, there are many variables which are not certain.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For instance, how will our lifespan change and what is the extent to which our seniors will continue to be healthy?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And how would new drugs, new treatment methods change the cost structure and change the life expectancy?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And I think even if you ask all our doctors here, they would not be able to give you a definitive answer because there is a wide range of uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, we must plan on the long-term basis.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And we are not just having an ageing population, we are also having ageing infrastructure, as Ms Tin Pei Ling reminded us.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As I said in my Budget speech, we are also looking at all of these long-term needs very carefully and we will share this when ready.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I want to revisit this idea of, not a cohort-based health benefits scheme for our seniors but something more permanent.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My point really comes back to some of the other issues that were raised by Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat and some of the other Members.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The argument really is, the Government will not know how much its surplus would be through the course of the term before it decides how much it can give out for these packages.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Be that as it may, I would like to make a quick reference to the Singapore Perspectives background paper which was released in 2018.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This was an Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) survey that was carried out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If I may, Mr Speaker, can I just pass it to the Minister of Finance?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second question is: should NIR used to fund social expenditure for the current generation be increased and the amount reserved for future generations likewise decreased?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The survey notes that while there were more neutral responses with the question on using a larger share of the returns from investing national Reserves to finance higher social spending, more respondents agreed to the statement than disagreed with it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: To a large extent, it is not surprising, People would react emotionally to issues of taxation, how it is funded and so forth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I think what was interesting was the final analysis from the IPS researchers which was, for both questions, respondents aged 45 to 64 – and I am assuming Ah Seng and Ah Kong are part of this – respondents aged 45 to 64 were more likely to disagree to pay higher taxes rather than tapping on national Reserves and to agree to using a larger share of the NIR to finance current social spending for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This is the interesting part: this age group experiences the highest tax burden and may be feeling the greatest uncertainty about financing their own post-retirement living expenses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, with that as a gauge, I have to put the issue again about NIRC for which NII is a component.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If you look at the Merdeka package about $6.1 billion, $8 billion with interest, and other components coming in, it is still a small percentage of the overall NIRC revenue that the Government is constitutionally allocated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In that context, is it possible to still consider moving away from cohort-based packages to something more permanent and universal, but with, of course, the additional MediSave top-ups and other issues which I raised in my speech as optional items, so to speak.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That is my first clarification and I apologise if I went too long.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Similarly for this year, we support the Budget, but our position on the GST has not changed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I just want to put that down for the record.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But if Members have heard me carefully during the round-up, MOH already have many, many permanent schemes, many permanent subsidies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We spent a lot of time thinking about how best we can do this in a sustainable way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, the Member was citing the IPS survey and so on.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The NIRC comes in as a big pot, and that helps us to fund a number of other things.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The packages that we have, specifically target that group and the funds come from what we have today in current Reserves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As I said earlier, the Reserves are a strategic asset for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: You do not know how the global situation will develop and it is important for us to have that strategic asset for the long term.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is why my whole Budget round-up speech is about planning for the long term, while you address and adapt for changes for short-term developments.
